fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Branches of the external carotid artery can be remembered with the mnemonic (Some Anatomists Like Freakout Out Poor Medical Students)

S - {{c1::Superior thyroid artery}}
A - {{c2::Ascending pharyngeal artery}}
L - {{c3::Lingual artery}}
F - {{c4::Facial artery}}
O - {{c5::Occipital artery}}
P - {{c6::Posterior auricular artery}}
M - {{c7::Maxillary artery}}
S - {{c8::Superficial temporal artery}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
- Maxillary artery gives off various branches including; MMA, which supplies the dura mater / periosteum; Sphenopalatine artery (which anastomosis with branches of ophthalmic and facial artery to form kiesselbachs plexus and also contributes to woodruffs plexus - cause of posterior nosebleeds)

- the meningeal branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery passes through the foramen lacerum, along with emissary veins

- Facial artery courses over mandible anterior to the insertion of the masseter muscle to supply the oral, nasal, and bucccal regions; anterior nosebleeds (in Kiesselbachs plexus) are commonly due to injuries to superior labial artery

- the Occipital artery arises opposite the facial artery and courses posteriorly to supply the SCM and posterior scalp

- The superficial temporal artery can characteristically get inflamed in temporal arteritis (giant cell arteritis)

Comment: Arteries of the oral and pharyngeal regions arise principally from branches of the external carotid artery. The external carotid gives rise to 8 branches:the superior thyroid artery, lingual artery, facial artery, ascending pharyngeal artery, occipital artery, posterior auricular artery, maxillary artery, and superficial temporal artery. 

The maxillary artery contributes many branches to the infratemporal region, nasal cavities, and muscles of mastication. Descriptively, the maxillary artery is divided into 3 parts (some of its branches are shown in this figure). 

The 1st (retromandibular) portion of this artery gives rise to branches supplying the tympanic cavity and membrane, dura, mandibular teeth and gums, ear, and chin. The 2nd (pterygoid) portion supplies the muscles of mastication and the buccinator. The 3rd (pterygopalatine) part supplies the maxillary teeth and gums, portions of the face, orbit, palate, auditory tube, superior pharynx, paranasal sinuses, and nasal cavity. 

Anastomoses among the branches of the facial and maxillary artery are common.

fields.name: Front
fields.value: c-ANCA is associated with which vasculitis?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener)

In general, ANCA is positive in 90% of patients. C-ANCA in 80% of patients and p-ANCA in 20% of patients.

GPA
Epidemiology
Affects males and females equally, peak incidence is 40-60 years, prevalence is 3 in 100,000

Pathophys
Aberrant epigenetic expression of proteinase-3 on cell membrane of neutrophils and subsequent antibody formation against the proteinase. When antibodies bind to the proteinase it activates neutrophils which causes the release of inflammatory mediators, complement activation and damage to the endothelial cells of small blood vessels

Clinical Features
Const: fevers, night sweats, weight loss
ENT: (typically first clinical manifestation)
  • chronic rhinitis/sinusitis ->septal perf -> saddle nose
  • Subglottic stenosis
  • chronic otitis
  • oral ulcers
  • strawberry gingivitis (painful, erythematous petechiae that resemble surface of strawberry
Lower respiratory: Pneumonia, cough, dyspnea, hemotpytis
Renal: 
  • Pauci-immune glomerulonephritis (little evidence of immune complex/antibody deposits on biopsy) -> crescentic glomerulonephritis
  • Hematuria, RBC casts in urine
Skin lesions
Eys: conjunctivitis, episcleritis, corneal ulcerations
Heart: 
  • Pericarditis
  • Vasculitis of coronary arteries that can lead to MI

Dx
Labs
Elevated ESR or CRP
normocytic anemia
Elevated creatinine and BBUN
ANCA (c-anca) is positive in 90% of patients (PR3-ANCA in 75% and MPO-ANCA (p-anca) in 20%)

Imaging
CXR may show nodular lesions
Consider kidney ultrasound
CT sinus
EKG if cardiac symptoms

Biopsy
  • Must be obtained from affected tissue
  • Intra and extra vascular granulomas, vasculitis of small and medium sized vessels.


Differential is microscopic polyangiitis which is not granulomatous and more often is caused by p-ANCA.

Tx
  • Rheum needs to be involved as well as other organ systems as affected.
  • Goal to achieve remission in 3 months
  • Plasmapharesis with patients with Goodpastures to protect the kidneys (antibodies against type IV collagen
  • Induce remission with steroids and methotrexate if non-severe or steroids and rituximab if severe (cyclophosphamide has more side effects)
  • Once remission, slowly taper glucocorticoids to minimum effective dose. Keep on steroids and methotrexate for at least 18 months.
ENT disease should be treated with topical nasal abx, lubricants or steroids. Refer to plastics if cosmetic concerns.

Prognosis
Without treatment 80% of patients die within 1 year. 5 year survival with good treatment is 80%. Most common cause of death is diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.

fields.value: Surgery near the parotid glands

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Which condition involves gustatory sweating often after surgery near the parotid glands?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Frey syndrome

Frey's syndrome is a rare complication of surgery or an injury of the salivary (parotid) gland in the cheek.
Symptoms include sweating and flushing on the cheek or temple, or near the ear, particularly when eating foods with more-intense flavors, such as sour, spicy, or salty foods.
Various treatments have been tried, but their effectiveness is limited.

mets are often detected before the primary tumor

80% of thyroid cancers.

fields.value: Is Ludwig angina often polymicrobial?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Yes!


Polymicrobial infection occurs in over 50% of cases. The most commonly cultured organisms include Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Bacteroides species. The infection is typically caused by seeding from a tooth. Management is with IV antibiotics. Surgery is not usually necessary since the disease is cellulitic rather than suppurative.

fields.value: PPI can be used in the treatment of which cause of hoarseness?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR)

LPR is sometimes called silent GERD because, although the mechanism is basically the same as GERD (acid from stomach moving superiorly), patients may not have the typical symptoms of GERD. The presenting symptoms of LPR are different than that of GERD.

LPR symptoms are chronic hoarseness (wrose in the morning), chronic cough, throat irritation, frequent throat clearing, a mucus sensation in the throat and globus sensation.

GERD symptoms are heartburn, acid brash, regurgitation.

May present as white spot (Herald patch)

If you do need to treat due to the lesion being in a sensitive area (periorbital region, airways, gi tract), use propranolol. If that doesn't work then use cryotherapy, laser therapy, or resect.

You would probably treat this kid since it is around his eye.

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Which subtype of tracheomalacia is due to weak or absent tracheal cartilage?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Intrinsic tracheomalacia

Presents with expiratory or biphasic stridor
associated with tracheoesophageal fistula as well as preemies on prolonged intubation

See Pasha for management

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Which subtype of tracheomalacia is due to a structure compressing the trachea?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Extrinsic tracheomalacia
Presents with biphasic stridor

Generally vascular compression from double aortic arch, right aortic arch, anomalous innominate artery, anomalous left common carotid, left aortic aarch with right escending throacic aorta, pumonary artery sling, retroesophageeal right subclavian artery (dysphagia lusoria)

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Administration of {{c1::Amoxicillin::drug?}} can cause a(n) "{{c2::salmon}}"-colored rash in patients with {{c3::Mononucleosis::disease?}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Historically, older studies reported rates as high as 80–100%, which is why many of us learned that amoxicillin + mono = rash.
More recent studies suggest the true incidence is much lower, roughly 30–70%, with some reports even lower depending on how mono was confirmed and how the rash was defined.

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Peritonsillar abscess occur between which structures?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Tonsilar capsule
Superior pharyngeal constrictor

You can think of the superior pharyngeal constrictor, palatoglossus, and palatopharyngeus as making a groove in the lateral portion of the oropharynx.

fields.name: Front
fields.value: What are the most common causes of Velopharyngeal insufficiency (2)?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Cleft palate
Submucous cleft

In a submucous cleft, the palate has not formed but tissue is over the top of the bony defect on oropharyngeal exam. In cleft palate, you can see the defect.
A bifid uvula may be present in submucous cleft

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Which common pediatric surgery can cause Velopharyngeal insufficiency?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Adenoidectomy

1 in 1500 procedures. 50% of these patients have underlying 22q11.2 deletion
In order to avoid this, leave a portion of Passavant's ridge (fibers of the palatopharyngeus and superior constrictor that form a U shaped muscle loop in posterior pharyngeal wall under the mucosa.)

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A(n) “{{c1::beard}}”distribution of hemangioma may indicate a subglottic hemangioma

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: aka segmental infantile hemangioma, associated with PHACES

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Surgical removal of which congenital neck mass requires preoperative thyroid ultrasound?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Thyroglossal duct cyst

This is because the thyroid tissue within the cyst may be the patient's only functioning thyroid tissue. This would be problematic if removed.

Thyroglossal duct cyst
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JNCJ5NPAhDA&t=8s

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Which congenital midline mass contains all three germ layers?

fields.name: Back
fields.value: Teratoma

fields.name: Front
fields.value: What is the most common midline nasal mass?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Nasal dermoid cyst

Most commonly at nasal dorsum but can occur anywhere from glabella to nasal tip

Hair on cyst is pathognomonic

Consider that it could also be herniation of brain tissue or heterotic brain tissue (glioma). If you do suspect the latter, get a CT head to look for bony defect.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Positive staining for {{c2::GLUT1}} is suggestive of {{c1::infantile hemangiomas::which common vascular tumor?}}

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Infantile hemangiomas typically present at which age?

fields.name: Back
fields.value: 2 to 4 weeks

fields.name: Front
fields.value: What are the absolute indications for treatment of Infantile hemangiomas?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Ocular obstruction
Airway compromise


Other indications include large ulcerated lesions with hemorrhage or infection, those prone to functional compromise (ear/nose) or long-term cosmetic deformity, and those that are a source of psychosocial trauma to the child

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Port-wine stain in the V<sub>1</sub> distribution is associated with which syndrome?

fields.name: Back
fields.value: Sturge-Weber syndrome

fields.name: Front
fields.value: What is the strength layer of the scalp?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Galea aponeurosis

  • S: Skin
  • C: Connective tissue
  • A: Aponeurosis (Galea Aponeurotica)
  • L: Loose areolar tissue
  • P: Pericranium

fields.name: Front
fields.value: Which muscle is the sole elevator of the brow?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Frontalis

The forntalis is the forntal part of the epicranius. All of the other muscles of the brow cause depression of the brow. These include the procerus, pared corrugator supercilii, and the parired orbicularis oculi.

fields.name: Front
fields.value: What is the surgical treatment for internal nasal valve incompetence?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Cartilage spreader graft

The Latera nasal implant can also be used to correct nasal valve incompetence but I am not sure if it is internal, external, or both.

fields.name: Front
fields.value: What is the surgical treatment for external nasal valve incompetence?

fields.name: Back
fields.value:
Alar batten graft

Latera implant is now also used for this

Skin graft take occurs in three phases:
{{c1:: imbibition (PO 24-48 hours), inosculation (POD1-2), and revascularization ( POD4-7) }}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
First you drink (imbibe), then you inosculate (kiss), then you make a baby (neovascularization).

Plasmatic imbibition refers to the first 24 to 48 hours after skin grafting, during which time a thin film of fibrin and plasma separates the graft from the underlying wound bed. It remains controversial whether this film provides nutrients and oxygen to the graft or merely a moist environment to maintain the ischemic cells temporarily until a vascular supply is re-established. After 48 hours a fine vascular network begins to form within the fibrin layer. These new capillary buds interface with the deep surface of the dermis and allow for transfer of some nutrients and oxygen. This phase, called inosculation, transitions into revascularization, the process by which new blood vessels either directly invade the graft or anastomose to open dermal vascular channels and restore the pink hue of skin. These phases are generally complete by 4 to 5 days after graft placement. During these initial few days the graft is most susceptible to deleterious factors such as infection, mechanical shear forces, and hematoma or seroma. (See Schwartz 9th ed., Chapter 45, Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.)

This is a good segway into the four phases of wound healing hemostasis, inflammation, and maturation

Indications for lymphoscintography (sentinel lymph node biopsy) in head and neck cancer
{{c1::malignant melanoma, oral squamous cell carcinoma, merkel cell carcinoma::3}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
There is a lot of nuance, read the Iowa Protocols website as well as the controversy regarding the value of SLN biopsy (exerpt and link below)
  • Malignant melanoma
    • Breslow depth of invasion greater than 1 mm - may consider in thinner (>0.75 mm) melanoma in high risk sites
    • Thin melanoma <1mm if mitotic rate 1 or more or if ulceration present
    • Melanoma with status other than Tis (melanom in situ) or T1a 
    • Currently felt that for pure desmoplastic melanoma of the head and neck,  the high incidence of negative sentinel lymph node biopsies as well as the  low incidence of neck recurrence, argues against use of sentinel lymph node biopsy for this rare subset of melanoma (Eppsteiner et al 2012, Mohebati et al 2012)
  • Oral squamous cell carcinoma
    • T1N0 or T2N0  (ACOSOG protocol)
  • Merkel cell carcinoma
    • Stage I (localized tumor)
  • Consider use with sebaceous carcinoma
Further Reading
https://medicine.uiowa.edu/iowaprotocols/sentinel-lymph-node-biopsy

fields.value: The most common type of malignant sinonasal tumor is {{c1::squamous cell carcinoma}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
It is more common in males, typically seen in the 6th or 7th decade, and usually seen in the maxillary sinuses.

The second most common is adenocarcinoma, followed by adenoid cystic carcinoma, sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma, and many others.

Imaging of SCC typically shows aggresive bony destruction.

Tx is with surgery and sometimes chemoradiation

It used to be believed that there was a correlation between tobacco use and SCC. However, now that global smoking rates have decreased and sexual habits have changed, HPV is being found more commonly in patients with sinonasal SCC. HPV SCC is more commonly found in the nasal cavity than the maxillary sinus.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Chronic rhinosinusitis was often classified by phenotype such as chronic sinusitis with polyposis (CRSwP) or chronic sinusitis without polyposis (CRSsP), etc. More recently, efforts have been made to classify the disease based on underlying molecular mechanisms, termed endotyping. 

There are three predominant endotypes. Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3. Type 2 is the most common endotype in the west and is characterized by elevated IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13. It has an eosinophilic character. and generally leads to a CRSwNP phenotype. Cells implicated include TH2 cells and mast cells.

Non-type 2 CRS is highly heterogenous.

Up to 15% of patients with CRSwNP have omorbid asthma and an intolerance to inhibitors of COX, commonly referred to aspirin exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD). 

Treatment of chronic rhinosinusitis starts with medical managment which is often courses of antibiotics and a steroid tapaer. If symptoms are refractory to medication, endoscopic sinus surgery can be considered. Many patients with CRS have recurrence of symptoms after surgery in which case revision surgery or use of biologic medications such as dupilumab are considered.

  • Endotypes of chronic rhinosinusitis: Relationships to disease phenotypes, pathogenesis, clinical findings, and treatment approaches - 10.1111/all.15074

You diagnose laryngomalacia in an otherwise healthy infant. What is the next step in management?
{{c1::Reassure and observe}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Laryngomalacia is a benign condition that is is the result of weak cartilage of the aryepiglotic folds that results in an omega shaped epiglottis. It typically self-limited and will resolve spontaneously by age 2. 

Consider surgery if the patient has severe hypoxemia, apnea, or failure to thrive

🦀 🦀 🦀 CrabsMcChaffey Light Year ENT Deck 🦀 🦀 🦀 
Deck Index

What is the origin story of CrabsMcChaffey?
{{c1::IYKYK}}

I originally overhauled the ENT light year deck in 2022 and have since updated it throughout my sub-I’s. It uses ENT Secrets by Scholes & Ramakrishnan and  Otolaryngology, Head & Neck Surgery: Clinical Reference Guide by Pasha as its primary resources. It also has cards associated with AAO Primary Care Otolaryngology.
 

🦀 🦀  Changes from Light Year ENT 🦀 🦀 
  1. More images in existing cards
  2. More cards from ENT Secrets
  3. Cards for prepping cases
  4. More resources
  5. Consolidated redundant information into single notes
  6. Elaboration of concepts in the EXTRA field
  7. Links to useful references
  8. Mnemonics
  9. Memes
  10. Improved tagging
  11. Made it Pretty💃🕺
  12. Basically every tag below that starts with “Crabs” is new

🦀 🦀 How to Use 🦀 🦀 
  • Search “tag:Crabs::Index Deck” to see all of this information within Anki
  • The cards are not detailed enough that you can get away with doing them without reading the associated text. You will also may find it beneficial to supplement the material with Google and Amboss. Remember, Anki is a retention tool, not a learning tool. Buy and use the primary resources.
  • First time through (ie for your elective clerkship): 
    • Not interested in a career in ENT. Read AAO Primary Care Otolaryngology and do the corresponding cards.
    • Interested in a career in ENT. Read AAO Primary Care Otolaryngology and do the corresponding cards. Read the chapter in ENT Secrets, then do the corresponding Anki cards by searching the tags as noted below. 
  • Second time through (ie before/during sub-i/aways): read the corresponding sections of Pasha and the additional resources associated with each note (this will make more sense as you do the cards). 
    • Additional resources include but are not limited to Iowa Protocols, Mayo Clinic Otolaryngology Surgical Atlas videos, and PubMed journal articles.
    • Before specific cases: unlock by the procedure tag, read the suggested text, and watch the Mayo Atlas videos on the procedure index card (see Procedures below). Then do the anki cards.
  • Residents: Read the corresponding sections of Pasha and then do the cards. Supplement with the Crabs::Procedures cards

🦀 🦀 Tags 🦀 🦀 
I am making the assumption that you are familiar with the syntax that can be used to search for tags within Anki. If you are not, consult the Anki manual and/or the plethora of videos regarding searching for tags on the Anking YouTube channel.

🦀 Redundancy 🦀 
  • If you use Anking, some of the cards will be duplicate information. In addition, some of the cards from the original Lightyear ENT deck are low yield. These cards are tagged tag:Crabs::duplicates_didnt_study

🦀 Extra anatomy 🦀 
  • The original Lightyear ENT deck had some anatomy cards but if you want to study more cards then unlock the cards tagged with Crabs::extra_anatomy. It may be helpful to narrow the search with another tag. ex. tag:Crabs::Specialty::HeadandNeck tag:Crabs::extra_anatomy

🦀 Pimp Questions 🦀 
  • Questions I was actually pimped on throughout my rotations. tag:Crabs::Pimped

🦀 By depth of Knowledge 🦀 
Some of the concepts are more advanced/detailed and above what would be expected of you during a third year clerkship. Thus you can filter based on your level of experience.
  • For third year rotations use Crabs::Elective
  • For sub-i’s/aways study the Crabs::Sub-I in addition to the Elective cards
    • Before starting the relevant rotation on your sub-I: read ENT Secrets then create a filtered deck with the specialty, secrets tag, and extra anatomy. ex. (tag:Crabs::Specialty::Laryngology* tag:Secrets_ENT*) OR (tag:Crabs::Specialty::Laryngology* tag:Crabs::extra_anatomy*).
  • For residents use Crabs::Residency

🦀 By resource/subspecialty 🦀 
All of the sections use the relevant chapters of ENT Secrets 2nd edition,  AAO Primary Care Otolaryngology , and Pasha are included with additional information added in the extra section from The Handbook of Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery 2nd edition by Goldenberg and Goldstein. You can search for the relevant text sections by using the Secrets_ENT, Crabs::AAOHNS_PrimaryCareOtolaryngology, or Crabs::Pasha tags. They are labeled with the same name as the book chapters. You can also search for tags based on subspecialty by using Crabs::”name of subspecialty”. The section headings below are the names of the subspecialty and listed in the order they appear in ENT Secrets.  Additional resources are briefly summarized in the relevant extra section of each note and the URL is provided for a deeper dive. 🦀 By Procedure 🦀 
Use Crabs::Procedures* to find cards for specific ENT operations. These cards include background information, pertinent anatomy, indications, complications, alternative management, and procedure steps. There are also links to relevant videos in the Mayo Surgical Video Atlas. Use these cards after reading the relevant chapters in a textbook such as Operative Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery by Myers or Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery by Flint. You can access them online through your school’s library at www.clinicalkey.com. Remember, Anki is a retention tool, not a learning tool. I included the relevant extra_anatomy tags to the relevant procedures. By tagging this way, I tried to ensure that you would see all of the relevant anatomy, regardless of which procedure tag you started with. This means there is overlap for the anatomy between procedures (ex laryngeal anatomy is covered in total laryngectomy and partial laryngectomy). If this ends up being too many cards or you are already comfortable with the anatomy then add -tag:Crabs::extra_anatomy* to your search. ex. tag:Crabs::Procedures::EndoscopicSinusSurgery* -tag:Crabs::extra_anatomy*.  If you previously unsuspended the anatomy cards, you may not see them again when you are studying for a case. To remedy this, I recommend creating a filtered deck using the procedure tag, Crabs::extra_anatomy, and Crabs::duplicates_didnt_study in order to make sure you see all of the relevant cards again before you go into the OR. This will keep the anatomy at the top of your mind. To just see the summary section with the recommend readings, videos, and bullet points (to cram on your phone right before a case). Search for the procedure tag with tag:Crabs::Index. You can also find PDF’s of all of the procedures at this link. You can import them into your favorite notes app.

fields.value:
The MCID for the SNOT-22 score in CRS
Medically managed = {{c1::12 }}
Surgically managed = {{c2::9}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Even if a patient does not have MCID based on score, if they have improvement in the nasal subdomain, they are more likely to report overall improvement in CRS symptoms.

Patients with a SNOT-22 score between 10-19 are unlikely to have an MCID after ESS. Patients with a score >30 have a >75% chance of acheiving an MCID.

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Adenoidectomy

Operative Video(s): Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy using Electrocautery Technique

Indications
  • Pediatric patients with otitis media with effusion (more than 90 days), chronic sinusitis, or OSA

Contraindications
  • Cleft palate
  • Submucous cleft palate or velopharyngeal insufficiency

Complications
  • Trauma or burns, airway complications, pulmonary edema, bleeding, injury to the Eustachian tube, regrowth of the adenoid, nasopharyngeal stenosis, Grisel syndrome, velopharyngeal insufficiency

Relevant Anatomy
  • The adenoid is located on the roof of the nasopharynx
  • The anterior boundary of the nasopharynx is the choanae
  • Care must be taken to avoid damage to the Eustachian tube while performing an adenoidectomy. The slit-like recess formed by the Eustachian tube is called the pharyngeal recess or the fossa of Rosenmuller. The torus tuberous is the nasopharyngeal end of the Eustachian tube.
  • Blood supply is from the ascending palatine branch of the facial artery, ascending pharyngeal artery, pharyngeal branch of the internal maxillary artery, and ascending cervical branch of the thyrocervical trunk

Steps
  1. Palpate palate to rule out the sub mucous cleft
  2. Pass catheter through each nostril and retrieve from the oral cavity
  3. Identify the torus tubarius bilaterally
  4. Use curette to remove adenoid tissue (can also use coblation or electrocautery)
  5. Consider leaving a strip of tissue in Passavant’s ridge to prevent velopharyngeal insufficiency
  6. Irrigate with saline through the nose
  7. Visualize the choanae

Post-Op
  1. Pain (acetaminophen and ibuprofen)
  2. Hydration

Suggested Reading: Cummings Otolaryngology, Primary Sinus Surgery
Operative Video: Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery for Chronic Rhinosinusitis -https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rab4PQueSqg
  • Major complications of endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) include cerebrospinal fluid leak, blindness, diplopia, internal carotid artery injury, and death.
  • Common causes of failure of ESS include lateralized middle turbinate, failure to incorporate maxillary ostium in the middle meatal antrostomy, maxillary ostium stenosis, frontal recess scarring (which can be the result of only partially resecting the agger nasi), residual ethmoidal air cells, and adhesions.

Relevant Anatomy
  • During ESS, the uncinate process is removed in order to gain access to the maxillary sinus
  • The oblique part of the basal lamella is the only part of the middle turbinate that can be sacrificed without compromising the integrity of the turbinate
  • The oblique part of the MT basal lamella separates the anterior and posterior ethmoidal cells.
  • The ethmoid bulla is the largest and most prominent cell of the ethmoid complex
  • The ager nasi is the most anterior of all ethmoidal cells
  • An infraorbital ethmoidal cell (IOC) aka Haller cell, is an anterior ethmoidal cell that pneumatizes into the orbital floor and may compromise the latency of the maxillary sinus.
  • The most common failure of maxillary antrostomy is not incorporating the tru maxillary sinus osmium into the surgical antrostomy
  • The sphenoid ostia is typically two thirds up the anterior wall of the sinus and always lower than the level of the maxillary roof and medial to the superior turbinate
  • The frontal sinus ostia is the narrowest portion of the frontal sinus.
  • Supraorbital ethmoidal cells can complicate surgery on the frontal sinuses
  • On preoperative surgery, be sure to identify low-lying ethmoidal arteries. They normally are enclosed in the skull base but sometimes make their way into the ethmoidal space.

Complications
Epistaxis, hyposmia/anosmia, adhesions, headache, ecchymosis, dental or facial pain, nasolacrimal trauma, carotid injury, orbital hematoma, blindness, CSF leak, or meningitis

{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Horizontal Partial Laryngectomy

Operative Video(s): Laryngectomy: Partial Horizontal Supraglottic Open Laryngectomy

Relevant Anatomy
Partial Laryngectomy
  • Superior laryngeal nerves
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Hypoglossal nerve
  • Lingual artery
  • Epiglottis
  • Vocal cords
  • Base of tongue
  • Thyroid cartilage
  • The level of the true cords is half the height between the superior and inferior thyroid notch

Indications
Partial Laryngectomy
  • Highly selected glottic, supraglottic, and subglottic cancers. The indications are nuanced, read the text.

Alternatives
  • Chemoradiation. There is a rich history of primary surgery versus chem-radiation based on the VA Laryngeal Cancer Group Study in the 1990’s
  • Palliative care

Complications
Partial Laryngectomy
  • Aspiration pneumonia, Bleeding, damage to surrounding structures, infection, subcutaneous emphysema, dysphagia, delayed cannulation, airway obstruction

Steps
Partial Laryngectomy
  1. Visualize space with laryngoscopy
  2. Perform tracheostomy with apron flap 
  3. Transect strap muscles
  4. Open vallecula
  5. Incise the thyroid cartilage
  6. Incise the aryepiglottic fold
  7. Connect the end-laryngeal and thyroid cartilage incision
  8. Place nasogastric tube in pharynx
  9. Reconstruct the pharynx by suturing the cricoid perichondrium to the fibroadipose tissue of the tongue 12 to 15 mm deep to the mucosa. This prevents post-op dysphagia

Post-Op
Partial Laryngectomy
  1. Avoid emesis
  2. Attempt to deflate cuff of tracheostomy on PO#3
  3. Perform flexible laryngoscopy on POD#5
  4. Transition to uncuffed tube and then capping of tube as able
  5. Start swallow therapy once patient is using speaking valve or cap

{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Selective Neck Dissection; Operative Otolaryngology: Central Neck Dissection; Cummings Otolaryngology: Overview of Diagnostic Imaging of the Head and Neck

Operative Video(s): Select Neck Dissection Levels II-IV, Neck Dissection: Levels I-III

Other Resources: Radiologic Lymph node levels

Relevant Anatomy
  • Neck dissection removes lymphoareolar tissue between the superficial and deep layers of the deep cervical fascia
  • Level I: Superior: Mandible  Inferior: hyoid bone Anterior: Anterior belly of digastric Posterior:  posterior belly of digastric
  • Level II Superior: Skull base Inferior: hyoid bone  Anterior:  stylohyoid muscle Posterior: Posterior border of SCM
  • Level III Superior: Hyoid bone  Inferior: Cricoid cartilage Anterior: Sternohyoid muscle Posterior:  Posterior border of SCM
  • Level IV Superior: Cricoid cartilage Inferior: Clavicle Anterior: Sternohyoid muscle Posterior: posterior border of SCM
  • Level V Superior: Skull base Inferior: Clavicle Anterior: Posterior border of SCM Posterior:  Trapezius
  • Level VI Superior: Hyoid bone Inferior: sternal notch  Lateral: Carotid arteries 
  • Level 1 contains the facial artery and vein, marginal mandibular nerve, lingual nerve, and hypoglossal nerves
  • Thoracic duct
  • Sympathetic trunk
  • Level Va contains the accessory lymph node group. Level Vb contains the supraclavicular and transverse cervical lymph nodes
  • Level VI contains the prelaryngeal, pretracheal, and paratracheal lymph nodes
  • Erb’s point
  • Cervical plexus

Indications
  • Generally clinically N0 neck and risk of occur metastases greater than 15% to 20%
  • Clinically N1 neck with metastases in the first echelon level
  • Low volume clinical N2 Neck without fixation of surrounding soft tissue invasion

Contraindications
  • Distant metastases
  • Unresectable primary cancer

Complications
  • Shoulder dysfunction, chyle leak, infection, bleeding, edema, nerve damage, skin and ear numbness, dysphagia, Horner’s syndrome

Steps
Level Ib
  1. Protect the marginal mandibular nerve
  2. Dissect the submandibular gland from the inferior border of the mandible
  3. Ligate the facial artery and vein
  4. Identify the lingual and hypoglossal nerves as they cross the hyoglossus muscle
  5. Ligate the submandibular duct as anteriorly as possible

Levels II-IV
  1. Elevate fascia along anterior border of SCM and preserve the great auricular nerve
  2. Identify CN XI
  3. Start dissecting the level II packet
  4. Extend the dissection inferiorly along the deep posterior portion of the SCM to the posterior belly of the omohyoid.
  5. Dissect from posteriorly to anteriorly from the SCM to the carotid sheath. Leave the deep cervical fascia intact on the deep muscles of the neck to protect the phrenic nerve and brachial plexus.
  6. Dissect the jugular chain lymph nodes

Level V
  1. Identify the spinal accessory nerve, skeletonize it, then protect it for the rest of the dissection
  2. Dissect packet off of the splenius capitus, elevator scapulae, and scalene muscles.

Level IV
  1. Identify and preserve the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroid glands.
  2. Skeletonize the RLN and remove tissue deep to the nerve

Post-Op
  • Sound care
  • Drain monitoring
  • Shoulder PT starting POD 1 or 2

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology Superficial Parotidectomy and Deep Parotidectomy
Operative Video(s): Superficial Parotidectomy; Deep Parotidectomy

Relevant Anatomy
  • Tragal pointer
  • Mastoid tip
  • Posterior belly of digastric
  • Greater auricular nerve
  • Deep lobe of parotid

Complications
Hematoma, Frey Syndrome, injury to facial nerve, infection, sailocele formation, recurrent tumor, fistula. First bite syndrome in deep parotidectomy due to dissection into the parapharyngea space

Steps
  1. Modified Blair incision
  2. Separate SMAS
  3. Identify great auricular nerve
  4. Dissect to posterior belly of digastric
  5. Follow digastric back to the mastoid
  6. Dissect to identify the facial nerve
  7. Dissect the branches of the facial nerve

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Partial Glossectomy
Operative Video(s): Partial Glossectomy with Primary Transverse Closure

Relevant Anatomy
  • Lingual artery
  • Lingual nerve

Indications
  • Stage I and II tumors partial glossectomy, often perform a selective neck dissection with it

Contraindications
  • T3 and T4 tumors which often require hemiglossectomy or subtotal glossectomy
  • T4 tumors which may require transcervical delivery or mandibulotomy
  • Bone invasion for tongue cancer for which a segmental mendibulectomy is performed

Alternatives
  • Radiation
  • Palliative care

Complications
  • Hemorrhage from lingual artery
  • Communication with neck dissection 
  • Tongue edema
  • Injury to lips/dentition
  • Infection
  • Dysarthria

Steps
Dependent on location of tumor
  1. Panendoscopy
  2. Approximate 1 cm margins circumferentially and 1 cm deep
  3. Identify, clamp, and ligate the lingual artery

Post-Op
  • Diet
  • Pain
  • Nutrition
  • Speech

fields.value:
{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Otitis Media, Myringotomy, Tympanostomy Tube, and Balloon Dilation
Operative Video(s): Myringotomy with PE tube placement

Indications
  • Recurrent AOM is defined as three episodes of AOM in 6 months or 4 episodes in 12 months
  • Chronic otitis media is effusion lasting longer than 3 months
  • Persistent AOM is when an infection fails to resolve with appropriate antibiotic therapy or when two episodes of otitis media occur in 1 month

Contraindications
  • CSF
  • Vascular anomaly

Complications
  • Bleeding, infection, tube obstruction, granulation, premature extrusion, TM tube retention, myringosclerosis, TM perforation, middle ear tympnaostomy tube, damage to ossicular chain and chords tympani

Steps
  1. With myringotomy knife, make 2mm incision away from the posterior-superior quadrant
  2. Aspirate the middle ear with suction
  3. Place tube in the pars tensa away from the posterior superior quadrant, in the myringotomy site
  4. Position the tube with a pick
  5. Achieve hemostasis with cotton soaked in 1:1000 epinephrine

Post-Op
  • Drops depending on if there is drainage
  • Post-operative audiogram and tympanogram
  • Routine follow-up every 3-6 months after post op visit

fields.value:
{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Phonomicrosurgery for Benign Vocal Fold Lesions

Operative Video(s): Microdirect laryngoscopy with microflap for removal of a vocal cord cyst, Microdirect laryngoscopy with vocal cord polyp removal

Relevant Anatomy
  • The interface between the mucosa and deeper lamina propria and muscles allows for the creation of a mucosal wave.
  • Subepithelial plane, vocal ligament
  • The most medial aspect of the muscle that runs from the vocal process of the arytenoid to the thyroid cartilage is named the vocals muscle
  • Excluding epithelial disease, all benign vocal fold lesions arise from the lamina propria. The majority com from the sub epithelial space.

Indications
  • All nonsurgical therapies have been exhausted

Contraindications
  • Poor patient compliance with voice therapy

Complications
  • Injury to teeth, injury to the lingual nerve, no voice improvement, postoperative scarring

Steps
Microflap
  1. Intubate and suspend patient
  2. Inject epinephrine at the base of the lesion
  3. Make incision just lateral to the lesion to minimize damage to normal mucosa
  4. Develop plane using elevator
  5. After removal of lesion, visually inspect the micro-flap and then retrace it over the defect

Truncation (for pedunculate polyps)
  1. Do not inject epinephrine into the submucosa
  2. Grasp the pathology and retract medially then cut the stalk at the level of the vocal fold mucosa
  3. Achieve hemostasis with epinephrine soaked pledgets

Post-Op
  • Voice rest
  • Acid suppression if indicated
  • Hydration
  • Smoking cessation
  • Voice therapy

{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Septoplasty, Development and validation of the Nasal Obstruction Symptom Evaluation (NOSE) scale, Anatomy and Physiology of Nasal Obstruction

Operative Video(s): Endoscopic Septoplasty

Complications
Disarticulation of quadrangular cartilage (leads to loss of dorsal height), mucosal tears, loss of dorsal/tip support, bleeding, sinusitis, septal perforation, septal hematoma, toxic shock syndrome, CSF leak (make superior bone cut before making inferior bone cuts), anosmia, need for revision surgery, change in external appearance

Relevant Anatomy
  • The internal nasal valve is the narrowest portion of the nasal airway and thus comprises the area of greatest overall resistance to airflow
  • The septum and turbinates are the most common anatomic causes for nasal obstruction
  • The purpose of the nose is to warm, humidify, and filter inspired air before it reaches the pulmonary system
  • Optimal nasal airflow requires patent nasal passages, intact mucociliary function, normal functioning receptors for airflow, and absence of mucosal inflammation
  • The anatomy of the nose is divided into thirds: the osseous nasal vault, the upper lateral cartilages, and the lower lateral cartilages
  • The caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage, nasal septum, floor of the nose, and head of the inferior turbinate form the internal nasal valve
  • Nasal septal swell body is a widened region of the anterior nasal septum that is located anterior to the middle turbinate

Steps
  1. Hemitransfixion incision in caudal edge of septum
  2. Elevate the submucochondrial and submucoperiosteal flaps using Woodson and Cottle elevators
  3. Separate the quadrangular cartilage from the bony septum posteriorly, do not disarticulate
  4. Cut perpendicular plate high then low (over the maxillary crest), remove bone with rongeur
  5. Remove quadrangular cartilage with 15 blade if necessary. Make sure to preserve at least 1 cm of dorsal septal strut and 1 cm of caudal septal strut.
  6. Remove inferior bony septal spurts of the maxillary crest by elevating the mucoperiosteium over the lateral aspect of the crest and then removing the bone with a wronger or chisel or osteotome.
  7. Correct caudal septal deformities
  8. Make sure you can visualize the axilla of the middle turbinate
  9. Close hemitransfixion incision then approximate the septal flaps with quilting
  10. Place silastic splints bilaterally and secure anteriorly with suture

Post-Op
  1. Antibiotics while splints in place
  2. Patients should use nasal rinses
  3. Remove splints at POD#5-7

{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology, Open Thyroidectomy; Operative Otolaryngology: Central Neck Dissection; Cummings Otolaryngology: Overview of Diagnostic Imaging of the Head and Neck
Operative Video(s): Thyroid lobectomy; Total Thyroidectomy with Central Neck Dissection

Indications
Total thyroidectomy: this is nuanced but in generally large differentiated tumors and poorly differentiated tumors of any side.
Thyroid Lobectomy: small well differentiated tumors, nodules with suspicion of cancer, benign nodule greater than 4cm

Relevant Anatomy
Superior thyroid artery off of the external carotid (16% branch off of the common carotid)
Inferior thyroid artery: branch of the thyrocervical trunk
Thyroid ima artery supplies isthmus in 2-12% of patients.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve: travels in the tracheoesophageal groove, Simon’s triangle, Berry's ligament
Superior laryngeal nerve: Joll’s triangle 

Complications
Injury to the recurrent (hoarseness and vc in the paramedic position) or superior laryngeal nerves (difficulty projecting voice with poor pitch control in high frequencies), devascularization of the parathyroids, interoperative hemorrhage, hematoma

Steps
  1. Make horizontal neck incision
  2. Divide and lateralize the straps muscles
  3. Ligate the superior vascular bundle, make sure the SLN is not within the pedicle
  4. Mobilize the thyroid medially (ligate the middle thyroid veins)
  5. Identify the RLN. Once identified,  transect Berry’s ligament
  6. Dissect and lateralize the parathyroid glands (usually get blood supply form the inferior thyroid arteries)
  7. Deliver the lob and ligate the inferior pole (repeat on other side if doing a total thyroidectomy)
  8. Achieve homeostasis
  9. Wound closure  (straps with 3-0 vicryl and skin with 4-0 monocryl

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Tonsillectomy

Operative Video(s): Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy using Electrocautery Technique, Cold Steel Tonsillectomy, Intracapsular Tonsillectomy

Indications
  • #1 Sleep disordered breathing
  • #2 Recurrent pharyngotonsillitis, seven episodes in 1 year, five in each of the last 2 years, or three in each of the last 3 years
  • After peritonsillar abscess
  • After Lemierre syndrome
  • After acute upper airway obstruction due to enlarged tonsils

Complications
Pain, nausea/vomiting, dehydration, bleeding, post-obstructive pulmonary edema, laryngospasm, airway fire, TMJ dysfunction, burns

Relevant Anatomy
  • Palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus.
  • Peritonsillar potential space
  • Ascending palatine, lingual, facial, and maxillary arteries of the external carotid.
  • Tonsillar veins of external palatine, pharyngeal, and facial veins
  • Internal carotid artery lies 2-2.5cm posterolateral to the tonsil in the poststyloid parapharyngeal space
  • Sensation from lesser palatine and CNIX
  • Lymphatic drainage to Level II and retropharyngeal lymph nodes

Steps
  1. Grasp tonsil with Allis clamp and retract medioinferiorly
  2. Make incision superolaterally at the anterior tonsillar pillar
  3. Identify the tonsillar capsule then retract the tonsil inferiorly and begin dissection from superior to inferior
  4. Leave areolar tissue in the peritonsillar potential space
  5. Irrigate pharynx with saline
  6. Control bleeding
  7. Stay in room until patient is ventilating independently

Post-Op
  1. Pain (acetaminophen and ibuprofen)
  2. Hydration

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology, Open Tracheostomy
Operative Video(s): Open Tracheostomy

Preoperative Preparation
Typically, cuffed tubes are placed in adults to reduce aspiration of secretions
If the patient requires higher than 30% oxygen to maintain Saturn, then electrocautery should not be used wen the trachea is open

Post-Operative Care
The tube should not be changed until 3-5 days postoperatively when adhesion form between the overlying soft tissues and the trachea

Relevant Anatomy
  1. Thyroid notch
  2. Cricoid cartilage
  3. Sternal notch
  4. Anterior jugular veins
  5. Trachea
  6. Layers (skin, platysma, straps, pretracheal fascia, trachea)

Complications
Hemorrhage, tracheoesophageal fistula, pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum, flash pulmonary edema, fire, tube obstruction, tube displacement, infection, granulation tissue

Steps
  1. Transverse incision ~1cm above the suprasternal notch or 2 cm below the cricoid cartilage. This is usually 2 finger breadths above the sternal notch.
  2. Rakes to separate the subcutaneous tissue horizontally
  3. Split the straps muscles vertically and retract using blunt retractor or Weitlander
  4. Retract the thyroid isthmus superiorly
  5. Place tracheal hook under the cricoid to immobilize the trachea
  6. Notify the anesthesiologist that you are going to be entering the trachea, they may need to partially retract the endotracheal tube. Then make a transverse incision between the second and third or third and fourth tracheal rings. If doing a Bjork flap, make vertical incisions at each end of the transverse incision and then suture the flap to the skin
  7. Insert the tracheostomy tube and secure it by string the neck plate to the skin. Velcro the strap to the patients neck. if the patient is not undergoing subsequent head and neck surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Transoral CO 2 Laser Microsurgery for Cancer of the Larynx
Operative Video(s): Transoral Laser Co2 Microsurgery of the Larynx - Type I and Type III cordectomy

Relevant Anatomy
Depends on approach, see text
  • Vocal ligament
  • Thyroarytenoid muscle
  • The European Laryngological Society (ELS) is the classification system used for endoscopic cordectomy

Indications
  • T1 or T2 glottic cancer
  • Treat sequelae of CO2 laser or radiation

Alternatives
  • Chemoradiation or hemilaryngectomy for glottic cancer
  • Supraglottic or supracricoid laryngectomy for supraglottic cancers

Complications
  • Traumatic injury
  • Airway fires
  • Laser burns
  • airway obstruction
  • bleeding
  • aspiration
  • damage to lingual nerve from upward traction
  • poor voice quality

Steps
General
  1. Panendoscopy
  2. Protect laryngoscope with moist material
  3. Put moist material around endotracheal tube


Glottic Cancer
Superficial: 
  • 1 mm margins, low power laser (1.5-3 W) in continuous SP mode. 
  • Make initial incision then grasp the epithelium with micro forceps to continue dissection off of the vocal ligament

Deep: 
  • ELS type II to IV, >1 mm margin, slightly higher power (3-5 W) and normal SP mode. 
  • Consider ventriculectomy to improve visualization of the cords. 
  • In order to judge the depth of the cancer during transoral laser microsurgery you breadslice the lesion. 
  • Resect the cancer in piecemeal fashion

Supraglottic cancer
  • Laser at >5 W, SP mode to cut and coagulate. Margins >5mm. 
  • Use distended laryngopharyngoscope. 
  • Bisect the suprahyoid epiglottis in a sagittal plane
  • Clip the superior laryngeal vessels as they traverse the pharynoepiglottic folds.
  • Dissect the pre-epiglottic space
  • Bisect the infra hyoid epiglottis in a sagittal plane
  • Secure hemostasis with bipolar

Cancer of hypopharynx
  • 5-10 mm margins. Laser at >5 W and on CW mode.
  • Be wary of the carotid sheath

Post-Op
  • Pain management
  • Nutrition
  • Airway management

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Surgery of the Turbinate, Development and validation of the Nasal Obstruction Symptom Evaluation (NOSE) scale, Anatomy and Physiology of Nasal Obstruction

Operative Video(s): Submucosal Inferior Turbinate Reduction

Complications
MT: Bleeding, synechiae, sinusitis, injury to the lacrimal duct, empty nose syndrome
IT: Bleeding, synechiae, sinusitis, CSF leak

Relevant Anatomy
  • IT = inferior turbinate branch of the posterior nasal artery. 
  • MT = hiatus semilunaris and ethmoid bulla, cribriform plate, basal lamella
  • The internal nasal valve is the narrowest portion of the nasal airway and thus comprises the area of greatest overall resistance to airflow
  • The septum and turbinates are the most common anatomic causes for nasal obstruction
  • The purpose of the nose is to warm, humidify, and filter inspired air before it reaches the pulmonary system
  • Optimal nasal airflow requires patent nasal passages, intact mucociliary function, normal functioning receptors for airflow, and absence of mucosal inflammation
  • The anatomy of the nose is divided into thirds: the osseous nasal vault, the upper lateral cartilages, and the lower lateral cartilages
  • The caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage, nasal septum, floor of the nose, and head of the inferior turbinate form the internal nasal valve
  • Nasal septal swell body is a widened region of the anterior nasal septum that is located anterior to the middle turbinate

Preoperative
  • Ask about laterality, aggravating/alleviating factors, previous surgery, and medications
  • Look valve collapse

Steps
Inferior Turbinate
  1. After decongestion and vasoconstriction, make stab incision in the anterior inferior turbinate
  2. Elevate mucosa
  3. Use microdebrider to remove redundant tissue
  4. Consider using through cutting instrument to remove excess bone
  5. Use an elevator to out fracture the turbinate

Middle Turbinate
  1. Make stab incision into concha bulls lateral to the medial vertical attachment
  2. Use through cutting/microdebrider to remove the concha bulllosa. Do not go more posterior than the basal lamella.

Post-Op
  1. Pain management
  2. Irricgation
  3. If splints, remove after POD#3-5

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Parathyroidectomy for Primary Hyperparathyroidism and Nonlocalizing Hyperparathyroidism 
Operative Video(s): Parathyroidectomy for Parathyroid Adenoma

Background
  • Primary hyperthyroidism is 4 times more common in females. 
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism is most commonly associated with parathyroid adenoma (80%), followed by glandular hyperplasia, double adenoma, and carcinoma.
  • MEN1 and MEN2 are familial conditions associated with hyperparathyroidism
  • Hypercalcemia: stones, groans, psychiatric overtones. May also be asymptomatic.
  • Initial imaging study for suspected parathyroid adenoma is ultrasound. Traditionally, it was a sestamibi scan.

Relevant Anatomy
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • The location of the superior parathyroid glands can be estimated 1 cm above and below the intersection between the RLN and inferior thyroid artery. In closes proximity to the cricothyroid junction
  • Inferior parathyroid glands are most commonly found in the thyrothymic tract as the level of the inferior aspect of the thyroid lobes. They have higher location variability than superior parathyroids
  • The RLN is anterior to the superior parathyroid and posterior to the inferior parathyroids

Indications
  • Sympomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, familial primary hyperparathyroidism , suspicion for cancer, asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism  given specific features (see text)

Contraindications
  • Contralateral RLN injury, cervical disc disease

Alternatives
  • Medications, though these will not cure primary hyperparathyroidism 

Complications
  • Injury to RLN, operative failure, bleeding, hypocalcemia (Hungry bone syndrome), infection, thyroid dysfunction 

Steps
  1. Preoperative PTH level
  2. Kocher skin incision
  3. Raise subplatysmal flaps
  4. Split straps muscles
  5. Rotate thyroid medially
  6. Identify RLN
  7. Find parathyroid glands
  8. Dissect glands circumferentially and send for frozen
  9. Consider intraoperative PTH monitoring to guide surgery. The Loma Linda University protocol requires measurement of PTH: preincision and 10, 15, and 10 minute post incision levels. A PTH decline rather than 50% compared to precision level suggests cure.
  10. If two enlarged glands are found ipsilaterally, convert to bilateral neck exploration
  11. Approximate strap muscles and platysma then close skin

Post-Op
  • Pain management
  • Labs 2 weeks post surgery and 6 months post surgery.
  • Bone scan 18 months post surgery

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Medialization Laryngoplasty and Arytenoid Adduction
Operative Video(s): Type 1 thyroplasty with arytenoid adduction

Relevant Anatomy
  • Inferior border of the thyroid cartilage
  • Posterior border of thyroid cartilage
  • Cricoid cartilage
  • Cricopharyngeus muscle
  • Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle
  • Muscular process of arytenoid (grain of rice)

Indications
  • Symptomatic glottic insufficiency

Alternatives
  • Observation, injection laryngoplasty with adipose or other material

Complications
  • Infection, bleeding airway obstruction, implant migration, persistent dysphonia

Steps
Medialization laryngoplasty (Type I thyroplasty)
  1. 4-5 cm incision along the inferior border of the thyroid all
  2. Elevate subplatysmal flaps
  3. Divide straps
  4. Incise thyroid cartilage longitudinally and elevate to identify the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage
  5. Use caliber to measure posterior to thyroid cartilage and superior to the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage
  6. Place needle into the thyroid cartilage and visualize with laryngoscopy
  7. Create window based on implant material
  8. Insert implant being sure to slightly overmedialize the cord to account for itraoperative edema of the vocal fold and prevent undermedialization post op, then secure the implant with a suture
  9. Reapproximate the thyroid perichondrium, and straps, and close the skin

Arytenoid Adduction
  1. 4-5 cm incision along the inferior border of the thyroid all
  2. Elevate subplatysmal flaps
  3. Divide straps
  4. Transect 1 cm of medial aspect of the sternohyoid muscle blow insertion on hyoid
  5. Incise thyroid cartilage longitudinally and elevate to identify the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage
  6. Continue dissection around the posterior border of the thyroid all and skeletonize the inferior cornu then dissect up towards the superior cornu
  7. Release the criopharyngeus from the inferior cornu
  8. Dissect the pyriform sinus off of the posterior cricoid cartilage and identify the posterior cricopharyngeus muscle
  9. Remove small portion of posterior thyroid cartilage
  10. Suture arytenoid cartilage then place the suture through the window and suture through the circothyroid membrane and the thyroid cartilage.

Post-Op
  • Pain management
  • Reevaluate in 4 weeks in clinic

Background
  • The Voice Handicap Index (VHI) can be used to monitor the response to treatment of vocal fold injection

Relevant Anatomy
  • Superior arcuate line
  • Vocal process

Indications
  • Symptomatic glottic insufficiency
  • Trial VFI

Alternatives
  • Injection under local
  • Voice therapy
  • Swallowing therapy
  • Compensatory streatgies for dysphagia

Complications
  • Airway compromise
  • Vocal fold hemorrhage
  • Injury to teeth and gums
  • Inadequate augmentation
  • Superficial injection (can present with worsened voice qualtiy)
  • Persistent symptoms
  • Airway compromise

Steps
  • Place and suspend laryngoscope
  • Visualize true vocal folds
  • Find injection location at the intersection of the superior arcuate line and the vocal process
  • Prepare injection material
  • Deploy injection material at depth of 3-5 mm. Make sure needle bevel is anterior and medial.
  • Suction excess material
  • Control bleeding
  • Remove laryngoscope and check teeth and tongue for trauma

Post-Op
  • Voice rest
  • pain management

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Endonasal Approach to the Sella and Parasellar Areas 
Operative Video(s): Endoscopic Transsphenoidal Approach for Pituitary Tumor Resection

Relevant Anatomy
  • Sphenoid ostium
  • Vomer
  • Sella
  • Planum sphenoidale
  • Clival recess
  • Cavernous sinus
  • Internal carotid artery.
  • Lateral opticocarotid recess
  • Vidian nerve
  • CN V2
  • Sphenopalatine artery

Indications
  • Pituitary tumors

Contraindications
  • Pathology deep to a nerve or vessel

Alternatives
  • Medical management
  • Stereotactic radiation

Complications
  • CSF leak, carotid artery injury, cavernous sinus hemorrhage, nerve injury, endocrinopathies, epistaxis, hematoma, synechiae, septal perforation, meningitis, 

Steps
  1. Outfracture the turbinates
  2. Resect or lateralize the superior turbinates
  3. Bilateral sphenoidotomies
  4. Posterior septectomy
  5. Elevate nasoseptal flap if needed
  6. Remove intersinus septum and rostrum of sphenoid
  7. Remove posterior ethmoid cells
  8. Remove mucosa over the sella with Cottle elevator and suction
  9. Drill bone over sella to expose dura and cavernous sinus
  10. Let the neurosurgeon do their thing
  11. Reconstruct the defect. If the ICA is exposed, use the nasoseptal flap for coverage 

Post-Op
  • Evaluate vision
  • Antibiotics if packing in place
  • Access Pituitary function
  • In office debridements

Operative Video(s): Microdirect Laryngoscopy with CO2 Laser Wedge Excisions for Subglottic Stenosis

Background
  • The subglottis is the laryngeal region most susceptible to stenosis
  • Etiologies include external trauma, intubation, tracheotomy, endoscopy, caustic burns, radiation, nasogastric intubation, infectious/granulomatous/autoimmune processes, lymphoproliferative disorders, and GERD 
  • Acquired laryngeal stenosis from endotracheal tubes usually affects the posterior glottis. Generally presents as progressive dyspnea beginning 4-8 weeks after extubation. 
  • Elective tracheostomy is recommended when intubation is expected to be needed for longer than 10 days. 
  • Trach cuff pressures should be kept below 22 mm Hg to reduce the risk of cartilage necrosis and tenses or malacia.
  • Caustic ingestion usually damages the supraglottisSofferman syndrome is trauma of the posterior cricoid associated with the nasogastric tube
  • Mitomycin C is an alkalating agent that is often used during surgery. It must be applied to tissues for a total of 4 minutes.

Relevant Anatomy
  • Larynx

Indications
  • Dysphagia and dyspnea

Contraindications
  • Uncontrolled diabetes, current smoking

Complications
  • Dental injury, tongue numbness, loss of airway, bleeding, infection, subcutaneous emphysema, laser injury

Steps
  • There are many different approaches. Read the text

Post-Op
  • Depends largely on type of surgery
  • Elevate the head of the bed
  • Flexible laryngoscopy

Background
  • RRP is more aggressive in children
  • Pulmonary involvement of RRP is associated with poor prognosis
  • Potassium titanic-phosphate (KTP) laser treatments effects are described using a 5 point classification system
  • RRP is a disease of the epithelium
Relevant Anatomy
  • Larynx
  • Anterior commissure 

Indications
  • Dyspnea, dysphonia, globus sensation

Alternatives
  • cidofovir, interferon, bevacizumab, I3C, HPV vaccine

Complications
  • Injury to surrounding structures,, airway fire, dental injury, worsened voice or breathing

Steps
  1. Evaluate airway
  2. Place moist pledge in sub glottis
  3. Use cold instrumentation to remove small portion of mucosa and send for pathology
  4. KTP: “Inside-out”, “outside-in”. Cold steel. CO2 laser. Microdebrider. To remove papillomas.
  5. Achieve hemostasis
  6. Consider staging removal of papillomas from the anterior comminsure to prevent an anterior laryngeal web, anterior glottic web

Post-Op
  • 4-6 week follow up

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Transcranial and Endonasal Approaches to the Anterior Cranial Base
Operative Video(s): Combined Endoscopic and Open Craniofacial Resection for Esthesioneuroblastoma; Endoscopic Endonasal Approach for Craniopharyngioma Resection with Nasoseptal Flap Reconstruction


Relevant Anatomy
  • Anterior cranial fossa
  • Cranial nerves I, II, III, IV,VI, and the frontal branch of VII
  • Orbit
  • Ethmoid, sphenopalatine, internal maxillary, and carotid arteries

Indications
  • Tumors of the anterior skull base

Contraindications
  • Bilateral orbital, cavernous sinus, or ICA involvement
  • Gross intracranial extension (for sinonasal tumors)

Alternatives
  • Induction chemoradiation

Complications
  • bleeding, stroke, vision loss, CSF leak, meningitis, epistaxis, facial nerve weakness, nasal obstruction, SIADH, diabetes insidious, DVT, Pneumocephalus, scalp necrosis, chronic rhinitis

Steps
Bicoronal Approach
  1. Incision at least 2 cm posterior to the hairline from the preauricular skin bilaterally
  2. Dissect in the smbgaleal plane posteriorly being cognizant for the superficial temporal artery
  3. Laterally, separate the deep temporal fascia from the temporal muscle
  4. Release supraorbital vessels and nerves
  5. Elevate temporalis off of the temporal bone
  6. Neurosurgeon performs craniotomy
  7. Perform lateral rhinology or facial devolving if necessary
  8. After removal of tumor, repair defect with a pericardial flap.
    1. Suture to the dura from posterior to anterior
    2. Strip mucosa from the frontal sinuses to allow for cranialization
    3. Use temporals muscle plugs to obliterate the frontal recesses bilaterally
    4. Replace the craniotomy and supraorbital bones. Remove 2-3 mm of bone to avoid compressing the pericardial flap at the inferior edge of the supraorbital bone
  9. Secure Jackson Pratt drain
  10. Repair scalp in layered fashion

Endoscopic Approach (multiple approaches can be used depending on the location of the tumor. Review the text as well as the other Rhinology procedure tags)
  1. Vasoconstriction
  2. Use bottle elevator to discern tumor attachment
  3. Debulk tumor
  4. Expose non-involved sinuses to evaluate lateral and posterior margins
  5. Perform Draf III to evaluate anterior margins
  6. Detach vomer from sphenoid rostrum
  7. Expose ethmoid arteries laterally where the fovea ethmoidalis attaches to the lamina papyracea
  8. Perform craniotomy
  9. Release the crest gallic and fax cerebra in anterior to posterior direction
  10. Reconstruct defect

Post-Op
  • ICU monitoring
  • Close neurologic assessment
  • Drain management
  • Post op imaging
  • Nose blowing and lifting limitations

Relevant Anatomy
  • Sphenopalatine artery

Indications
  • Dural defect after tumor or encephalocele excision
  • Post-op CSF leak after sinonasal surgery
  • Extra dural defects

Complications
  • Damage to flap pedicle or perforation of flap, CSF leak, pneumocephalus, hemorrhage, mucocele

Types of flaps
  • Free mucosal graft from the nasal floor
  • Free mucosal graft from nasal septum
  • Free mucosal graft from middle turbinate
    • Use cutting instrument  to cut anterior to posterior just below the axilla.
    • Avoid extending the incision superiorly
    • Transect the horizontal (oblique) portion of the basal lamella
    • Cauterize the middle turbinate branch of the sphenopalatine artery
  • Nasoseptal flap
    • Make inferior incision inferolateral to the sphenoid osmium and extend medially to the posterior china
    • Continue inferior incision over the posterior aspect of the nasal septum
    • Begin superior incision at the sphenoid ostium and then continue over the face of the sphenoid. Carry this anteriorly.
    • Join the parallel incision at the level of the anterior head of the inferior turbinate
    • Elevate the flap from anterior to posterior
    • Place the flap in the nasopharynx or maxillary sinus until needed
  • Fascia Lata Flap
    • Make 3-5cm longitudinal incision along the lateral thigh down to the ileotibial band
    • Make medial then lateral longitudinal incisions then distal and proximal transverse incisions of fascia
    • Close in layered fashion

Steps
  1. Make sure all mucosa is stripped from the defect site
  2. Place allogenic material or collagen matrix as the subdural inlay graft
  3. Lay free mucosal or nasoseptal flap as an onlay
  4. Bolster flap with absorbable packing
  5. Place Foley balloon catheter or packing sponges to stabilize the grafts

Post-Op
  • Elevation of bed
  • Stool softener
  • Remove nasal packing on POD#3-5
  • Saline irrigation after removal of packing
  • Debridement 2 weeks s/p
  • Debridement 4 weeks s/p
  • Activity restriction until 6 weeks s/p

  • Sphenopalatine artery
  • Nasal nerves
  • Sphenopalatine ganglion
  • Sphenopalatine foramen

Indications
  • Rhinitis refractory to medical managment

Complications
  • Bleeding
  • Dry eyes

Steps
  1. Elevate mucoperiosteal flap from the inferior turbinate to the oblique portion for the ground lamella of the middle turbinate off of then perpendicular plate of the palatine bone
  2. Cut posterior inferior nasal nerves with laser
  3. Dissect the periosteum of the sphenoplatine foramen to reveal the sphenopalatine artery
  4. Remove branches of posterior superior nerve with small forceps
  5. Replace flap

Suggested Reading: Cummings Otolaryngology: Skin Flap Physiology and Wound Healing

Background
  • An acute wound becomes a chronic wound when healing is delayed by more than 3 weeks.
  • Smoking, radiation and diabetes increase the risk of flap failure.
  • Critical closing pressure is a concept  based on the idea that there is a not at which capillary blood flow will cease. It is a zone II phenomenon.
  • Creep referee to the increase in strains when constant forsce is applied to the skin.
  • Stress relaxation refers to the decrease in stress that occurs when skin is held under tension at a constant strain.
  • The precapillary sphincter controls the amount of nutritive blood flow to the skin
  • Blood flow in capillaries is dictated by Poiseuille’s law
  • Generally tissues can tolerate 6 hours of complete ischemia
  • No-reflow is the condition in which zone 1 perfusion has been reestablished but Zone II or II failure prevailed.
  • Neovascularization  begins 3 or 4 days after flap transposition. The free flap is typically not monitored after 1 week.
  • The four classifications of flaps based on their principal blood supply are random, arterial cutaneous, fasciocutaneous, and musculocutaneous.
  • Delay phenomenon is raising part of the flap and then laying it back down in its original position

Operative Video(s): Latissimus dorsi free flap

Background
  • The latissimus dorsi is the largest muscle in the body by surface area

Relevant Anatomy
  • Thoracodorsal artery and vein
  • The thoracodorsal vessels originate from the subscapular vessels
  • The thoracodorsal medical enters the latissimus doors 8-12 cm proximal to the humeral attachment of the muscle. It then divides into two branches
  • Thoracodorsal nerve innervates the latissimus doors and often intertwines the vascular pedicle
  • Most of the perforators are located at the lateral, superior aspect of the muscle
  • Thoracoacromial pedicle

Indications
  • Reconstruction of lateral neck, oral, oropharyngeal, and skull base or scalp defects.

Contraindications
  • Inability to position in lateral decubitus position
  • Contralateral or midline defects

Complications
  • Bleeding, infection, loss of flap (arterial compromise, venous compromise, hematoma, dehiscence), scarring, damage to surrounding structures like the brachial plexus

Steps
  1. Make incisions along the lateral edge of the axilla
  2. Elevate anterior flap to expose serratus muscle (long thoracic nerve and lateral thoracic artery)
  3. Identify thoracodorsal pedicle and trace to its origin. Ligate arteries to serratus and teres major.
  4. Identify and divide the thoracodosal nerve
  5. Elevate flap in distal to proximal direction
  6. Elevate the medial portion of the flap
  7. Create tunnel between the pectorals muscles. Visualize the thoracoacromial pedicle
  8. Dissect clavicular head of pectorals major muscle
  9. Divide the humeral tendon of the latissimus
  10. Rotate the flap through the tunnel and reconstruct
  11. To close, place suction drain and close primarily.

Post-Op
  • Flap monitoring
  • Drain monitoring
  • Pain control
  • PT

Operative Video(s): Any of the “Free Flap” videos

Background
  • Radial forearm free flap
  • Anterolateral thigh flap
  • parascapular and scapular free flaps, rectus abdomens and deep inferior epigastric perforator flap
  • fibula free flap
  • jejunal free flap
  • latissimus dorsi free flap (can also be a regional flap)
  • Anterolateral thigh flap is most common
  • The fibula will pride up to 26 cm of bone vascularized by the perineal artery
  • An Allen test should be performed prior to harvesting a radial forearm free flap (RFFF)
  • Before harvesting a rectus abdomens, iliac crest or jejunal free flap, determine whether the patient has a hernia
  • Confirm the presence of a palpable dorsals pedis and posterior tibial pulse prior to harvesting a fibular free flap
  • Resection of the anterior mandible can result in a(n) Andy Gump deformity

Relevant Anatomy
  • Recipient vessels: facial, superior thyroid, transverse cervical arteries, external carotid
  • Veins in zones I and V of neck as well as the external jug

Indications
  • Mandibulectomy defects (fibula free flap, osteocutaneous radial forearm free flap, pectorals flap, soft tissue free flap)
  • Glossectomy defects (rectus abdominis free flap, anterolateral thigh free flap)
  • Pharyngectmy free flap (anterolateral thigh free flap, radial forearm free flap, jejunal free flap)
  • Midface and matxillectomy defects (fibula free flap, anterolateral high free flap)
  • Skull base defects (local: pericardial or temoroparietal fascial flap, free: rectus abdominis, anterolateral thigh, latissimus myocutaneous, serratus free flap)

Complications
  • Bleeding and infection
  • Flap failure
  • Donor site morbidity

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Skin Grafting
Operative Video(s): Full-thickness skin graft harvested from the inside of upper arm; Split-Thickness Skin Graft Technique; Harvesting a full thickness skin graft. #33

Background
  • Full thickness contains epidermis and dermis
  • Split thickness contains epidermis and some dermis
  • Full thickness better approximates skin texture and color than split thickness
  • Split thickness has a higher rate of survival on wound beds with minimal vascularity due to decreased metabolic demand
  • Common donor sites for full thickness grafts include the supraclavicular fossa, post auricular, preauricular or upper eyelid.
  • Split thickness can be meshed at ratios of 1:1.5 or 1:3. If harvesting from the thigh, make sure you are at least four finger breadth from the patella to avoid interfering with knee flexion and extension
  • For large full thickness skin grafts, the supraclavicular region is often best as a donor site. Avoid closing the defect over the clavicle
  • For female, a preauricular skin graft often provided appropriate skin color match
  • In males, the post auricular skin is appropriate because it is usually hairless
  • Graft thickness is typically 0.012 inches

Contraindications
  • Areas prone to poor graft “take” such as avascular defects, radiated tissue, exposed cortical bone, cartilage, and/or tendon

Complications
  • Skin graft failure (technical error, hematoma, mobilization of graft), eschars

Alternatives
  • Local flaps, skin substitutes, allografts, xenografts

Steps
Split thickness
  1. Select plate that is 10-15% wider than the size of the defect
  2. Lubricate the donor site with mineral oil
  3. Engage skin at 30-45% angle and keep dermatome on until the entire graft is harvested
  4. Inject lidocaine and pinephrine into the donor site
  5. Apply semioccluzive dressing to the donor site and then Tegadrm.
  6. Mesh graft if indicated
  7. Draft graft over the recipient site. Secure the graft circumferentially
  8. Apply boldster and secure with sutures in a star-burst pattern.

Full thickness
  1. Use tell to make a template of the surgical defect and make it oversized by ~10%
  2. Harvest graft deep to the dermis.
  3. Use iris scissor to remove excess subcutaneous adipose tissue
  4. Place graft into the donor site and suture in an interrupted fashion circumferentially
  5. Make slits in the center of the graft to prevent hematoma
  6. Bolster as per split thickness above

Post-op
  • Revascularization is typically 6-7 days post-op and bolsters can be removed at this time

  4. Expose periosteum along the temporal line and a vertical limb

{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Cummings Otolaryngology: Myringoplasty and Tympanoplasty
Operative Video(s): Tympanoplasty for tympanic membrane retraction; Butterfly graft tympanolasty

Background
  • Myringoplasty addresses only the tympanic membrane
  • Tympanoplasty incorporates inspection of the middle ear

Anatomy
  • Tympanomastoid and tympanosquamous suture lines
  • Ossicles
  • Facial nerve
  • Layers of TM

Indications
  • Repair of TM perforation to lift water restrictions
  • Prevention of recurrent otorrhea
  • Attempt to improve hearing (it will fix a conductive loss)

Contraindications
  • Caution if operating on an only hearing ear
  • Vestibulopathy

Complications
  • Worsening of hearing, vertigo, changes in test, facial paresis, infection, failure of graft to hear perforation, numbness of the superior auricle, blunting of anterior sulcus, epithelial cysts, lateralization (when graft not place medial to the malleus)

Alternatives
  • Conservative management with observation or amplification with a hearing aid

Steps
Myringoplasty
  1. Acute and small: unfold medial edges of perforation, place small pieces of ofloxacin soaked gel foam medial to perforation, place patch the the lateral surface of the TM
  2. Small chronic: apply phenol to edges of perforation, freshen the margins of the TM, apply patch to the lateral surface fo the TM. If paper patching has previously failed, use autologous adipose tissue

Tympanoplasty
  1. Cartilage inlay
    1. Freshen perforation edges
    2. Measure size of perf
    3. Harvest and size tragal cartilage
    4. Introduce cartilage into the perforation
  2. Lateral Grafting
    1. Create transmeatal vascular strip along the tymapnomastoid and tympanosquamous suture lines
    2. Join incision just lateral to the annulus
    3. Make post auricular skin incision (extension beyond the mastoid tip dangers the facial nerve)
    4. Dissect medially into the subcutaneous tissue
    5. Harvest temporalis fascia
    6. Elevate canal skin around the TM
    7. Enlarge the bony canal with butting burr (remember that the facial nerve is located posteriorly)
    8. Continue depithelialization
    9. Trim the dehydrated fascia graft and cut slit in 12 o clock position
    10. Place graft over the perforation (avoid putting the graft on the bony canal as this will cause blunting
    11. Replace the canal skin on the bony canal. If this tissue is folded, you can get an epithelial cyst.
    12. Place gleam into the anterior sulcus
  3. Medial Grafting
    1. Inject edges of perforation
    2. Make incision in the tympanomastoid and tympanosquamous sutures
    3. make post auricular incisions and harvest fascia graft
    4. Retract the auricle anteriorly
    5. Elevate the tymapnomeatal flap and annulus to enter the middle ear. Make sure to identify the chords tympani
    6. Inspect the ossicular chain
    7. Place graft on the medal aspect of the TM perforation
    8. Return tymapnomeatal flat to anatomic position

Post-op
  • Ensure TM is intact by third post-op week
  • Audiometric testing at 2-3 months after surgery

Operative Video(s): Revision Middle Ear Exploration, Ossicular Chain Reconstruction (OCR) with Clip Prosthesis

Anatomy
  • Same as myringoplasty
  • Jugular vein
  • Pyramidal eminence
  • Cochleariform process
  • Horizontal (tympanic) segment of facial nerve

Indications
  • Conductive hearing loss with ossiucular etiology
  • When the ossicular chain must be misarticulated for access to other middle ear pathology
  • Extruding prosthesis from previous surgery

Contraindications
  • An only hearing ear
  • Conductive loss due to middle ear tumor or infection with involvement of dura or brain
  • Contracted middle ear space
  • Limited AB gap in revision cases

Complications
  • Hearing loss, dizziness, infection, extrusion of prosthesis, ossicular erosion, TM perforation, cholesteatoma, taste disturbances, facial nerve weakness

Alternatives
  • Frequent aural toilet
  • Amplification

Steps
Dependent on the type of reconstruction, read the text

Post-op
  • Water restriction
  • Avoid blowing nose
  • Avoid air travel
  • Packing removed 7-10 days post-op

Suggested Reading: Cummings Pediatric Otolaryngology: Cleft Lip and Palate
Operative Video(s): Cleft Lip (Millard’s); Cleft palate (2 flap)

Background
  • The most common syndrome associated with cleft lip is van her Woude syndrome and typically present with lower lip pits. It is a mutation in the interferon regulatory factor 6 gene and autosomal dominant
  • The most common syndrome associated with Pierre Robin Sequence is Stickler syndrome. PRS, sensorineural hearing loss, myopia, and MSK anomalies.
  • The most common syndrome associated with isolated cleft palate is 22q11 deletion syndrome.

Anatomy
  • Cupids bow
  • Columella
  • Oral commissure
  • Orbicularis oris
  • Philtrum
  • Nasal ala
  • Incisive foramen
  • Greater palatine foramen

Technique
Cleft lip
  • Millard
  • Veau
  • Manchester
  • Use of preoperative nasoalveolar molding

Cleft palate
  • Complications: oronasal fistula (severity of cleating and type of cleft are the main risk factors), velopharyngeal dysfunction (most common, lower with double opposing Z-plasty)
  • Two flap - alveolar cleft is not closed and the palate is not lengthened
  • Double opposing Z-plasty (Furlow Palatoplasty) - lengthens the sot palate and reconstructs the muscle sling, often used for secondary cleft palate.
