Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Transoral and Robotic Tonsil Surgery for Cancers of the base of tongue and Pharynx
Operative Video(s): Transoral robotic tonsil resection

Indications
  • Primary T1, T2, T3, or some T4 lesions
  • Recurrent cancer of the oropharynx (after radiation)
  • Metastatic cancer to the neck

Contraindications
  • Retropharyngeal course of carotid artery
  • Involvement of carotid artery

Complications
  • Hemorrhage (most common), dehydration, injury to teeth, injury to the lingual nerve, injury to the hypoglossal nerve

Alternatives
  • Chemoradiation
  • Open surgery

Anatomy
  • Lingual artery
  • Carotid artery
  • Facial artery
  • Blood supply to tonsils (see tonsillectomy note)
  • Medial pterygoid
  • Styloglossus
  • Stylopahryngeus
  • Prevertebral facia and longus coli muscle
  • Glossopharyngeal nerve during tongue base incisions may be encountered deep to the styloglossus

Technique
  1. Make index incision along the soft palate
  2. Deepen the incision to the medial pterygoid
  3. Continue the incision inferiorly toward the base of the tongue
  4. Join the incision to the superior aspect of the soft palate
  5. Identify the styloglossus and stylopharyngess muscles
  6. Connect the medial mucosal incision with the lateral pterygomandibular raphe incision and extent posteriorly to the prevertebral fascia over the longs coli muscle
  7. Dissect the tongue base, up to half of the bae of the tongue can be resected without adverse effects on swallowing
  8. Dissect the styloglossus and stylopharyngeus muscles. The glossopharyngeal nerve may be encountered while dissecting the styloglossus

fields.value:
{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology Brow lift
Operative videos: Midforehead Brow Lift; https://youtu.be/ooRSLxncDWU?t=102
  • Not long lasting because they do not address the ligaments
This approach to brow lift can be effective in men with unpredictable hairlines. The resulting scar is particularly well concealed when the technique is used in patients with deeper preexisting static forehead rhytids. 2 Given the incision placement proximity to the more mobile inferior forehead tissues, it affords excellent control of brow position along the entire width of the brow. Using a potentially broader horizontal incision than the direct brow lift, it is somewhat better at addressing medial brow/glabella ptosis than direct brow lift, but not as good as other approaches using superiorly based incisions (see Fig. 157.4 ). The obvious downside to using this technique is a potentially visible scar positioned in the midforehead (see Fig. 157.1 ).
  1. 1. After marking the incision site with the patient in the upright position, 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine is injected to the incision site and supraorbital rim area.
  2. 2. Half-strength betadine solution (betadine solution mixed 50:50 with balanced salt solution) is used to sterilize the brow and eyelid area. Full-strength betadine is used to sterilize the remaining field.
  3. 3. A fusiform horizontal incision is created in the midforehead down to the level of the frontalis muscle taking care to bevel the incision to allow for eversion of the skin edges on closure. The contralateral brow lift incision site should be planned in an asymmetric fashion with each incision site centered on a horizontal rhytid of varying vertical position. This asymmetric scar placement will allow for greater concealment potential. The horizontal length of the incision can be extended to overlap at different heights medially for correction of medial forehead/glabella ptosis and may extend laterally past the lateral edge of the frontalis muscle.
  4. 4. Limited subcutaneous superior dissection is performed to allow some eversion of this skin margin upon closure. The inferior subcutaneous undermining may be carried inferiorly more extensively in the plane just above the frontalis muscle to the level of the brow if necessary. Great care must be taken in lateral dissection to avoid injury to the frontal branch of the facial nerve and in medial dissection to avoid the supraorbital neurovascular bundle.
  5. 5. The amount of skin removed is based on the lift required and takes some experience to judge adequately. Over excision of skin must be avoided. Fixation is achieved using 4-0 prolene to secure the soft tissues of the brow and orbicularis to superior periosteum.
  6. 6. Sharp dissection near the midline allows transition to a deeper subperiosteal plane of dissection giving access to the glabella musculature. Surgical sectioning of the corrugator and procerus muscles, if deemed necessary, is possible using this approach.
  7. 7. After meticulous hemostasis is achieved with bipolar electrocautery, the wound is approximated using 4-0 PDS simple interrupted subcutaneous sutures. 6-0 prolene simple interrupted or vertical mattress sutures allow surface closure with an emphasis on eversion of the wound edges.

Suggested Reading: Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery: Frontal Sinusotomy-Draf I and IIa; Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery: Frontal Sinusotomy-Draf IIb; Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery: Frontal Sinusotomy-Draf III

Operative Videos: Endoscopic Frontal Sinusotomy, Draf IIa Procedure; Draf III (Endoscopic Modified Lothrop) Procedure

Anatomy
  • Anterior ethmoid artery
  • Agger nasi cell
  • Interfrontal sinus septal cell
  • Supraorbital ethmoid cell
  • Suprabullar cell
  • Frontal Bullar cell
  • Frontal recess cell
  • Anterior fossa
  • Cribriform plate
  • Middle turbinate
  • Nasofrontal beak

Technique 
Draf I and IIa
  1. Identify the anterior ethmoid artery
  2. Identify the natural drainage pathway (usually posterior-medial to the posterior wall of the agger nasi cell)
  3. Remove the posterior wall of the agger nasi
  4. Remove surrounding bony partitions
  5. Remove the agger nasi cap
  6. Expand the posterior frontal recess

Draf IIb
Indications are generally failed prior frontal surgery, mucocele, frontal sinus unobliteraion, tumor, repair of CSF leak. Contraindications are narrow AP diameter (between he anterior cribriform and frontal sinus).
  1. Draf IIa
  2. Partial resection of the anterior middle turbinate
  3. Use punch to remove frontal sinus floor
  4. If necessary, use drill to further expand ostium
  5. Optimize the new ostium

Draf III
Indications include inflammatory sinus disease since it allows for instillation of topical medication. Also included are patients with failed prior ESS or salvage after tumor surgery. It also provides better access to sinosasal and skull base neoplasms.
  1. Dissect the anterior ethmoid air cells and identify the medial orbital wall
  2. Expose the nasofrontal beak and dissect to the first olfactory neuron (this is the posterior limit of the surgery)
  3. Make mucosal incisions along the point below the frontal sinus and the septum. Then push cautery through the septal wall
  4. Raise mucosal flaps
  5. Create septal window
  6. Drill to define the lateral limits
  7. Drill away the nasofrontal beak
  8. Square off the frontal sinus cavity
  9. Consider using posterior turbinate mucosal graft
  10. Place silastic sheets

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Anterior Antrostomy: The Caldwell-Luc Operation

Operative Videos: Caldwell-Luc Procedure for Maxillary Sinus Schwannoma

Anatomy
  • Gingivobuccal sulcus
  • Canin tooth roots
  • Canine fossa
  • Infraorgital nerve
  • Inferior meatus
  • Orbit

Indications
  • Inflammatory sinusitis
  • Neoplastic disease
  • Access tot he petrygopalatine fossa
  • Initial step in medial maxillectomy
  • Access to orbital floor
  • Closure of oroantral fistula

Contraindications
  • Medical commorbidities
  • Pediatric patients without secondary dentition
  • Initial approach to sinus disease (use ESS first)

Complications
  • Injury to tooth roots, orbital floor, infraorbital nerve, nasolacrimal duct, superior alveolar nerve.
  • Oroantral fistula

Alternatives
  • Endoscopic sinus surgery

Technique 
  1. Bovie horizontally along the alveolar bone just inferior to the ginggivobuccal sulcus
  2. Elevate tissue with periosteal elevator and identify and protect the infraorbital nerve (provides sensation to the cheek, upper, lip, lateral aspect of nose, and upper teeth.)
  3. Create opening over the canine fossa (the indentation just lateral to the tooth root), then remove additional bone with rongeur
  4. If maxillary antrostomy is being used, out fracture the inferior turbinate and use bovie to incise the inferior meatus. Then enter the sinus using a hemostat or elevator (~1-2 cm behind the anterior aspect of the inferior turbinate)

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Excision of Cancer of the Floor of the Mouth

Background
  • FOM cancer makes up 30% of cancers of the head and neck
  • SCC is the most common subtype

Anatomy
  • hyoglossus
  • geniohyoid
  • mylohyoid
  • Salivary glands
  • Lingual, hypoglossal, and mental nerves
  • Lingal artery

Indications
  1. Wide local excision if involving soft tissue only and not approaching or involving the mandible
  2. Marginal mandibulectomy = cancer involving periosteum but not invading cortex, cancer in close proximity to periosteum, cancer abutting healthy dentition
  3. Segmental mandibulectomy = cancer invasion into the cortex or deeper, cancer abutting diseased dentition
  4. Mandibulotomy = access to the anteriorly based cancers of FOM

Complications
  • Orocutaneous fistula, hematoma, infection, damage to hypoglossal nerve, damage to lingual nerve, pathologic fracture, mandibular non-union

Alternatives
  • Radiation, chem-radiation, brachytherapy

Technique for WLE
  1. Perform neck dissection first
  2. Mark lesion with 1 cm margins
  3. Excise to a depth at the level of the sublingual glands
  4. If necessary, reroute the submandibular duct by incising it along its length and marsupializing it to the floor of the mouth mucosa
  5. Reconstruct generally with split-thickness skin graft

See relevant notes for information regarding marginal mandibulectomy, segmental mandibulectomy, and flaps that can be used for reconstruction

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Marginal Mandibulectomy

Background
  • Invasion of the inferior alveolar nerve is more common in edentulous patients since bone resorption causes it to lay more superficially in the mandible

Anatomy
  • Mandible - first branchial arch, note mandibular height, location of mental foramina, and position of the mylohyoid line
  • Inferior alveolar nerve

Indications
  • Marginal mandibulectomy = cancer involving periosteum but not invading cortex, cancer in close proximity to periosteum, cancer abutting healthy dentition

Contraindications
  • Gross destruction of bone
  • Invasion of the mandibular canal
  • Edentulous patient with reduced vertical height
  • Previously radiated mandible

Complications
  • Fracture of mandible

Technique 
  • Mark area to be excised
  • Use monopoly to incise through the periosteum down to bone.
  • Elevate the mucoperiosteum off of the mandible
  • Extract teeth if necessary. Make osteotomy in the middle of the tooth socket. Make sure to stay at least 7mm away from the mental foramen. Make osteotomies using a saw.
  • Deliver tissue en-bloc
  • Reconstruct (more recent research suggests using free tissue transfers for sizable resections to prevent radio necrosis)

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Segmental Mandibulectomy

Operative Video: Segmental Mandibulectomy

Background
  • Most patients with need a tracheostomy
Anatomy
  • Divided into lateral and anterior defects by the mental foramen. Lateral defects have less morbidity.
  • Lingual and hypoglossal nerves
  • Patients will have post-op permanent numbness of the lower jaw due to transaction of the inferior alveolar nerve
  • Inferior alveolar artery
  • Submandibular duct
  • Facial artery
  • Marginal mandibular nerve
Indications
  • Segmental mandibulectomy = cancer invasion into the cortex or deeper, cancer abutting diseased dentition
Complications
  • Injfection
  • dental malocclusion
  • Nonunion
  • Dysphagia, dysarthria
  • Aspiration
Alternatives
  • Radiation, chemoradiation
Technique 
  • Tracheostomy
  • Mark cancer with 1-2 cm margins
  • Often a lip splitting incision with concurrent neck dissection incision.
  • Make intramural incisions along the gigivolabial and buccal sulcus and sacrifice the mental nerve
  • Carry the dissection along the mandible to the anterior aspect of the messier muscle. Identify the marginal branch of the facial nerve as well as the branches of the facial artery.
  • Consider preplanning the mandible
  • Determine the osteotomy sites, remove teeth if necessary. Make sure to extent the anterior margin at least 2cm to include the mental foramen. Use saw to complete anterior and posterior osteotomies.
  • Complete mucosal incisions to excise tumor.
  • Perform neck dissection
  • Reconstruct

fields.value: The ~30 dB figure represents impedance-matching/transformer gain from the TM-to-stapes area ratio (~25 dB) + ossicular lever (~2 dB). Rhinoplasty
If a bony hump is removed, the patient is left with a(n) {{c1::open roof deformity}} that must be closed by medializing the lateral osteotomies.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: A {{c1::rocker deformity}} results when the medial osteotomy creates a cephalic fracture higher in the thicker part of the frontonasai junction

fields.name: Extra

fields.value:
Major nasal tip support mechanisms
  1. {{c1::Strength of the lower lateral cartilage}}
  2. {{c2::Attachment of the medial crura to the septum}}
  3. {{c3::Attachment of the upper lateral cartilage to the lower lateral cartilage (scroll region)}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
These somewhat correspond to the ligaments within the area
  • pitanguys ligament, septocolumellar ligament, scroll ligament - https://academic.oup.com/asj/article/38/4/357/4816879
Minor tip support mechanisms
  1. Dorsal septum
  2. Intermodal ligaments
  3. membranous septum
  4. Nasal spine
  5. Surrounding skin and soft tissue
  6. Alar sidewalls

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A(n) {{c1::inverted V}} deformity is when the nasal bones are wider than the upper lateral cartilage

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
It is the result of a dorsal resection without providing support to the midvault. The attachment between the ULC's and the nasal bones are disrupted
Treated with providing this support, often by using spreader grafts to the cartilaginous dorsum

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A(n) {{c1::polybeak}} deformity is dorsal fullness and can result from over-resection of the nasal bones, under-resection of the cartilaginous septum, or scarring of the supratip region and is treated with steroid injection in the case of scarring or secondary rhinoplasty to address the anatomic cause

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: {{c1::Bossae}}—are the result of irregularities in the tip cartilages, which can be symmetric or asymmetric and visible. These are treated with secondary rhinoplasty to address the specific cause of the bossae.

Anatomy
  • Glabella
  • Nasion/radix
  • Rhinion
  •  Supratip
  • Tip
  •  Infratip lobule
  • Anterior septal angle
  • Posterior septal angle
  • Head of inferior turbinate
  • Septum (cartilaginous and bony)
  • Nasal bones
  • Upper lateral cartilages
  • Lower lateral cartilages
  • Maxillary spine
  • Nasal-columellar angle
  • Columellar artery off the superior labial artery offf the facial artery

Indications
  • Improve appearance of nose
  • Improve function of the nose (septorhinoplasty)

Contraindications
  • Medical commorbidities
  • Unrealistic patient expectations
  • Active nasal vasoconstrictor use

Complications
  • Valve collapse (manipulation of the lower lateral cartilages)
  • scarring
  • Epistaxis
  • Septal perforation
  • CSF leak

Alternatives
  • Hyaluronic acid fillers

Technique 
  1. Inject local
  2. Open the nose by making incisions in the lateral crura and transversely along the collumela
  3. Dissect tissue off of the crura to the upper lateral cartilage and then to the nasion
  4. Dissect the medial crura and retract them laterally to expose the caudal septum.
The rest of the technique is dictated by what the patient needs to have done to have an aesthetic nose. See the linked videos above.

At the conclusion of the procedure, reap proximate the skin and suture.

{{c1::Index}}
Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Paramedian Forehead Flaps

Operative Videos: Paramedian Forehead Flap for Nasal Reconstruction

Anatomy
  • Supratrochelar artery (1.25-1.5 cm lateral to the midline at the orbital rim, superficial to the corrugated supercilious and deep to the orbiculares oculi and frontal muscles, pierces the frontal muscle to become subcutaneous 1 to 2.5 cm superior to the orbital rim)
  • Corrugator supercillii
  • Orbicularis oculi
  • Frontalis
Indications
  • Năsal cutaneous defects
  • Some periorbital and cheek defects

Contraindications
  • Significant scarring, previous radiation to the forehead, active smoking

Complications
  • Flap loss, hematoma, infection, scalp numbness (the supratrochelear and supraorbital nerves), brow/hariline distortion

Technique 
  • Localize the supratrochlear artery
  • Outline the flap with a marker
  • Make a template of the flap
  • Procedures are often staged, so the incision will include full thickness of the frontal muscle at the distal end fo the flap
  • Inset flap into the nasal defect
  • The pedicle will need to be divided at a later stage after neovascularization has occurred.
  • Close the donor site primarily (generally)

fields.value: The supratrochlear artery exits the supratrochlear foramen {{c2::1}} cm medial to the supraorbital foramen and {{c1::1.7-2.2}} cm from midline and pierces the orbital septum, courses within the {{c3::corrugator}} and deep to the {{c3::orbicularis}} muscles and then pierces the {{c4::orbicularis}} and {{c4::frontalis}} muscle at the level of the {{c5::brow}} to run subcutaneously

fields.value: In the {{c1::extended deep plane}} face lift, inferior dissection continues to the border of the {{c2::mandible}} and {{c3::the cervical retaining}} ligaments are released.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Think of the cervical retaining ligaments as little fibrous tethers holding the platysma down to the deeper neck.
Normally you have:
skin → fat → platysma → deep cervical fascia/muscles
The platysma isn't just freely sliding over everything underneath it. Along its lateral/posterior portion, near the anterior border of the SCM, fibrous connections run between the platysma and the deep cervical fascia:
Platysma
↕️ cervical retaining ligaments

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Face lift

Operative Videos: Extended Deep Plane Facelift

Anatomy
  • Skin: laxity and rhytids
  • Muscles: zygomaticus major and minor, masseter, platysma, orbicularis oculi, frontalis, procerus, corrugator supercili, orbicularis oris, masseter, depressor anguli oris, sternocleidomastoid, temporalis
  • Distribution of adipose tissue
  • Nerves: facial nerve-temporalis, zygomaticus, buccal, marginal, cervical, greater auricular, trigeminal-supraorbital, infraorbital, supratroclear, mentalis
  • Vessels: facial artery and vein, superficial temporal artery and vein, jugular vein, external and internal, carotid artery
  • Salivary glands: submandibular gland, parotid gland, and Stensen duct
  • Skeletal: cervicomental angle, mandible, zygoma, mastoid, frontal bone, zygomatic arch
  • Retaining ligaments: zygomatic, masseter, mandibular, parotid

Contraindications
  1. The overly narcissistic patient
  2. The single immature male who is obsessive neurotic (SIMON) patient
  3. The body dysmorphic patient
  4. The unstable patient undergoing major lifestyle changesâ€”for example, loss of job, divorce
  5. The culturally estranged patientâ€”desires major change to alter natural culture features
  6. The exceptionalism patientâ€”the patient who refuses to talk to staff, fill out paperwork, refuses to follow medical instructions, overly demanding
  7. The unrealistic patientâ€”brings photos of his or her youthâ€”wedding photo, graduation photoâ€”and expects to have the surgeon recreate
  8. The multiply operated patientâ€”lavishes praise on you and denigrates prior surgeons

Complications/errors in technique
  • Hematoma, damage to great auricular nerve, altered hairline, injury to Stenson duct, injury to accessory nerve, injury to facial nerve, cobra neck deformity

Technique 
Largely dependent on the approach used. In general:
  1. Make initial incision
  2. Design flap, elevate to the facial nerve using dissecting scissors
  3. Undermine the skin in the cheek and neck area to avoid tension and the risk of a pixie ear deformity
  4. Consider removing excess adipose tissue of the flap
  5. Decide on imbrication or plication

S lift
UOM purse string sutures to secure the lateral and vertical SMASectomies as well as the molar fat pad.

Deep plane face lift
  • Uses deep plane face lift in sub-SMAS dissection plane in the lower face as well as a supra-SMAS dissection plane in the upper cheek.
  • Plane of dissection is superficial to the zygomaticus major and minor muscles
  • The zygomatic cutaneous ligaments are released at McGregor’s patch.
  • Anchor the flap to the deep temporal fascia in the preauricular area
  • In the extended deep plane face lift, inferior dissection continues to the border of the mandible and the cervical retaining ligaments are released.

Background
Nasal fractures should be reduced within 2 weeks of the time of injury

What key features need to be evaluated in nasal trauma?
External exam: deformity, mobility, step-offs, and telecanthus
Internal exam: septal deviation, mucosal tears, septal hematoma, CSF leak

In acute setting, the fracture can be reduced 1 to 2 hours following the fracture or after swelling has subsided (5-10 days).
Chronic nasal fractures (>10 days) may require full healing (3-6 months) followed by a formal septorhinoplasty

Anatomy
  • Nasal bones

Indications
Closed reduction
  • Unilateral or bilateral nasal bone fracture without significant dislocation
Open Reduction
  • Extension fractures with dislocation
  • Open septal fracture or persistent deviation following closed reduction

Contraindications
  • Isolated nasal fracture repair in context of severe nasoethmoid complex fracture.

Complications/errors in technique
  • Septal hematoma, epistaxis, infection, facial edema, CSF leak
  • Unfavorable cosmetic appearance

Technique 
Closed
  • Palpate nasal bones
  • Perform endonasal exam
  • Measure the distance between the superior aspect of the nasal bones and the external nasal valve
  • Reduce

Open
See septorhinoplasty note

Operative Videos: 
Open Reduction and Internal Fixation for Parasymphyseal Mandibular Fracture
Open Reduction and Internal Fixation (ORIF) of Mandibular Angle Fracture with Champy Plate

Assessment
  • Laterality, subside of mandible, type of fracture (simple/comminuted, open), if mandibular angle: whether the fracture is favorable or unfavorable.
  • Numbness of the skin (damage to V3 and more common in parasympheal fractures)

Background
  • Fractures of the mandibular angle have the highest rate of complication due to proximity to inferior alveolar nerve and the masseteric and facial vessels
  • If patient is edentulous, you need to use rigid fixation. You cannot use load sharing devices because edentulous jaws have poor cross sectional rigidity
  • Angle system of occlusion: Class 1 = normal, Class 2 = retrognathia, class 3 = prognathia

Anatomy
  • Marginal mandibular nerve
  • Cervical nerve
  • Mental nerve
  • Dental roots
  • Facial artery/vein
  • Tail of parotid
  • Attachment site of geniglossus
  • Platysma

Indications
Any mandibular angle fracture needs operative repair
ORIF Condyle Fractures
  1. Displacement into the middle cranial fossa
  2. Difficulty establishing dental occlusion with closed treatment
  3. Lateral extra capsular displacement of the condyle
  4. Presence of a foreign body
  5. Open fracture

In general
  • Restore facial form/function
  • Restore occlusion
  • Restore mandibular ROM
  • Reduce fracture to stop bleeding

Contraindications
  • Neurologically unstable, hemodynamically unstable, acute infection

Complications
  • Loss of tooth vitality, malocclusion, exposure of hardware, non-union, paresthesias, infection, bleeding.

Alternative
  • No surgical intervention in non displaced fracture without evidence of malocclusion in a patient that is willing to be compliant with a liquid diet

Technique 
Dentoalveolar fractures
  1. Reimplant teeth within 1 hour
  2. Make sure there are no foreign bodies
  3. Reduce fracture and splint for 2-3 weeks

Symphysis/Parasymphysis Fracture (Maxillomandibular fixation [MMF] or ORIF)
  1. If the fracture line is appropriately reduced, use MMF
  2. Otherwise, make vestibular incision 8-10mm below the mucogingival junction for ORIF
  3. Expose the fracture and reduce it
  4. Place tension plate and insert mono cortical screws 2-2.5 cm below the incise edges of the incisors.

Mandibular Body Fractures
  1. Determine optimal occlusion. 
  2. If non-displaced, can be treated with MMF for 6 weeks
  3. Otheris make transoral incision 8-10 mm below the mucogingival junction.
  4. Identify and skeletonize the mental nerve
  5. Apply tension band and Place two mono cortical screws on either side of the fracture.
  6. Screw in the fracture plate with minimum two bicrotical screws on either side of the fracture

Angle Fractures
  1. Can be done intraoral or extraoral
  2. Dissect carefully to avoid the marginal mandibular and cervical branches of the facial nerve if using extraoral technique
  3. Place tension band superiorly and fixate with two monocrotical screws on either side of the fracture. Secure fracture plate on the inferior border with 2-3 bicortical screws on either side of the fracture

Condylar/Subcondylar fracture
  1. Unless the condylar head is dislocated, can be managed with MMF
  2. Often use a submandibular incision along with a preauricular incision to get exposure to the fracture

Ramus Fracture
  1. Treat with MMF for 4 weeks
  2. ORIF if significant malocclusion or facial asymmetry is present using a submandibular or retromandibular incision.

Atrophic mandible fractures
  1. Can do extraoral or transoral
  2. The inferior alveolar nerve can be closer to the superior aspect of the alveolar crest
  3. Must be rigidly fixed with a 2.0mm plat or compression plate
  4. Wound dehiscence is common

Suggested Reading: Operative Otolaryngology: Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Therapy

Operative Videos:
Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulator Implantation via Two Incision Approach
Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulator Implantation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea

Background
  • Neuromuscular control of breathing. Afferents from the pharynx through he superior laryngeal nerve to the nucleus solitaires. Efferents form the hypoglossal nerve motor nucleus to the genioglossus.
  • Outcomes are better in patients with an anterior-posterior pattern of collapse and worse in patients with a complete circumferential pattern.
  • MRI is currently contraindicated
  • Medial branch innervates the geniohyoid and genioglossus muscles. The lateral branch innervates the styloglossus and hyoglossus muscles.

Anatomy
  • Digastric tension and submandibular gland
  • Mylohyoid muscle
  • Hyoglossus muscles
  • Hypoglossal nerve
  • Pectorals fascia
  • 5th or 6th intercostal space, external intercostal muscle, superior border of the rib

Indications
  • Moderate to severe OSA after failure of positive pressure therapy in patients that are not severely obese
  • Have undergone a drug induced sedated endoscopy (DISE)

Complications
  • Bleeding
  • Injury to CNXII or marginal branch of CNVII
  • Pneumothorax
  • Inadequate sensor placement
  • Device malfunction

Technique 
  • Typically right side with mostly standard submandibular incision
  • Pulse generator is placed ipsilateral to planned neck incision ~4cm below the clavicle and medial to the deltopectoral groove
  • Sensing need is placed ipsilaterally overlying the 5th-6th rib space at the intersection of the anterior axillary line and the nipple line
Cuff
  1. Carry incision through he platysma to expose the junction of the digastric tendon and the atneroinferior border of the submandibular gland
  2. Retract the gland and the free edge of the mylohyoid to expose the floor of the submandibular triangle to expose the hypoglossal nerve
  3. Clamp and divide the ranine vein
  4. Exclude the retractor branches of the XII nerve (lateral branches) which are located superiorly to the protrusion branches (medial branch). 
  5. Place the cuff around the distal protrusion branches and secure it to the digastric tendon. Consider including C1 in the cuff.
Pulse Generator
  1. Make incision as specified above and create a subcutaneous pocket. Then place the generator.
Respiratory sensor
  1. Make incision at location specified above.
  2. Carry the dissection to the chest wall and stay inferior to the pec and anterior to the stratus until you reach the external intercostal muscle. 
  3. Place the sensor into a tunnel between the external and intercostal muscles.

Confirm the device is functioning
Get post-op radiographs

Drug-Induced Sleep State Endoscopy (DISE) for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Evaluation

Background
  • DISE is more accurate than the Muller maneuver
  • DISE resembles non-REM rapid eye movement sleep
  • An inferiorly positioned hyoid bone greater than two finger breadths below the mandibular pane is evidence of an unfavorably elongated airway.
  • VOTE (velum, oropharyngeal lateral walls, tongue, epiglottis)

Anatomy
  • Velum
  • Salphingopharyngeus
  • Palatopharyngesus
  • Palatoglossus
  • Palatine tonsils
  • Tongue
  • Larynx
  • Jaw
  • Nasal airway

Indications
  • During nasal surgery to evaluate for persistent collapse
  • To evaluate for candidacy for hypoglossal nerve stimulation therapy
  • Pediatric patients with persistent OSA after adenotonsillectomy

Complications
  • Mucosal irritation and bleeding
  • Oversedation

Technique 
  1. Give glycopyrolate pre op to reduce oronasal secretions
  2. Pass scope through nasal cavity
  3. Ensure correct depth of sedation (unresponsive to verbal commands and signs of periodic obstructive breathing.) Observe for paradoxical breathing
  4. Assess laxity of the jaw
  5. Observe each location for at least two respiratory cycles.
  6. Read the VOTE article above for more detail on what to assess

Operative Videos:
Sistrunk Procedure for Excision of a Thyroglossal Duct Cyst

Background
  • Differential includes dermoid, lymph node, lipoma, hemangioma, radula, and inflammatory lesion.
  • Most are present at the level of the thyrohyoid membrane but can also be found in the supra hyoid location  or at the level of the hyoid.
  • Usually 1-2 cm but can be up to 10 cm
  • Dx with US

Anatomy
  • Foramen cecum
  • Hyoid bone
  • Thyroid notch
  • Cricoid cartilage
  • Lingual artery
  • Pharynx
  • Vallecula
  • Floor of tongue (take 1 cm cuff of tongue tissue posterior to the hyoid bone)
  • Hypoglossal nerves
  • Superior laryngeal nerves

Indications
  • Midline mass in the neck
  • Recurrent infections
  • Failed prior resections or incision and drainage procedures

Complications
  • Recurrence
  • hemorrhage from the lingual artery
  • Hematoma/infeciton
  • Pharyngocutaneous fistula

Alternative
  • Slcerotherapy

Technique 
  1. Transverse incision in neck crease
  2. Identify the cyst
  3. Grasp the hyoid and skeletonize it
  4. Transect the affected hyoid with a bone cutter
  5. Reapproximate the straps
  6. Close skin

Suggested Reading: 
Operative Otolaryngology: Total Glossectomy

Relevant Anatomy
  • Lingual artery
  • Lingual nerve
  • Mylohyoid line
  • Insertion of genioglossus onto superior genial tubercle
  • Insertion of geniohyoid onto the inferior genial tubercle
  • Insertion of digastric onto mandible
  • Sublingual salivary glands
  • Pre-epiglotic space
  • Hyoid bone
  • Superior laryngeal neves
  • Mental Nerve

Indications
  • Advanced cancers of the tongue

Contraindications
  • Medically unfit
  • Unable to achieve clear margins
  • Distant mets

Alternatives
  • Radiation
  • Palliative care

Complications
  • Hematoma
  • Flap loss
  • Dysphagia/aspiration

Steps
  1. Panendoscopy
  2. Temporary Trach
  3. Open neck and perform neck dissections
  4. Incise the mandibular periosteum
  5. Transect the anterior bellies of the digastric and divide the mylohyoid
  6. Strip tissues from the inner aspect of the mandible
  7. Free the geniohyoid from its insertion
  8. Start mandibulectomy
  9. Resect the cancer with sufficient margins and deliver the mandible, floor of mouth, and tongue as one unit
  10. Reconstruct (see flap procedures). The reconstruction should be convex in shape to prevent forming a sump where food can collect.
  11. Suspend the hyoid bone from the anterior arch of the mandible with two non absorbable sutures

Post-Op
  • Abx x 24 hrs
  • Flap monitoring
  • Remove drains when adequate
  • Trach cares
  • Enteral feeding until decannulated
  • Speech/swallow eval
  • Chemorads within 6 weeks

Relevant Anatomy
  • The level of the floor of the anterior cranial fossa corresponds with anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina along the frontoethmoidal suture line
  • There is 5-11 mm between the posterior ethmoidal foramen/artery and the optic nerve/optic foramen

    • Infraorbital artery (in the infraorbital groove and with the infraorbital nerve)
    • Sphenopalatine artery (through sphenopalatine foramen)

      • Posterior septal artery (crosses above the posterior china)

  • Internal Carotid artery

    • Posterior ethmoid
    • Ophthalmic artery
  • V2 through the foramen rotunda into the pteryopalatine fossa

Background

  • OSA is not caused or exacerbated by ankyloglossia

All are rare

Cummings Pediatric Otolaryngology: Velopharyngeal Dysfunction

Operative Video
Pharyngeal Flap for Velopharyngeal Insufficiency
Sphincter Pharyngoplasty Video 1
Sphincter Pharyngoplasty Video 2


Background
  • /n/, /m/, and /ng/ are phonemes that require nasal air escape. (nasal phonemes)
  • Incompetence of the velopharyngeal mechanism leads to hypernasality
  • Nasal obstruction leads to hyponasality
  • The velopharynx most commonly closes in a coronal pattern
  • Cleft palate is the most common congenital anatomic condition affecting velopharyngeal function
  • Velopharyngeal insufficiency is structural defects that result in insufficient tissue to accomplish closure
  • Velopharyngeal incompetence is impairment of motor control
  • Velopharyngeal misleading is from factors independent of structural defects or neuromotor pathology
  • Children with VPD of unknown etiology should be tested for 22q11.2 deletion with FISH and microarray testing.
  • Facial grimacing is often seen during production of oral phonemes in patients with VPD.
  • Speech endoscopy is the first line assessment tool for BPD.
  • Speech therapy is best used in patients with mild or intermittent VPD

Relevant Anatomy
  • Tensor veli palatini
  • Levator veli palatini (main muscle mass of the velum, pulls palate up)
  • Musculus uvulae
  • Palatoglossus (pull palate down)
  • Palatopharyngeus (pull palate down, widens the velum)
  • Superior pharyngeal constrictor (contributes to lateral wall motion)
  • Passavant ridge (uppermost fibers of the superior constrictor and palatopharyngeus muscles)

Indications
  • Structural causes of VPD
  • VPD persisting after speech therapy

Complications
  • OSAS, bleeding, infection, damage to nearby structures, post-op dysphagia

Techniques
  • Intravelar veloplasty
  • Furlow double-opposing z-plasty
  • Sphincter pharyngoplasty
    • Decreased risk of post-op airway obstruction compared to other techniques
    • Best suited for coronal and circular closure patterns.
    • Flaps from either side of the lateral pharyngeal wall are based and inserted into an incision on the posterior nasopharyngeal wall.
    • The posterior incision is made at the level of maximal palatal excursion.
    • The lateral flaps may include the palatopharyngeal muscle or the constrictor muscles
  • Pharyngeal flap
    • Brings posterior wall tissue to the center and leaves lateral ports on either side.
    • Best for sagittal or circular VPD patterns
    • Elevate in the prevertebral fascial plane
  • Posterior Wall Augmentation

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
A Randomized Trial of Adenotonsillectomy for Childhood Sleep Apnea (CHAT) - Marcus 2013
  • School aged (5-9)
  • Early T&A versus watchful waiting
  • Severe OSAS, extreme obesity, recurrent tonsillitis, and meds for ADHD were excluded
  • Endpoints were executive function, teacher behavior ratings, beds sleeps questionnaire, QOL questionnaire, and sleep study results
  • OAI<1 post op 79% vs 46% 
  • AHI -1.6 vs -3.5 from baseline post-operatively

fields.name: Text

What is the name of the trial(s) that investigated the role of T&A for recurrent strep pharyngitis?
{{c1::Paradise}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Efficacy of Tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection in severely affected children - Paradise 1984
  • Criteria
    • 7 in 1, 5 in 2, 3 in 3.
    • Episodes had to show fever, adenopathy, exudate, and/or positive culture in clinical record
    • Significantly fewer throat infections in the 1 and 2 year follow up groups (3 versus 1.2 and 2.66 versus 1.61)
Tonsillectomy and Adenotonsillectomy for Recurrent Throat infections in Moderately Affected Children - Paradise 2002
  • Less stringent criteria than the 1984 trial. This is outlined in the appendix of the paper. There was less stringent # of episodes and less stringent documentation of episodes
  • Two arms of the trial
    • tonsillectomy, adenotonsillectomy, or control
    • adenotonsillectomy or control
  • Significantly fewer episodes of throat infections in the surgical group but the control group also had low incidence of throat infections
  • If patients do not have obstructing adenoids, don’t take them out
  • Use the more stringent criteria from 1984 trial in deciding who gets a tonsillectomy

Bilateral Choanal atresia repair

Background
  • Result of failure of the nasobuccal membrane to rupture in the fifth and sixth weeks of development
  • 1 in 5000 to 1 in 8000 live births
  • Most common on the right side
  • 75% of patients with bilateral disease have underlying congenital anomalies (CHARGE, polydactyly, Crouzon syndrome, etc)
  • Diagnosed clinically by failure to pass a 6Fr catheter through the nose
  • Unilateral presents later in life while bilateral presents in the neonatal period. 
  • Treatment of unilateral atresia can be delayed for several months. Bilateral atresia requires acute intervention

Relevant Anatomy
  • Vomer
  • Ptyergoid bone
  • Middle turbinate

Complications
  • Bleeding, synechiae, recurrence

{{c1::Index}}
Cummings Pediatric otolaryngology: Diagnosis and Management of Tracheal Anomalies and Tracheal Stenosis

Suggested Reading: 
Operative Otolaryngology: Surgery for Aspiration; Laryngeal Cleft Repair and Laryngotracheal Separation

Operative Video
Animation Video

Background
  • The majority of cases of pediatric dysphagia are neurological in nature
  • Incidence is 1:10,000-1:20,000 newborns.
  • Laryngeal clefts are the result of incomplete development and fusion of the tracheoesophageal septum.
  • The Benjamin Inglis System is the most commonly used classification system for Laryngeal clefts.
  • Presentation in grades 1 and 2 are subtle (hoarseness, mild stridor, chronic cough, URI, recurrent pneumonia). Grades 3 and 4 are more obvious.
  • Are associated with Optiz-Frias, Pallister Hall Syndrome, VACTERL, and CHARGE

Technique
Type 1: Injection augmentation (can be used to diagnose type I clefts when a temporary substance is used)
  • Insert needle into the apex of the cleft, bevel aimed posteriorly
  • Inject until the notch is reduced, do not overinject as this can cause airway compromise or dysphagia
  • Monitor overnight, consider using steroids
Type 1 and 2: Endoscopic
  • Incise cleft with laser or knife
  • Use scissors to achieve appropriate depth
  • Suture the left esophageal flap to the right esophageal flap
  • Suture the left laryngeal flap to the right laryngeal flap
  • Observe overnight and give 24 horus of steroids
Type 3 and 4: Open
  • Horizontal skin incision then divide down to airway at midline.
  • Dissect superiorly to expose the thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage
  • Open the airway vertically
  • Incise the cleft bilaterally form the inferior aspect of the arytenoids to the apex of the cleft and dissect in the anterior laryngotracheal mucosal plan and pharyngoesophageal mucosal plane.
  • Close the posterior plane with sutures
  • Place rib graft in anterior plane then suture into place

Suggested Reading: 
Operative Otolaryngology: Rib Graft

Operative Video
Rib Graft

Background
  • Most commonly harvested form the fifth, sixth, and seventh ribs
  • Harvest alternative bones rather than sequential
  • Eval for injury to the parietal pleura and pneumothorax before closure
  • Can harvest bone (calvarial recon), costal cartilage (LTR, microtia, rhinoplasty[columellar struts, spreader grants, dorsal grafts]), or composite grafts (mandibular condyle and TMJ arthroplasty)
  • Cartilage can warp 0-25%

Contraindications
Concomitant lung disease

Complications
  • Pneumothorax
  • Injury to surrounding vessels and nerves
  • Scarring
  • Chest wall deformity

Anatomy
  • manubriosternal junction is the location of the second rib
  • Costal margin
  • Breast fold in females to hide the incision

Technique
  1. Incise thought eh superficial thoracic fascia directly down to the rib
  2. If harvesting cartilage, incise fascia and retrace the muscle of the rectus abdominis laterally.
  3. Incise rib longitudinally over the central portion of the rib. The final incision should look like an “H”
  4. Rase the periosteum and perichondrium off of the anterior rib
  5. Free graft using elevators and knife
  6. Check for pleural tears
  7. Close (may place suction drain)

Operative Otolaryngology: Dysfunction of the Upper Esophageal Sphincter

Operative Video
Open Repair of Zenker’s Diverticulum

Background
  • Pharynx innervated by the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves
  • Cricopharyngeus normally relaxes during swallowing
  • False diverticulum
  • Can be due to failure of cricopharyngeal relaxation or poor elevation of the laryngeal complex
  • Dysphagia to solids more than liquids

Indications
  • Moderate to severe dysphagia symptoms wit poor UES opening on modified barium swallow

Contraindications
  • Diffuse pharyngeal motor abnormalities and poor anteroom superior laryngeal elevation (think of comorbid conditions such as ALS, Parkinson’s, etc)
  • Conditions affecting the opening of the lower esophageal springer (achalasia, structure)
  • Uncontrolled GERD

Complications
  • Bleeding, infection (mediastinitis), salivary leak or fistula

Anatomy

  • Zenker diverticulum is posterior to esophagus between the inferior pharyngeal constrictor (superiorly) and cricopharyngeus (inferiorly)
  • Lainer diverticulum is posterior to esophagus and inferior to the cricopharyngeus
  • Killian Jamison is lateral to esophagus and inferior to cricpoharyngeus
  • Cricoid cartilage marks the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle
  • RLN relative to the cricothyoird joint
  • Cricopharyngeus muscle has horizontal orientation of fibers. Inferior pharyngeal constrictor are oblique fibers

Suggested Reading: 
Operative Otolaryngology: Surgical Management of Hereditary Hemorrhagic telangiectasia

Operative Video
Coblation of HHT

Background
  • Autosomal dominant disorder
  • Dx using the Curacao criteria
  • Most common Ssx is recurrent epistaxis
  • Can use the epistaxis severity score to get a sense of epistaxis

Indications
  • severe, recurrent, debilitating epistaxis refractory to conservative medical management such as humidification and nasal emollients 
  • severe, recurrent epistaxis requiring blood transfusions

Contraindications
  • Medical comorbidities
  • Optimize other medical morbidities such as hypertension and coagulopathy

Anatomy
  • Common sites to AVMs oar the nasal septum, inferior turbinate, floor of nasal cavity, and head of the middle turbinate
  • Preserve the perichondrium in septodermoplasty

Technique
Coagulation
  • Best for limited telangectasias
  • Can use bipotlar or laser (Nd:YAG, KTP, diode, or argon can be used)
  • Coblation mimeses injury to surrounding tissues by emitting a radio frequency that excites electrolytes in a conductive medium and forms a plasma field at temperature between 40 and 70 celsius.
Septodermoplasty
  • Best when a patient continues to have severe epistaxis after laser or radiofrequncy coagulation has been attempted.
  • Get STSG from donor site
  • Remove the septal mucosa with a microdebrider making sure to preserve the perichondrium
  • Insert the STSG intranasally and suture in.
Young Procedure
  • 80% of patients have complete cessation of epistaxis but need to give up breathing through their nose
  • Elevate alar mucosa flaps and suture them together at the midline of the nare


Complications
  • Septal perforation if ablate/coagulate bilaterally
  • bleeding
  • graft loss in septodermoplasty if perichondrium is not preserved
  • synechiae
  • dehiscence of closure in Young procedure

External dacryostorhinostomy

Background
  • In newborns and infants, the most common site of obstruction is distally at the valve of Hasner. This will resolve by age 6-12
  • Excessive tearing can be caused by hypersecration or impaired drainage
  • Physical obstruction may occur at the level of the punctum, canaliculus, common canaliculus, lacrimal sac, or nasolacrimal duct. The latter two account for about 74% of lacrimal outflow obstructions and are treated with greater than 90% success by external DCR surgery.

Indications
  • Acquired obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct
  • Acute dacryocystitis with an abscess unresponsive to antibiotic therapy

Contraindications
  • Mass is suspected or found at surgery

Anatomy
  • Nasolacrimal but is located beneath the inferior turbinate
  • Upper system (puncture, canaliculus, and common canaliculus)
  • Anterior lacrimal crest is the anteriormost border of the orbit and part of the ascending process of the maxilla
  • Nasal osmium should be made just anterior to the tip of the middle turbinate
  • bone removal should not proceed more than 2mm above the medial cantonal tendon

Complications
  • Erosion of lacrimal punch due to placing silk suture to deep and thus too much tension on the silicone stent
  • damage to the ncanalicular mucosa due to failure to put lateral traction on the eylid while passing a lacrimal probe.
  • CSF leak if the bone punch is twisted when directed superiorly

Operative Otolaryngology: Excision of Submandibular Gland

Operative Video
Submandibular Gland Excision

Background
  • Located in submandibular triangle
  • Excretory but is the Wharton’s duct which passes deep to the mylohyoid and parallels the course of the lingual nerve
  • The narrowest point of the submandibular duct is at the orifice
  • 80% of salivary calculi are found in Wharton’s duct
  • Most stones are calcium phosphate but you can see uric acid calculi in patients with gout
  • 90% of stones are radiopaque
  • Glands become ptotic with age

Indications
  • Neoplasm or suspected neoplasm
  • Sialolithiasis when sialoendscopy does not work (if the stone is in the gland parenchyma)
  • Chronic sialorrhea in patients with neuromuscular swallowing disorders

Contraindications
  • Acute infection

Anatomy
  • marginal mandibular nerve
  • Hayes-Martin maneuver is elevating the facial vein over the marginal mandibular nerve to protect it
  • Anterior belly of digastric
  • Mylohyoid muscle (the lingual nerve and Wharton’s duct lie immediately deep)
  • Nerve to mylohyoid
  • Lingual nerve
  • Facial artery
  • hypoglossal nerve

Complications
  • Marg injury
  • retained calculi if there is not dissection of Wharton’s duct all the way to the floor fo the mouth
  • Bleeding
  • Lingual nerve injury (leads to loss of sensation of the tongue)
  • Hypoglossal nerve injury

{{c1::Limberg}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
It is a transposition flap. It is differentiated from a Dufourmental flap in that it is constructed of equal length segments of 2 120° and 2 60° angles.

Advantages: better distrubtion of tension
Disadvantage: forces a facial defect into an arbitrary design
Common Use: cheek, temple

  • Type: Rhombic transposition flap
  • Geometry: Rhombus with 60° and 120° angles; all sides equal
  • Design: Flap extends from the short diagonal; flap sides equal the sides of the defect
  • Movement: Flap transposes/pivots into the primary defect; donor site closed primarily
  • Tension: Greatest closure tension occurs at the donor site, approximately 20° from the short diagonal across the flap base
  • Key planning principle: Choose the flap orientation based on skin mobility and extensibility so donor-site tension falls in the most favorable direction
  • Undermining: Wide surrounding undermining has minimal effect on wound-closure tension
  • Advantage: Recruits adjacent similar tissue while redirecting tension away from the primary defect
  • Pearl: Multiple Limberg flap designs are geometrically possible → choose the one with the best donor-site laxity and scar orientation

  • Can be designed four different ways

fields.value: {{c1::Alexander's}} Law states that a pathologic peripheral nystagmus intensity will increase when gaze is in the direction of the fast phase and slow when in the direction of the slow phase

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Alexander is intense


Right vestibular neuritis

Ewald’s laws → Why does it beat LEFT?
The horizontal semicircular canals work as a push-pull pair. For the horizontal canal, ampullopetal endolymph flow is excitatory, and excitation produces a stronger response than inhibition.
Normally, the right and left sides have balanced tonic firing.
With right vestibular neuritis:
↓ right vestibular firing → unopposed relative LEFT-sided activity
Functionally, the CNS interprets this asymmetry as leftward head rotation.
Ewald's principles predict the VOR associated with that apparent leftward rotation:
Relative LEFT excitation
→ eyes driven slowly RIGHT
→ corrective saccade LEFT
→ LEFT-beating nystagmus
Remember, nystagmus is named by the fast phase.
Alexander’s law → Why does it get worse looking LEFT?
Alexander's law says:
Vestibular nystagmus becomes stronger when the patient looks in the direction of the FAST phase.
The fast phase in this patient is LEFT.
Therefore:
Look LEFT → stronger left-beating nystagmus
Look straight → less intense
Look RIGHT → weakest

Put them together

Ewald explains the direction; Alexander explains the gaze dependence.
RIGHT vestibular neuritis
→ ↓ RIGHT vestibular tone
→ relative LEFT vestibular excitation
→ Ewald: apparent LEFT head rotation → slow phase RIGHT → fast phase LEFT
→ LEFT-beating nystagmus
→ Alexander: looking toward the fast phase increases nystagmus
→ worse with LEFT gaze
So the compact rule is:
Weak RIGHT ear → beats LEFT → worse looking LEFT.

fields.value: {{c1::Neoadjuvant}} chemotherapy is chemotherapy given before local treatment modality (surgery, radiation, chemoradiotherapy)

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
aka induction chemotherapy

Advantages: may allow better drug penetration before tumor vascularity becomes impaired from radidation or surgery, may also reduce tumor bulk to make surgery possible
Disadvantache: chemotherapy can increase complications of surgical intervention or radiotherapy

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Concomitant}} therapy is concurrent chemotherapy and radiation

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
either given continuously or interrupted
Advantages: may syndergistically maximize therapeutic effect
Disadvantages: increased side effects

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Adjuvant}} chemotherapy is therapy after primary treatment modality to control microscopic disease.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Generally indicated is locally advanced disease, ENE, positive margins, and/or recurrent
Advantages: may improve survival
Disadvantages: chemotherapy side effects

Reoxygenation
Repopulation
Repair}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• Reassortment: fractionation allows cells to proceed to more
radiosensitive stages in their cell cycle
• Reoxygenation: fractionation allows for reoxygenation of previously
more hypoxic cells (making them more susceptible)
• Repopulation: prolonged waiting between fractions results in
regrowth of tumor cells from sublethal damage
• Repair: normal tissue tends to have better repair than tumor cells,
recovers more quickly from sublethal damage

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In the {{c1::pterygopalatine}} fossa the {{c2::vidian}} nerve gives rise to the {{c1::pterygopalatine}} ganglion

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Pterygopalatine ganglion aka Meckel's ganglion, nasal ganglion, or sphenopalatine ganglion.

Parasympathetic
Superior salivatory nucleus → nervus intermedius (CNVII) → Greater petrosal nerve (in middle ear) → vidian nerve (with deep petrosal nerve) → pterygopalatine ganglion (synapse)

Sympathetic
Superior cervical ganglion → internal carotid artery → deep petrosal nerve → vidian nerve (with greater petrosal nerve) → pterygopalatine ganglion (passes through)
These nerves supply the lacrimal gland, paranasal sinuses, glands of the mucosa of the nasal cavity and pharynx, the gingiva, and the mucous membrane and glands of the hard palate.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c2::vidian}} nerve is made up of the {{c1::greater petrosal and deep petrosal::2}} nerves

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Pterygopalatine ganglion aka Meckel's ganglion, nasal ganglion, or sphenopalatine ganglion.

Vidian contains the greater petrosal and deep petrosal nerves. Only the greater petrosal nerve synapses with the ganglion since it is parasympathatic. The deep petrosal nerve just passess through the ganglion since it is already post-synaptic sympathetic. 

Parasympathetic
Superior salivatory nucleus → nervus intermedius (CNVII) → Greater petrosal nerve (in middle ear) → vidian nerve (with deep petrosal nerve) → pterygopalatine ganglion (synapse)

Sympathetic
Superior cervical ganglion → internal carotid artery → deep petrosal nerve → vidian nerve (with greater petrosal nerve) → pterygopalatine ganglion (passes through)

These nerves supply the lacrimal gland, paranasal sinuses, glands of the mucosa of the nasal cavity and pharynx, the gingiva, and the mucous membrane and glands of the hard palate.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::otic}} ganglion is located immediately below the {{c2::foramen ovale}} in the {{c3::infratemporal fossa}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Provides functional innervation to the parotid gland
Parasympathetic
Inferior salivatory nucleus of CNVIII → tympanic nerve (Jacobson's nerve) → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion (synapse) → auriculotemporal nerve → parotid gland
Sympathetic
superior cervical ganglion (synapse) → middle maningeal artery → otic ganglion (pass through) → auriculotemporal nerve → parotid gland

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Parasympathetic innervation for the {{c1::parotid::parotid or submandibular/sublingual}} gland(s) derives from the {{c2::inferior::inferior/superior}} salivatory nucleus

fields.name: Extra

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:

SSN = superior salivatory nucleus

fields.name: Text
fields.value: From the pterygoplatine ganglion parasympathetic/sympathetic innervation reach the glands of the {{c2::eye, nasal cavity, palate, and pharynx::4}} by jumping onto {{c1::CNV2 (maxillary nerve)}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Lacrimal gland = zygomatic nerve of V2
Nasal gland = nasopalatine nerve of V2
Palatine gland = nasopalatine, gretaer palatine, and lesser palatine of V2
Pharyngeal gland - pharyngeal nerve of V2



Parasympathetic
Superior salivatory nucleus → nervus intermedius (CNVII) → Greater petrosal nerve (in middle ear) → vidian nerve (with deep petrosal nerve) → pterygopalatine ganglion (synapse)

Sympathetic
Superior cervical ganglion → internal carotid artery → deep petrosal nerve → vidian nerve (with greater petrosal nerve) → pterygopalatine ganglion (passes through)

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::submandibular}} ganglion is attached inferiorly to the {{c2::lingual}} nerve

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Parasympathetic
superior salivatory nucleus → nervus intermedius → chorda tympani → chorda tympani/lingual nerve → submandibular ganglion (synapse) → submandibular gland or back to the lingual nerve to connect to the sublingual gland

Sympathetic
Submandibular gland
Superior cervical ganglion (synapse) → external carotid artery → facial artery → submental artery → submandibular gland
Sublingual gland
Superior cervical ganglion (synapse) → external carotid artery → facial artery → submental artery → anastomosis with sublingual artery from the lingual artery → sublingual gland

fields.value:
Rhinoplasty grafts
{{c1::Spreader graft}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
extended spreader grafts can be used for correction of dorsal septal deviation and to provide additional support to patients with saddle nose deformity. They extend past the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage to the anterior septal angle

Traditional spreader grafts are placed between the nasal bones and the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage

Spreader grafts also help to widen the angle of the internal nasal valve and decrease internal nasal valve narrowing

Spreader grafts can also help to fix an inverted V deformity

Need to consider the width of the middle vault to determine whether you need to separate the ULC's from the septum or if you can just creat a pocket for the grafts under each ULC

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Rhinoplasty grafts
{{c1::Lateral crural strut grafts}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Helps to correct a cephalically malpositioned lateral crura ( see red line on image below) where the long axis of the lateral crus is oreinted toward the medial cantus rather than the lateral canthus. This results in a narrow external nasal valve.

LCS grafts can also be used to correct a sagitally oriented lateral crura but the lateral crura must first be separated from the scroll region via cephalic trim.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Sympathetics anatomy
The {{c4::superior cervical ganglion}} is located posteriorly to the {{c3::common carotid}} artery and anterior to the {{c2::C1-4}} vertebrae and just lateral to the {{c1::longus colli}} muscles bilaterally.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The superior cervical ganglia usually lie anteromedial or medial to their respective internal carotid arteries.
They are typically at level C1 and C2 but can be variable.

Branches coming off of the superior cervical ganglia include the:
  • Pharyngeal branch
  • The communicating branch of the cervical nerve
  • The internal carotid branch
  • The communicating branch of the pharyngeal mucosa
  • The communicating branch of the vagus nerve
  • The communicating branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
  • The laryngeal branch
  • The communicating branch of the internal jugular vein

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The Anterior Ethmoid Artery (AEA) typically crosses the ethmoid roof about {{c1::1 cm posterior }} to the frontal recess

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Buzz words are mesentery sign, string of pearls sign

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Endoscopically, the AEA runs {{c1::at or just anterior}} to the superior turbinate attachment to the skull base

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Buzz words are string of pearls sign and mesentery sign

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The AEA lies {{c1::just anterior}} to the basal lamella, marking the transition between anterior and posterior ethmoids.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Buzz words are string of pearls sign and mesentery sign

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The Posterior Ethmoid Artery (PEA) is typically located just anterior to the {{c1::sphenoid face/ostium}} at the skull base.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: The PEA aligns with the {{c1::posterior attachment of the superior turbinate and face of the sphenoid}}

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: The AEA and PEA are generally {{c1::10–12 mm apart::distance}}, which helps orient you during ethmoidectomy progression.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: The {{c1::PEA::AEA/PEA}} is more often enclosed in bone and carries a lower risk of catastrophic orbital hemorrhage if encountered.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: The basal lamella has {{c1::three::#}} components

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: The basal lamella of the middle turbinate has three components: a {{c1::vertical (coronal), oblique, and horizontal.}}

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: Peripheral vestibular lesions typically produce nystagmus that is {{c1::unidirectional}}, meaning it beats in the same direction regardless of the direction of gaze.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze (right-beating in right gaze, left-beating in left gaze) is characteristic of {{c1::central pathology}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Peripheral nystagmus {{c1::suppresses}} with visual fixation

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: whereas central nystagmus does not suppress or may even increase with fixation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: When reading CT for suspected ZMC fracture, start laterally at the {{c1::zygomatic arch / zygomaticofrontal (ZF)}} before focusing on the maxillary sinus.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Seeing a ZF fracture alone should immediately raise concern for a ZMC fracture, even if the arch looks intact.
Think of the zygoma like a table:
  • 4 legs (ZF, rim, buttress, arch)
  • A table does not need all 4 legs broken to collapse
  • Once 2–3 legs are gone, the structure is unstable
ZMC fracture = structural failure, not a checklist injury.

 
ZF suture

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For laser hair removal in Fitzpatrick III–VI skin types, {{c1::Nd:YAG}} is preferred due to lower risk of pigment alteration.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Nd:YAG has a longer wavelength with less epidermal melanin absorption, reducing hypo- and hyperpigmentation risk in darker skin types.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 50}} when performing a truly bilateral procedure in the same session if the CPT code itself is defined as unilateral.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Do not use modifier 50 if the CPT already describes a bilateral procedure. Ask: “Is laterality implied by the code?”

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 24}} for an unrelated E/M service performed by the same physician during a postoperative global period.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This prevents the unrelated E/M from being bundled into the global surgical package.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 57}} when an E/M visit represents the decision for surgery for a major procedure.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Do not use modifier 57 for routine preoperative visits already included in the global package.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Outpatient E/M code families are new patient {{c1::99202–99205}} and established patient 99212–99215.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Higher final digits generally reflect increasing complexity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If it is your first encounter with a patient during a hospitalization, bill {{c1::initial hospital care (99221–99223)}} even if they are an established outpatient.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consult codes are payer-dependent; many Medicare workflows use initial/subsequent hospital care codes instead.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 52}} to indicate reduced services when a procedure is partially reduced or discontinued at the physician’s discretion.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
You bill the full code; the payer determines the payment reduction.

5-2 Reduce

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 62}} when two surgeons perform distinct parts of the same procedure as co-surgeons.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Each surgeon dictates a separate operative note and lists the other as co-surgeon.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 25}} when a significant, separately identifiable E/M service is performed on the same day as a procedure.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Documentation must support a true, separate E/M beyond the procedure itself.
You can only document one CPT coe during an office visit so from a financial perspective you should document the one that bills the highest

ex

Clinic visit + flexible laryngoscopy

  • Patient presents with new hoarseness
  • You:
    • Take a history
    • Perform head & neck exam
    • Develop a differential (reflux vs malignancy)
  • You perform flexible laryngoscopy (minor procedure)

Billing

  • Office visit (9920x/9921x) + modifier 25
  • Flexible laryngoscopy CPT
Again: the E/M is separate and significant, not just “scope-only.”

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 51}} when multiple procedures are performed in the same session, listing procedures from highest to lowest value.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This signals multiple procedures rather than bundled work.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 22}} when procedural work is substantially greater than typically required and documentation supports the added complexity.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The justification lives entirely in the operative note.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Use {{c1::modifier 58}} for a planned, staged, or more extensive related procedure performed during a postoperative global period.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classic example: division and inset following a staged flap reconstruction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Retropharyngeal abscesses often present {{c1::off midline}} due to a midline raphe dividing the retropharyngeal space.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Children have retropharyngeal lymph nodes (nodes of Rouvière) that can suppurate after URI or nasopharyngeal infection.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The clinical hallmark of a {{c1::masticator space}} infection is trismus.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Trismus should immediately raise concern for masticator space involvement, even if you think you are just dealing wiht a run of the mill PTA

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Deep odontogenic infections most commonly arise from {{c1::mandibular molars::specific teeth}} in adults.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: In children, maxillary teeth are relatively more common sources; diabetes is a risk factor.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A walled-off abscess in the labial or buccal gingiva is called a {{c1::parulis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Extension into the alveolar mucosa forms a vestibular space abscess.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Preseptal cellulitis is {{c1::anterior}} to the orbital septum.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
whereas orbital cellulitis is posterior

This distinction drives urgency, imaging, and surgical decision-making.

fields.value: CT temporal bone with contrast showing mastoid air cell opacification with preserved bony septations is consistent with {{c1::uncomplicated (non-coalescent) mastoiditis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Key diagnostic divider: coalescent mastoiditis = bony destruction of mastoid air cell septae. This implies aggressive disease with poor response to antibiotics alone and a low threshold for mastoidectomy. CT (not labs or exam alone) establishes the distinction. Look for terms like “breakdown of septations
Coalescent


Non-coalescent

fields.name: Text
fields.value: CT temporal bone with contrast demonstrating loss of mastoid air cell septations and bony erosion defines {{c1::coalescent mastoiditis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Key diagnostic divider: coalescent mastoiditis = bony destruction of mastoid air cell septae. This implies aggressive disease with poor response to antibiotics alone and a low threshold for mastoidectomy. CT (not labs or exam alone) establishes the distinction. Look for terms like “breakdown of septations or subperiostial abscess" for coalescent
Coalescent


Non-coalescent

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bell’s palsy (clinical definition) should progress to maximum weakness within {{c1::72}} hours; slower progression → work up for other causes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: If slower than 72h: evaluate for alternative etiologies; consider imaging first, then biopsy as indicated.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lower lid: {{c1::arcuate expansion of Lockwood ligament}} separates {{c2::middle and lateral}} fat pads; {{c3::inferior oblique}} separates {{c4::medial and middle}} fat pads.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful intra-op orientation to avoid iatrogenic injury and to identify pads correctly.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common indication for lower blepharoplasty is {{c1::orbital fat pseudoherniation}}.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: Lower bleph does not correct {{c1::malar edema}}, {{c2::midface ptosis}}, or {{c3::fine rhytids}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consider adjuncts (midface lift, resurfacing) when those are the primary complaints.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c2::Transconjunctival::approach}} lower bleph is preferred when pseudoherniation is present with {{c1::no excess skin or muscle}} (no anterior lamellar pathology).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often younger patients; avoids external scar and lowers risk of lid retraction vs transcutaneous.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c4::Transcutaneous}} (skin–muscle flap) lower bleph is indicated when there is {{c1::anterior lamellar pathology}} (excess lower lid {{c2::skin}}, {{c3::muscle}}, or both).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Match approach to lamella that needs correction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Insurance often requires superior visual field loss of about {{c1::20}}%, or {{c2::14}} degrees, for upper bleph coverage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Orbit fat compartments: superior orbit {{c1::central + medial}} (lateral = lacrimal gland); inferior orbit {{c1::medial + central + lateral}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Helps avoid mistaking lacrimal gland prolapse for “lateral fat.”

fields.name: Text
fields.value: MRD1 is distance between {{c1::central corneal light reflex}} and {{c1::upper eyelid margin}}; MRD2 is distance between {{c2::central corneal light reflex}} and {{c2::lower eyelid margin}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: MRD1 + MRD2 approximates palpebral fissure height.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: MRD1 + MRD2 ≈ palpebral fissure height; average is about {{c1::9}} mm.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Leave at least {{c1::20}} mm of upper lid skin (lid margin → brow line/superior orbital rim) to avoid lagophthalmos.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: 20::measure

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Normal lateral canthus is {{c1::2–4}} mm higher than the medial canthus.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ptosis is defined as MRD1 ≤ {{c1::2.5}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Normal MRD is 3-4mm

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Scariest complication after bleph is {{c1::retrobulbar hematoma}} → open incisions + perform {{c2::lateral canthotomy/cantholysis}} to relieve pressure.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Treat as vision-threatening emergency; time-to-decompression matters.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) increases volume by stimulating collagen via {{c1::localized inflammatory response recruiting monocytes/macrophages/fibroblasts}}, not via TGF-β activation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: It is not a scaffold and does not release growth factors (per your note).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Calcium hydroxyapatite (CaHA) fillers provide immediate volume and stimulate collagen production, and {{c1::cannot be dissolved::dissolvable}} by any agent.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: cannot be dissolved::dissolvable? Osteogenesis has not been reported with skin injections (per your note).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: High molecular weight hyaluronic acid (HMWHA) acts as anti-inflammatory and suppresses {{c1::CD44}}; fibroblast stimulation occurs indirectly via cytokines {{c2::IL-4}} and {{c2::IL-13}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mechanism question favorite.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Aminoglycosides}} can potentiate botulinum toxin–induced paralysis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Think NMJ blockade synergy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Botulinum toxin serotypes vary in potency; {{c1::Type A}} is the most potent.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Different serotypes target different synaptic proteins.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Poly-methyl methacrylate (ArteFill)}} requires {{c2::skin testing 1 month prior}} due to {{c3::bovine collagen}} content.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Skin testing addresses hypersensitivity risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::CaHA}} (Radiesse) is contraindicated in the {{c2::glabella, lips, and tear trough::3 regions of face}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Approved for nasolabial folds

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dermal filler longevity/structural integrity are primarily determined by {{c1::degree of molecular cross-linking}} and the presence/amount of {{c2::hyaluronic acid}}

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Filler G’ (G-prime) reflects viscoelasticity; higher G’ = {{c1::denser/sturdier}} filler, lower G’ = {{c2::more flexible/watery}} filler.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Helps match product choice to anatomic plane.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Superficial rhytids are best treated with {{c1::hyaluronic acid filler}} placed in the {{c2::deep papillary or superficial reticular dermis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Plane matters for visibility/Tyndall and contour irregularity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Skin necrosis after filler injection occurs most frequently in the {{c1::glabella}} due to variable dependence on the supratrochlear artery.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Vascular complications with HA have been reported most often in this region

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Brow/forehead subunits: {{c1::central forehead; right lateral temporal; left lateral temporal; right brow; left brow::5}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Your source calls this “5 subunits.”

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Corrugator supercilii is the only muscle of facial expression that {{c1::arises from bone}} (medial supraorbital arch) and inserts into {{c2::frontalis and orbicularis}} → causes vertical/oblique rhytids.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield anatomy + wrinkle pattern linkage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lateral brow ptosis is more pronounced because of paucity of {{c1::lateral frontalis insertion}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Explains “why the tail droops.”

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Before planning surgery, determine whether ptosis is primarily from {{c1::brow}} vs {{c1::upper eyelid}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Prevent wrong operation (bleph when brow lift needed, etc.).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: To achieve a {{c1::10–12}} mm brow lift, often need to resect about {{c2::16}} mm of skin.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Rule-of-thumb planning number; adjust for laxity and vector.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Coronal forehead lift is good for generalized ptosis + upper-face rhytids with {{c1::normal/low}} hairline.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Contraindications: men with male pattern baldness; women with high hairlines. Disadvantages: raises frontal hairline, hypesthesia posterior to incision, possible hair loss if not closed in layers.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Direct brow lift is useful for correcting {{c1::brow asymmetry}} and {{c2::lateral brow ptosis}}, especially in men with bushy eyebrows or unilateral brow ptosis from facial nerve paresis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Tradeoff is visible scar; selection matters.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Endoscopic brow lift advantages: {{c1::smaller incisions}}, less sensory neuropathy/bleeding, faster recovery; disadvantage: {{c2::steeper learning curve}} and need long-term outcome data.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Your note: prospective study showed no significant difference in sensory deficits vs open.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The zygomaticotemporal (sentinel) vein is typically encountered {{c1::5–10}} mm lateral to the zygomaticofrontal suture and is close to the temporal branch of CN VII.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Key hazard structure during brow/temple dissection.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lateral eyebrow hooding is best corrected with a {{c1::brow lift}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
not a blepharoplasty.
Fix the true anatomic cause; avoids under-correction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Concurrent {{c1::blepharoplasty::procedure}} and {{c1::brow lift::procedure}} increases risk of lagophthalmos.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Stage procedures or be conservative with skin resection.
If you dont stage, do the browlift before the blepharoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Jessner’s solution removes the {{c1::stratum corneum}} and diminishes {{c2::intercellular keratinocyte connections}}; used as a {{c3::prepeel}} for medium-depth peels.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Helps even penetration and predictability.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Medium-depth peels treat dyschromias, mild acne scarring, actinic keratoses, fine rhytids; destruction extends into {{c1::papillary dermis and upper reticular dermis}}; commonly uses {{c2::TCA 45–50%}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Different types of peels are not usually performed in a series

fields.name: Text
fields.value: TCA peels use {{c1::frosting}} as a depth indicator.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: Classic deep chemical peel is Baker–Gordon: {{c1::3 drops croton oil::3}}, {{c2::8 drops Septisol::8}}, {{c3::3 mL 88% phenol::3}}, {{c4::2 mL distilled water::2}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Deep peels penetrate mid-reticular dermis; for deep rhytids (Glogau III–IV per your note).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In cleft lip repair, reconstructing the {{c1::orbicularis oris}} muscle layer is critical for acceptable dynamic outcome.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Muscle continuity is the functional repair.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On the cleft side, the orbicularis oris muscle fibers insert abnormally into the {{c2::lateral alar base}}, specifically at the {{c1::piriform aperture}} rather than forming a continuous sphincter across the lip.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: On the noncleft side, orbicularis oris inserts into the nasal spine and caudal septum

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common complication of congenital aural atresia repair is {{c1::meatal stenosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often due to circumferential scarring of the reconstructed canal; prevention relies on meticulous postop stenting and surveillance.

fields.name: Text
