fields.value: Sump syndrome is a complication of {{c1::dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Think functional failure despite creation of a patent ostium.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Sump syndrome after DCR results from {{c1::stagnation below the neo-ostium}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: A residual inferior lacrimal sac/duct segment acts as a “sump,” allowing debris/fluid accumulation → recurrent epiphora.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In dermabrasion, removal of epithelium is marked by the {{c1::nonbleeding, white epidermal–dermal junction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: First visual endpoint before dermal bleeding appears.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In dermabrasion, {{c1::punctate (pinpoint) bleeding::visual finding}} corresponds to the {{c2::superficial papillary dermis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classic safe therapeutic depth for resurfacing.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In dermabrasion, encountering the reticular dermis is suggested by a {{c1::yellow-white (“chamois”) appearance}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Indicates deeper injury with increased scarring and dyspigmentation risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Generally, dermabrasion treatment should not progress past {{c1::papillary dermis bleeding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Some sources allow superficial reticular dermis, but deeper penetration markedly increases fibrosis risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An absolute contraindication to dermabrasion is {{c1::scleroderma::medical condition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Poor wound healing and abnormal collagen deposition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most frequent complication of infant ear molding is {{c1::superficial skin excoriation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Usually mild; managed with brief device breaks and close follow-up.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ear molding should ideally be initiated between {{c1::birth and 6 weeks}} of age.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Maternal estrogen increases cartilage malleability (peak ~day 3, wanes by week 6).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Normal facial aging includes {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} orbital aperture size.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Normal facial aging changes include orbital aperture enlargement, maxillary retrusion, pyriform aperture expansion, and mandibular body thinning.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Normal facial aging includes {{c1::retrusion}} of the maxilla.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Normal facial aging changes include orbital aperture enlargement, maxillary retrusion, pyriform aperture expansion, and mandibular body thinning.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Normal facial aging includes {{c1::expansion}} of the pyriform aperture.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Normal facial aging changes include orbital aperture enlargement, maxillary retrusion, pyriform aperture expansion, and mandibular body thinning.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Normal facial aging includes {{c1::thinning}} of the mandibular body.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Normal facial aging changes include orbital aperture enlargement, maxillary retrusion, pyriform aperture expansion, and mandibular body thinning.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After facelift, postoperative hematoma risk increases when BP is >150/100 due to {{c1::uncontrolled hypertension}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: One of the strongest modifiable risk factors; postop BP spikes matter more than intraop bleeding.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After facelift, there is {{c1::no direct correlation::relationship}} between increased intraoperative bleeding and postoperative hematoma.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Hematoma risk tracks more closely with postoperative blood pressure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Intraoperative adjuncts that decrease hematoma risk after facelift include {{c1::TXA, tissue sealants, and blood pressure control::3}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Drains alone do not meaningfully reduce hematoma risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Postoperative drain placement after facelift {{c1::does not::does/does not }} reduce hematoma risk.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: May reduce seroma but not bleeding-related complications.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After facelift, the group at higher risk for postoperative hematoma is {{c1::men::gender}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often attributed to thicker skin/vascularity and higher HTN prevalence.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Stigmata of a primary facelift include (4)
{{c1::hairline distortion
platysmal banding
anteriorly displaced tragus
loss of temporal hair tuft}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Cluster of “operated-on” tells—often reflecting incision design and/or excessive tension vectors.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
The nose has {{c3::9::#}} aesthetic subunits:
paired {{c1::sidewalls, ala, soft tissue triangles::3}},
unpaired {{c2::tip, dorsum, columella}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Total = 3 unpaired + (3 paired × 2). Subunit principles guide flap design and excision planning.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: First-line treatment for lagophthalmos with poor lower lid globe apposition is {{c1::upper eyelid weight placement with lower eyelid suspension}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Protects the cornea while preserving vision better than permanent tarsorrhaphy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In congenital facial paralysis, nerve transfers are {{c1::not recommended::recommended/not recommended}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Typically due to aberrant development rather than acute denervation, so transfer won’t restore normal spontaneous circuitry.
Can use dynamic muscle slings such as gracilis or fascia though.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In facial reanimation, {{c1::cable grafting::procedure}} offers the best chance of restoring spontaneous facial function.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Particularly relevant when proximal and distal nerve stumps are available (e.g., radical parotidectomy).

Nerve cable grafting timing (facial nerve):
Best performed within 72 hours of injury.
Functional recovery remains reasonable up to ~6 months, declines significantly after that, and is poor after ~12 months due to irreversible motor end-plate degeneration and muscle atrophy.
Beyond 12 months, nerve transfers / dynamic reanimation are preferred over grafting.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Masseter, temporalis, and hypoglossal-driven transfers::facial nerve repair}} are typically not spontaneous.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: They are driven by clench or tongue activation rather than automatic emotional smile pathways.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Flaccid facial paralysis present for >2 years makes patients poor candidates for {{c1::nerve transfers}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Chronic denervation leads to irreversible facial muscle atrophy (often referenced as ~24 months in adults).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A straightforward option to restore resting symmetry in long-standing flaccid facial paralysis but may add bulk is {{c1::temporalis tendon transfer}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reliable symmetry; may add bulk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A more complex option to restore dynamic smile in long-standing flaccid facial paralysis is {{c1::gracilis free muscle transfer}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Microsurgical option that restores excursion and tone.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Common chemodenervation targets for synkinesis include {{c1::DAO and orbicularis oculi}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Also corrugator, buccinator, mentalis, and platysma depending on pattern.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In facial synkinesis chemodenervation, avoid injecting the {{c1::zygomaticus major::muscle}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Weakening this muscle directly compromises smile strength.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Hypoglossal nerve transfer::procedure}} provides the best improvement in facial tone.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Best considered before irreversible facial muscle atrophy—practically within about ≤2 years (≈24 months in adults) of flaccid paralysis for reinnervation-based strategies.

AO Reference

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c3::Zuker’s point}} is a landmark for identifying {{c1::zygomaticobuccal}} branches and is located at {{c2::the midpoint of a line from the root of the helix to the lateral oral commissure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Zygomaticobuccal branches are off of the main trunk. Visualize the point if needing to a retrograde dissection for the parotid or facial nerve paralysis work.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: First-line myectomy for synkinesis-related smile dysfunction is {{c1::depressor anguli oris (DAO)::muscle}} myectomy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mentalis or DLI myectomy can worsen smile asymmetry; platysma myectomy is not first-line if the goal is smile improvement alone.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A favorable facial nerve outcome on HB (House–Brackmann) is {{c1::I or II}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: HB I–II is generally considered “good” functional recovery (near-normal to mild dysfunction).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ENoG is best performed between {{c1::72 hours and 2 weeks::timeframe}} after onset of facial nerve symptoms.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Too early (before ~72 hours) risks underestimating degeneration; after the optimal window, prognostication utility decreases.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On ENoG, {{c1::90–95}}% degeneration portends about a {{c2::50}}% chance of a favorable outcome.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High degeneration = worse prognosis; interpret alongside clinical course.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After complete facial nerve transection, eyelid closure can be preserved for {{c1::1–2}} days.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Gravity can still drive closure until levator palpebrae superioris begins to contract unopposed (leading to lagophthalmos).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In adults, native facial musculature may remain receptive to reinnervation for up to {{c1::24}} months after denervation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
2 years

Evidence suggests possibly longer in children; “reinnervation window” concept drives urgency of nerve transfers/repairs.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In dense flaccid facial paralysis with no recovery by {{c1::12}} months, {{c2::nerve transfers::procedure}} should be considered.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Further observation at this point can worsen outcomes of later transfers (muscle atrophy/less receptive targets).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A good option when there is no recovery to facial nerve function by 12 months is {{c1::split-hypoglossal nerve transfer::procedure}} to the main trunk of CN VII.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Main trunk repairs/transfers aim to restore tone and some blink; meaningful expression recovery is uncommon at this stage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Targeted nerve transfers should be considered when minimal/no improvement is seen {{c1::7}} months after vestibular schwannoma resection with CN VII preservation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: In this setting, probability of ultimate meaningful expression recovery is <10%.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In late dense paralysis with minimal recovery, {{c1::ENoG and EMG::test}} are unlikely to change management.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Even if electrical activity is present, spontaneous recovery of meaningful facial movement is unlikely at this stage.

  • ENoG is only useful during the first 3–21 days after onset of complete paralysis.
  • EMG is most useful from about 2–3 weeks to 6 months after onset to assess reinnervation potential.
  • Once a patient has had persistent dense paralysis for >6–12 months with little or no recovery, electrodiagnostic testing rarely changes management because the discussion shifts toward reanimation procedures rather than waiting for spontaneous nerve recovery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A common targeted procedure for volitional smile reanimation is {{c1::nerve-to-masseter (V→VII) transfer::procedure}} to lower zygomatic branches.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Strong, reliable smile excursion; typically bite-driven (volitional).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A targeted procedure for {{c2::blink restoration}} is {{c1::cross-face nerve graft (CFNG)::procedure}} to upper zygomatic branches.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Aims to restore blink via contralateral facial nerve input.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A {{c2::Tinel}} sign after CFNG is an {{c1::electrical/buzzing/crawling}} sensation felt in the contralateral face when tapping the distal tip of the graft.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Many patients have it post-op; its presence or absence does not predict success.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Synkinesis typically develops {{c1::6–18}} months after in-continuity facial nerve insults.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Flaccid paralysis is denervation-dominant; synkinesis reflects miswiring during regeneration.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Common donor nerves for facial nerve grafts include the {{c1::great auricular, sural, and medial antebrachial cutaneous::3}} nerves.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Choose based on required length/caliber and donor morbidity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If the nerve gap is >10 cm, the preferred graft is often the {{c1::sural nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Sural nerve can provide up to 30 cm of graft length.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Primary nerve repair/nerve grafting should ideally be performed within the first {{c1::72}} hours after injury/sacrifice.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Wallerian degeneration begins around 72 hours; repair is still recommended even if post-op radiation is expected.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Current standard facial nerve repair technique is {{c1::epineurial suture repair}} with {{c2::fibrin glue stabilization}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Fascicular vs epineurial repair has no clear winner; epineurial is faster and more straightforward.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In facial reanimation terminology, “nerve grafting” means the {{c1::primary nerve provides motor input}} to the distal primary nerve via a graft.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Contrast: grafting uses the same source nerve; reinnervation uses a different donor nerve.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In facial reanimation terminology, “reinnervation” means a {{c1::different donor nerve provides motor input}} to the distal primary nerve.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Must occur within muscle receptivity window (~24 months adults).
This is also called nerve transfer

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Reinnervation procedures should be performed within {{c1::2}} year(s) following facial nerve injury.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reflects muscle receptivity window.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Common lower eyelid procedures in facial reanimation include {{c1::lateral tarsal strip}} and {{c2::fascia suspension}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Improve lid position and globe apposition.
Both of these are also used as management for ectropion
Lateral tarsal strip

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hyperlacrimation with salivation (crocodile tears) is {{c1::Bogorad syndrome::name of process}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Managed with botulinum toxin injection into the lacrimal gland.

Bogorad syndrome (crocodile tears) is caused by aberrant regeneration of the facial nerve (CN VII) after injury, most classically after Bell’s palsy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Glogau type I photoaging is {{c1::mild}} with {{c2::no wrinkles}} (age 28–35).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Glogau summary: I mild/no wrinkles; II moderate/wrinkles in motion; III advanced/wrinkles at rest; IV severe/only wrinkles.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Glogau type II photoaging is {{c1::moderate}} with {{c2::wrinkles in motion}} (age 35–50).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Glogau summary: I mild/no wrinkles; II moderate/wrinkles in motion; III advanced/wrinkles at rest; IV severe/only wrinkles.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Glogau type III photoaging is {{c1::advanced}} with {{c2::wrinkles at rest}} (age 50–65).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Glogau summary: I mild/no wrinkles; II moderate/wrinkles in motion; III advanced/wrinkles at rest; IV severe/only wrinkles.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Glogau type IV photoaging is {{c1::severe}} with {{c2::wrinkles everywhere}} (age 60+).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Glogau summary: I mild/no wrinkles; II moderate/wrinkles in motion; III advanced/wrinkles at rest; IV severe/only wrinkles.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An absolute contraindication to facial resurfacing is {{c1::isotretinoin::medication}} use.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Inhibits re-epithelialization; should be off isotretinoin for 1 year before resurfacing.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Relative contraindications to facial resurfacing include {{c1::connective tissue disorders, hypertrophic/keloid scarring, and prior radiation::conditions (3)}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Relative = increased risk; requires counseling.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Pre-resurfacing skin prep includes {{c1::topical hydroquinone}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reduces post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Pre-resurfacing skin prep can include tretinoin for 4–6 weeks, but it should be stopped {{c1::2}} weeks pre-op.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Tretinoin (not isotretinoin) thins epidermis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For patients with recurrent HSV, start antivirals {{c1::1–3 days::timeframe}} before facial resurfacing.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Prevents HSV reactivation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Collapse of the inner and/or external nasal valve with inspiration is termed {{c1::lateral nasal wall insufficiency (LWI)}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Dynamic lateral wall collapse.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In geometric broken line closure, the donor site should be {{c1::1}} mm larger than the recipient site.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Donor: excise outside marking; recipient: excise inside.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Keloid pathophysiology involves chronic inflammation of the {{c1::reticular dermis::skin layer (specific)}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Leads to excessive collagen/ECM deposition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: “5 As and one B” for keloid-prone repair: {{c1::atraumatic technique, asepsis, absence of raw surfaces, avoidance of tension, accurate approximation, and meticulous bleeding control}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Adjuvants: steroids, pressure therapy, or radiation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laser resurfacing is reserved for deeper {{c1::rhytids/photodamage}} and {{c2::acne scarring}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Used especially perioral, glabellar, lower eyelid.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For laser resurfacing, water-absorbed lasers include {{c1::CO2}} 10,600 nm and {{c2::Er:YAG}} 2,940 nm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: CO2 penetrates deeper; pulsed mode reduces scarring.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The laser {{c1::medium::what sets wavelength}} determines the laser wavelength.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Wavelength is fixed for a given laser type and determines which chromophore is targeted (e.g., water, hemoglobin, melanin).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laser {{c1::wavelength::fixed variable}} is determined by the laser type (medium), not by the operator.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Operators adjust fluence, spot size, and pulse duration, but wavelength is intrinsic to the device.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laser fluence is energy delivered per unit {{c1::area::definition}} (J/cm²).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Higher fluence increases ablative and thermal effect, but also raises complication risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The approximate fluence required to ablate skin is about {{c1::5}} J/cm².

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Board-style benchmark; actual clinical settings vary by device and skin type.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Larger laser {{c1::spot size::parameter}} allows deeper tissue penetration.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Larger spot sizes reduce scatter and increase effective depth of energy delivery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laser pulse duration should be shorter than the tissue {{c1::thermal relaxation time::TRT}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Pulse durations longer than TRT allow heat diffusion → greater collateral thermal injury.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lip defects >2/3 of lip width often require {{c1::free flap reconstruction::reconstruction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Local and regional options are usually insufficient at this size.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In a(n) {{c2::transposition}} flap, the point of greatest tension is at the {{c1::most distant donor site::tension point}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Advect | Transdonor
Advancement flaps move straight toward the defect, so the leading edge must stretch the most, concentrating tension at the defect. 
Transposition flaps rotate around a pivot point, so the tip travels the farthest along the arc and bears the greatest stretch at the most distant donor site.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In a(n) {{c2::advancement}} flap, the point of greatest tension is at the {{c1::primary defect::tension point}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Advect | Transdonor

Can distort free margins (e.g., cheek advancement causing lower eyelid ectropion).

Advancement flaps move straight toward the defect, so the leading edge must stretch the most, concentrating tension at the defect. 




Transposition flaps rotate around a pivot point, so the tip travels the farthest along the arc and bears the greatest stretch at the most distant donor site.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For scalp rotation flaps, the arc of rotation should be at least {{c1::6×::ratio}} the defect diameter.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Improves mobility and reduces closure tension.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For cheek rotation flaps, the arc of rotation should be about {{c1::4×::ratio}} the defect diameter.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Cheek tissue is more mobile than scalp.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Scalp flap undermining is performed in the {{c1::subgaleal::plane}} plane.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Preserves vascularity while maximizing mobility.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Exposed bone in scalp defects cannot reliably be covered with a {{c1::skin graft::contraindication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Requires vascularized tissue coverage.
Can consideer a skin substitute to create a layer of granulation tissue before trying a skin graft

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Adequate revascularization for flap pedicle division can occur as early as {{c1::7}} days.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Earliest reported timing; many surgeons still wait longer.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For interpolates flaps: Flap pedicle division is usually recommended after about {{c1::3}} weeks.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Waiting ~3 weeks improves reliability of neovascularization.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Concave facial surfaces ideal for secondary intention healing include the {{c1::temple, medial canthus, and conchal bowl::3 locations}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These sites often heal with acceptable cosmetic outcomes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Healing by secondary intention on the face typically takes {{c1::4–6::timeframe}} weeks.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Important counseling point for patients.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Axial cutaneous flaps have improved survival due to inclusion of a {{c1::septocutaneous artery::vessel type}} in the longitudinal axis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: More reliable vascular supply than random-pattern flaps.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Skin beyond the direct arterial supply of an axial flap survives via the {{c1::subdermal plexus::blood supply}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Distal perfusion physiology resembles random flaps.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The paramedian forehead flap is supplied by the {{c1::supratrochlear artery::artery}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Axial flap

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Abbe and Estlander lip crossover flaps are supplied by the {{c1::superior labial artery::artery}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Allows safe cross-lip tissue transfer.
Branch off of the facial artery

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The temporoparietal fascia flap is supplied by the {{c1::superficial temporal artery::artery}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Thin, pliable flap useful for coverage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Effective flap length is reduced by about {{c1::40}}% when pivoted 180 degrees.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Greater pivot angle increases standing cone formation and reduces reach.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Flaps should generally not be pivoted more than {{c1::90}} degrees.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Excessive pivot increases tension and dog-ear risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For open wounds >3 days old, consider a {{c1::5-day::duration}} course of oral cephalosporin before surgical repair.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reduces bacterial colonization of granulation tissue and risk of flap/graft failure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Yes/No: Increasing the width of a random flap’s pedicle increases perfusion pressure to the distal flap. {{c1::No::yes/no}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Pedicle width increases vessel number, not distal perfusion pressure.
Can help with venous drainage

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Increasing the depth of the pivot plane increases flap {{c1::advancement::effect}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Important principle for V-Y advancement flaps.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For a V-Y advancement flap, thicker underlying soft tissue generally allows {{c1::greater::more/less}} advancement distance.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Increased tissue bulk permits more movement when the pivot plane is deepened.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Poor response to mandibular distraction in {{c1::Pierre Robin sequence::disorder}} is associated with age, GERD, CNS anomalies, and intubation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These factors correlate with worse outcomes in retrospective studies.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Exposed cartilage in microtia reconstruction requires coverage with a {{c1::vascularized flap::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Cartilage does not need to be buried if it becomes exposed.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The Brent microtia technique is a {{c1::four::number}} stage reconstruction.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• Stages: framework placement, lobule transposition, auricle elevation, tragal construction + conchal refinement.
  • https://www.optecoto.com/article/S1043-1810%2817%2930034-9/fulltext

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The Nagata microtia technique is a {{c1::two-stage::number}} reconstruction.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Stage 1: framework + tragus + lobule transposition; Stage 2: auricle elevation with temporoparietal fascia flap + STSG. https://www.nagata-microtia.com/method.html

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The Reinisch microtia technique is typically a {{c1::one-stage::number}} reconstruction.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Medpor-based technique; second stage if postauricular sulcus contracts.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The Firmin microtia technique is a planned {{c1::two-stage::number}} reconstruction and uses an extra cartilage piece called {{c1::surelevation::term}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Similar to Nagata; surelevation improves tragal definition. https://otosurgeryatlas.stanford.edu/otologic-surgery-atlas/external-ear/microtia-repair/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most prominent ears are due to {{c1::antihelical unfurling::anatomic change}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Protruding ears most commonly result from underdevelopment/unfurling of the antihelical fold; it can be seen with prominent projection of the conchal bowl. Other associated deformities include superior pole deformity, prominent lobule, and Darwinian tubercle.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Obagi skin pinch test: pinch the {{c1::nasolabial fold::location}} to estimate nasal soft-tissue envelope thickness.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Thickness at the nasolabial fold is used as a surrogate for nasal skin/soft-tissue envelope.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Obagi classification: thin < {{c1::1}} cm, normal {{c1::1–2}} cm, thick > {{c1::2}} cm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Intermediate skin thickness is widely regarded as most conducive to a favorable cosmetic outcome. Extremely thin and extremely thick skin each have unfavorable physical characteristics and aberrant healing responses (thin skin shows irregularities; thick skin blunts refinement and prolongs edema).
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Oil glands reside in the {{c1::dermis::skin layer}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Oily skin has larger glands and therefore a thicker dermis; oily/thick dermis can make definition more challenging in rhinoplasty.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nasal {{c1::intermediate::best}} skin thickness is most conducive to favorable cosmetic outcome.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Extremes (very thin or very thick) are associated with worse/less predictable outcomes.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Which nasal skin thickness is most likely to impede a favorable cosmetic outcome? {{c1::Thick::skin thickness}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Thick skin’s bulk commonly limits definition and can “mask” refinement.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Normal internal nasal valve angle is {{c1::10–15::range}} degrees.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Key functional benchmark. https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nasal skin is thinnest at the {{c1::rhinion::location}} (≈2–2.2 mm).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Area where irregularities are most visible.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Upper lateral cartilages insert deep to the {{c1::caudal margin of the nasal bones::attachment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Relationship relevant to dorsal and middle vault work.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Diced cartilage should be cut into ~{{c1::0.5}} mm pieces to reduce risk of palpability.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Smaller pieces → smoother contour with diced cartilage techniques.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An alar batten graft augments {{c1::weak or absent lower lateral cartilage::indication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Supports external nasal valve / alar sidewall when LLC support is deficient.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Alar batten graft should extend from the supra-alar crease region (ULC/LLC junction) to over the {{c1::pyriform aperture::landmark}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Ensure adequate length and stable seating in a soft-tissue pocket for durable support.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Inverted-V deformity results from disruption of {{c1::middle vault support::cause}} after reduction rhinoplasty.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Classically from ULC separation/insufficient reconstruction after dorsal reduction.

Middle vault is the area between the nasal bones and ULCs https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Prevent inverted-V deformity with placement of {{c1::spreader grafts::prevention}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Restores middle vault and internal valve area after dorsal reduction.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Pollybeak deformity can result from disruption of {{c1::tip support::mechanism}} → tip ptosis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Avoid by supporting the tip before closure and appropriately managing dorsum/supratip.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dorsal hump reduction techniques: {{c1::structural (component reduction)::approach}} vs {{c1::dorsal preservation::approach}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Structural rhinoplasty removes the dorsal hump by component reduction and requires middle vault reconstruction, whereas dorsal preservation lowers the intact dorsum by subdorsal septal resection without dismantling the nasal roof.

Choice depends on ULC integrity and goals.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In spare-roof dorsal preservation (SRT), the first step is separation of the {{c1::middle vault::structure}} from the dorsal septum.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The middle vault is the central structural segment of the external nose, located between:
 • the upper nasal vault (bony vault)
 • and the lower nasal vault (tip / alar cartilages)

It is the portion of the nose that forms the internal nasal valve region, which is the narrowest and most critical area for nasal airflow.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dorsal preservation rhinoplasty has residual/recurrent hump rates of about {{c1::4.18::rate}}%.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Meta-analysis figure from your note.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: “Virgin nose” antibiotics: pre-op antibiotics and no more than {{c1::24}} hours post-op.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Contrast with revision protocols.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Revision rhinoplasty antibiotics: pre-op antibiotics + post-op {{c1::topical}} and oral antibiotics.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
From your note; institutional protocols vary.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Tension nose and saddle nose deformities are {{c1::opposites::relationship}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Conceptual pairing.
Tension nose


Saddle nose
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c2::Crumley (Crumley–Lanser)::eponym}} method measures nasal tip {{c1::projection::measurement}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Objective assessment of tip projection.


https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Geometric broken-line closure segments should ideally be ~{{c1::7}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Pattern planning pearl for camouflaging scars.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Endoscopic endonasal septal perforation repair with interpositional auricular cartilage graft is appropriate for anterior perforations <{{c1::20}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Large septal perforations (>20 mm) have high closure failure with purely endonasal techniques due to excessive tension and limited mucosal mobility. Definitive repair typically requires an open rhinoplasty approach with bilateral mucoperichondrial advancement and/or regional intranasal flaps (e.g., inferior turbinate, middle turbinate, FAMM), combined with an interpositional graft (temporalis fascia, ADM, cartilage/PDS) to achieve a tension-free, well-vascularized closure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After septoplasty, approximately {{c1::20–30::range}}% of patients have persistent symptoms.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Counseling estimate from your note.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common anatomic cause of persistent obstruction after septoplasty is {{c1::internal nasal valve narrowing::cause}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Chambers et al — revision cohort improved after valve correction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::zygomaticosphenoidal (ZS)::suture name}} suture alignment is critical in ZMC fracture reduction to reestablish {{c1::pre-traumatic orbital volume::goal}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Even though the ZS suture line is not typically fixated after reduction, its alignment is a key marker of accurate reduction and orbital volume restoration.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Common access for ZMC fracture reduction includes {{c1::upper blepharoplasty incision::approach}} or {{c1::lateral brow incision::approach}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Used to gain exposure for reduction; specific approach depends on fracture pattern and surgeon preference.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Fordyce granules are {{c1::ectopic sebaceous glands::what are they}} of the oral mucosa.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Benign yellow-white papules on buccal mucosa and vermillion border; reassurance/observation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In caustic ingestion, a repeat/relook endoscopic assessment around day {{c1::5::time}} can better predict later cicatrization/stenosis than day 1 EGD.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Day 1 EGD may overestimate injury; relook endoscopy better predicts esophageal and antropyloric stenosis (Kochhar et al., Endoscopy 2017).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The superior and inferior ophthalmic veins are {{c1::valveless::key feature}}, allowing communication between face/nose/sinuses, orbit, and the cavernous sinus.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mechanism for spread of infection and thrombosis along venous pathways.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c2::suprasternal space of Burns}} is formed by fascia surrounding the {{c1::intermediate tendon of the omohyoid::anatomic landmark}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
May contain a lymph node and a vessel bridging the two anterior jugular veins.

Surgical relevance

During:
  • tracheostomy
  • drainage of lower neck abscesses
  • exploration of deep neck infections
Surgeons must recognize this space to:
  • fully evacuate infection
  • avoid leaving a dependent pocket that will recollect
  • avoid injury to crossing venous structures
Failure to address it can explain persistent or recurrent infection after “adequate” drainage elsewhere.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Deep neck anatomy 'rule of two’s':
2 suprahyoid muscles ({{c1::masseter + anterior belly of digastric::pair}}),
2 crossing neck muscles ({{c2::trapezius + SCM::pair}}),
2 salivary glands ({{c3::parotid + submandibular::pair}}),
2 fascial compartments ({{c4::parotid + masticator::pair}}).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Mnemonic scaffold for visualizing spaces and contents in deep neck infections. 
https://radiopaedia.org/cases/74853/studies/85868?lang=us

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In deep neck infections, {{c1::Pseudomonas::organism}} is more likely in patients with HIV, and {{c2::Klebsiella::organism}} is more common in patients with diabetes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Microbial risks vary with host factors; tailor empiric therapy accordingly.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Delay in surgical drainage of deep neck abscess is associated with increased morbidity/mortality in {{c1::adults::adult/children}}, but not in {{c1::children::adult/children}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Still treat urgently in kids when indicated—this is a comparative outcome pearl, not a reason to delay care.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
The parapharyngeal space’s central location enables spread:
medially from {{c1::masticator space::source}},
anteriorly from {{c2::submandibular space::source}},
posteriorly from {{c3::retropharyngeal space::source}},
laterally from {{c4::parotid space::source}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Use this map to predict source of infection and complications. 


https://radiopaedia.org/cases/43811/studies/47296?lang=us

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::KTP::laser}} is used for {{c2::stapedectomy::procedure}} and {{c3::laryngeal/tracheal surgery::procedure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: KTP is a visible green laser (532 nm) with strong hemoglobin absorption, enabling precise cutting and coagulation in airway and middle ear surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Argon::laser}} emits blue-green light at {{c2::488–514::wavelength}} nm and is used for {{c3::stapedectomy::procedure}} and superficial {{c4::cutaneous vascular lesions::indication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Argon laser has superficial tissue penetration with strong hemoglobin absorption, ideal for surface vascular lesions and otologic applications.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Nd:YAG::laser}} is a near-infrared laser at {{c2::1064::wavelength}} nm used for {{c3::deep tracheobronchial lesion ablation::indication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Nd:YAG provides deeper tissue penetration than visible-spectrum lasers, useful for bulky airway and GI lesions.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Pulsed dye laser (PDL)::laser}} is {{c2::595::wavelength}} nm and treats superficial {{c3::infantile hemangiomas::lesion}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: PDL selectively targets oxyhemoglobin and is standard therapy for superficial infantile hemangiomas.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::KTP::laser}} is {{c2::532::wavelength}} nm and targets {{c3::hemoglobin::chromophore}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Frequency-doubled Nd:YAG; excellent hemostatic precision for vascular mucosal lesions.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::CO2::laser}} is {{c2::10600::wavelength}} nm and targets {{c3::water::chromophore}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: CO2 energy is absorbed by water, producing very superficial precise vaporization.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Median rhomboid glossitis is {{c1::benign::benign/malignant}} and associated with {{c2::Candida::etiology}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Smooth erythematous midline dorsal tongue lesion; treat with antifungals if symptomatic.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Orbital apex syndrome is distinguished by involvement of {{c1::optic nerve (CN II)::key distinction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Causes vision loss plus painful ophthalmoplegia due to crowded orbital apex anatomy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Orbital apex syndrome involves CN {{c1::II + III + IV + V1 + VI::which nerves}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Lesions at the orbital apex affect the optic canal and superior orbital fissure structures simultaneously.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Aspirin::medication}} irreversibly inhibits platelets for {{c2::5–7::timeframe}} days; {{c3::ibuprofen::medication}} is reversible; {{c4::DDAVP::medication}} can improve function.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: DDAVP increases vWF and platelet adhesion; useful in select bleeding states.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Best NPPV candidates: PaO2/FiO2 < {{c1::200::threshold}} or CO2 > {{c2::45::threshold}} with intact airway protection.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
NPPV most effective when respiratory failure is present without aspiration risk.

  • A patient on 50% oxygen (0.50 FiO2) with a PaO2 of 100 mmHg has a P/F ratio of 100/0.50 = 200, indicating significant lung impairment.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In children with peritonsillar abscess < {{c1::15::size}} mm, {{c2::medical management::management}} may be appropriate.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Smaller abscesses can respond to antibiotics and close observation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Viral causes of sialadenitis: {{c1::influenza::virus}}, {{c2::adenovirus::virus}}, {{c3::EBV::virus}}; {{c4::mumps::virus}} is uncommon.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consider viral etiologies when swelling is bilateral/systemic.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: There are {{c1::20::number}} primary teeth and {{c2::32::number}} permanent teeth; primary lack {{c3::premolars::missing teeth}} and {{c3::third molars::missing teeth}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Primary dentition includes incisors, canines, molars only.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The thyrohyoid membrane is the {{c1::anterior boundary::boundary}} of the prepiglottic space.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Key anatomic landmark for supraglottic disease spread.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After perc trach, tract maturation is {{c1::7–10::timeframe}} days; first trach change ~ post-op day {{c2::10::timeframe}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Perc trach tracts mature more slowly, increasing early decannulation risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Surgical trach tract matures in {{c1::3–5::timeframe}} days; early change ~ {{c2::72::timeframe}} hours.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Surgical stomas stabilize faster than PDT.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Fresh trach most dangerous for decannulation in first {{c1::48–72::timeframe}} hours due to {{c2::false passage::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Peristomal tract not yet formed early.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Suspect trach displacement if patient with fresh trach develops distress or suddenly can {{c1::speak::clinical clue}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Sudden phonation suggests partial decannulation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the oropharynx requires elective neck dissection due to {{c1::occult metastases::rationale}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High risk of microscopic nodal disease despite clinically negative neck.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The “resident’s best friend” landmark in the neck is the {{c1::digastric muscle::landmark}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Used for orientation in parotid/upper neck dissection—helps you quickly mentally “layer” what’s superficial vs deep. Superficial to the digastric: marginal mandibular nerve, great auricular nerve, and external jugular vein. Near the digastric but deep to it: hypoglossal nerve, lingual nerve, and facial artery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The RLN provides sensory innervation to the {{c1::subglottis::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: RLN = motor to intrinsic larynx (except CT) + sensory below the vocal folds (subglottis).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia transforms into invasive cancer at {{c1::64}}%.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: PVL is high-risk OPMD with substantial malignant transformation; requires long-term surveillance and low threshold for biopsy/re-biopsy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Oral lichen planus (OLP) malignant transformation risk is generally {{c1::low::risk level}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reported malignant transformation rates range from 0% to 3.5%. Risk increases with epithelial dysplasia, erosive/atrophic disease, and tobacco/alcohol use.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In high-risk cSCC, a major predictor of subclinical nodal metastasis is {{c1::depth of invasion (DOI)::predictor}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: In one prospective study: DOI ≥ 5 mm had ~19.7% nodal metastasis vs 0% when < 5 mm (p=0.01). Higher DOI further increases nodal risk and supports intensified nodal evaluation in deep tumors.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In deep neck space abscess in adults, if you think they’ll ultimately need surgery, perform surgical management {{c1::on the day of admission::timing}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Delaying drainage is associated with higher morbidity/mortality—early source control matters.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Strongest risk factors for life-threatening complications in deep neck infections are {{c1::multiple space involvement and diabetes mellitus::top risks}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-risk patients need aggressive monitoring, airway vigilance, and timely source control.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A right non-recurrent inferior laryngeal nerve is associated with a(n) {{c1::aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria)::association}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Arteria lusoria typically arises distal on the arch and courses retroesophageal. A retropharyngeal thyroid gland can also be associated with a right non-recurrent laryngeal nerve—any anatomic oddity suggesting aberrant arch development should raise vigilance during thyroid surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Peronea arteria magna::vascular variant}} = variant where the {{c2::peroneal artery::vessel}} is the sole blood supply to the foot.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Occurs in up to 5% of the population. Clinical relevance: fibula harvest planning—if peroneal is dominant/sole supply, harvest can threaten distal limb perfusion.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In free flap reconstruction, increased {{c1::operative time and crystalloid volume::2}} increases risk of wound-healing complications.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Longer cases correlate with physiologic stressors; excess crystalloid → tissue edema → higher wound complication risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Largest potential surface area musculocutaneous flap for H&N reconstruction: {{c1::latissimus dorsi::flap}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Can be pedicled or free flap; cited size ~20 × 40 cm.
It is off of the thoracodorsal artery

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Largest fasciocutaneous flap for H&N reconstruction: {{c1::anterolateral thigh (ALT)::flap}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
ALT is the large fasciocutaneous workhorse.
Off of the descending branch of the circumflex femoral artery

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For carotid body / “glomus” tumors: surgery is favored for {{c1::young, healthy, symptomatic::indications}} patients.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Goal: definitive management when operative risk acceptable.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Preop embolization is not required in selected small {{c1::Shamblin type I::classification}} carotid body tumors.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Small, low-encasement lesions may go straight to resection.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If patient is a poor surgical candidate with glomus tumor, treat with {{c1::external beam radiation::treatment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Nonoperative pathway when comorbidities/age make surgery high risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: FHH type 1 is associated with {{c1::loss-of-function CaSR mutation::mechanism}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Impaired sensing → inappropriately normal/high PTH with hypercalcemia + low urine calcium.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In FHH, 24-hour urine calcium is typically {{c1::low::lab pattern}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Contrasts with most primary HPT.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If evaluating suspected FHH vs primary HPT, calcium/creatinine clearance ratio < {{c1::0.01::cutoff}} supports FHH.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Ratio >0.01 supports primary HPT.
use the Cockcroft–Gault formula to calculate creatinine clearance

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Secondary hyperparathyroidism = elevated PTH due to chronic hypocalcemia ({{c1::e.g., CKD or vitamin D deficiency::examples}}).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: CKD: phosphate retention + decreased 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs when chronically hyperplastic glands begin {{c1::autonomous PTH secretion::transition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often after long-standing secondary HPT.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Parathyroid carcinoma is rare (~{{c1::1::frequency}}% of primary hyperparathyroidism).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consider with very high Ca, very high PTH, palpable mass.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Parathyroid carcinoma clue: serum calcium > {{c1::13::threshold}} mg/dL.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often with very high PTH.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On ultrasound, parathyroid adenoma is typically {{c1::hypoechoic and hypervascular::US appearance}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: US helps localization but misses deep adenomas.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hypopharyngeal cancer: subsite most associated with post-treatment dysphagia is the {{c1::postcricoid space::subsite}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Strong link to swallowing mechanics and fibrosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hypopharyngeal cancer 5-year survival is approximately {{c1::25–35::range}}%.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: ~75% present with T3/T4 disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Postcricoid hypopharyngeal cancer is associated with earlier fixation of the {{c1::arytenoid joints::structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Local invasion → impaired mobility.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hypopharyngeal cancer nodal presentation: {{c1::65–90::range}}% present with nodal disease.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Levels II–IV common; mediastinal nodes frequent.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A “nonfunctional larynx” after nonsurgical laryngeal preservation is suggested by gastrostomy dependence > {{c1::2::timeframe}} years.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Other criteria: permanent tracheostomy, functional laryngectomy, chronic aspiration.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For high-risk laryngectomy patients, {{c1::secondary TEP::procedure for voice}} is preferred to reduce pharyngocutaneous fistula risk.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Primary TEP safe overall; secondary preferred when PCF risk high.

High-risk features for pharyngocutaneous fistula (PCF) after laryngectomy:
• Prior radiation therapy (especially chemoradiation)
• Salvage laryngectomy
• Poor tissue quality / residual tumor at margins
• Malnutrition / low albumin
• Hypothyroidism
• Anemia
• Diabetes mellitus
• Active smoking
• Heavy alcohol use
• Advanced T stage / large pharyngeal defect
• Prior tracheostomy
• Bilateral neck dissection
• High-tension or poorly vascularized pharyngeal closure
• Infection / contaminated surgical field
• Steroid use / immunosuppression

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For T1 glottic cancer, {{c1::transoral laser microsurgery (TLM)::treatment}} is favored over radiotherapy for overal survival, disease free survival, and laryngeal preservation, with {{c2::similar local control::comparison}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Meta-analysis summary.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: 4D parathyroid CT localizes adenomas by rapid uptake and {{c1::washout on delayed/venous phase::imaging principle}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Protocol: noncontrast → arterial → venous/delayed.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Regional lymph node metastasis risk is higher for {{c1::supraglottic::laryngeal subsite}} laryngeal cancer.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Supraglottis includes false vocal folds and has richer lymphatic drainage than the glottis → higher nodal risk; early-stage glottic cancers are often managed without elective neck treatment. Approximate regional lymph node metastasis rate in supraglottic laryngeal cancer is ~55%.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Absolute contraindication to primary TEP is dissociation of the {{c1::party wall::structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: “Party wall” = shared tracheoesophageal wall; if it’s dissociated, primary TEP is contraindicated due to leak/fistula risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Secondary TEP after adjuvant radiation should be delayed at least {{c1::8::timeframe}} weeks for healing.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Minimum interval after RT before secondary TEP is ≥ 8 weeks.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Medications associated with MRONJ include {{c1::bisphosphonates::drug class}}, {{c2::denosumab::drug}}, and anti-angiogenic agents (e.g., {{c3::bevacizumab::drug}}, {{c4::sunitinib::drug}}, {{c5::aflibercept::drug}}).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Includes alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid, ibandronate, pamidronate, clodronate.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hyperbaric oxygen is {{c1::not recommended::recommended/not recommended}} for MRONJ.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Distinction: HBO is used for osteoradionecrosis (ORN), not medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ).

If doing HBO for ORN, make sure they dont have residual or recurrent cancer

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ORN typically occurs in the {{c1::posterior mandible::location}}, whereas MRONJ can occur {{c2::anywhere on the mandible::distribution}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Pattern recognition: ORN classically posterior mandible (radiation field/vascularity), MRONJ can present anywhere along the mandible.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Adjunct medical regimen sometimes used for MRONJ includes {{c1::pentoxifylline::medication}} + {{c1::alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E)::medication}} (“PENT-E”).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Is also used in ORN
Improves microcirculation + antioxidant effects; use varies by institution/stage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Routine SLN biopsy is {{c1::not recommended::recommended/not recommended}} for thin melanoma that is T1a (nonulcerated, Breslow < 0.8 mm).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: SLNB decision-making starts with Breslow depth + ulceration. T1a = nonulcerated <0.8 mm → generally no routine SLNB.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SLN biopsy may be {{c1::considered::considered/not recommended}} for thin melanoma that is T1b: Breslow 0.8–1.0 mm OR <0.8 mm with {{c2::ulceration::feature}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: T1b triggers SLNB discussion: either 0.8–1.0 mm thickness OR ulceration even if <0.8 mm.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SLN biopsy is recommended for intermediate-thickness melanoma (T2/T3): Breslow >1.0 mm to {{c1::4.0::max thickness}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Intermediate thickness (1–4 mm) → SLNB recommended (assuming no contraindications).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In mucosal melanoma staging, the lowest T category is {{c1::T3::lowest T stage}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mucosal melanoma staging starts at T3 due to aggressive biology and typical presentation; use site-specific AJCC schema.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Merkel cell carcinoma: overall survival is predicted by {{c1::T stage::factor}}, {{c2::nodal metastasis::factor}}, and {{c3::distant metastasis::factor}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Primary tumor stage + nodal status + distant mets drive prognosis; many series show improved outcomes with adjuvant RT depending on context.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Optimal treatment for Stage {{c2::III}} nasopharyngeal carcinoma is {{c1::concurrent chemotherapy and radiotherapy::treatment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Standard approach for locally advanced NPC: concurrent CRT (often with induction/adjuvant depending on protocol/risk).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Stage I and IIa nasopharyngeal carcinoma are treated with {{c1::radiotherapy alone::treatment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Early-stage NPC is highly radiosensitive; RT alone is standard for stage I/IIa in many schemas.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For SCC of the lip, strongest predictor of occult nodal metastasis is tumor {{c1::grade::predictor}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Then stage, then mucosal surface involvement (per Walton & Cramer 2020).

G3/4 are considered poorly differentiated
GradeDescriptionBehavior
G1 – Well differentiatedKeratin pearls, obvious squamous featuresSlowest growing, best prognosis
G2 – Moderately differentiatedPartial keratinization, less organizedIntermediate
G3 – Poorly differentiatedMinimal keratinization, high mitotic activityAggressive
G4 – Undifferentiated (rare)No squamous featuresWorst prognosis

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Leukoplakia 5-year transition rate to SCC is about {{c1::2.5::rate}}%.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful counseling number: low-but-real malignant transformation risk over 5 years (~2.5%).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common hematolymphoid tumor of the oropharynx is {{c1::diffuse large B-cell lymphoma::tumor type}}, most commonly arising from the {{c2::palatine tonsil::site}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Oropharyngeal lymphoma most often originates from the tonsil (Waldeyer ring). “Hematolymphoid tumor” framing helps prevent defaulting to SCC.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Maxillary (paranasal sinus) cancer T staging (orbit): T3 includes invasion of the {{c1::floor or medial wall of the orbit::orbital structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Orbit involvement shows up early as bony involvement rather than contents.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Maxillary (paranasal sinus) cancer T4a includes invasion of the {{c1::anterior orbital contents::what is invaded}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: (key structure: inferior rectus::key muscle}}).Anterior orbital contents marks transition from bony involvement to contents.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In a failed parathyroid exploration, {{c1::thyroid lobectomy::next step}} is typically reserved for after all other accessible neck locations have been explored.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Intrathyroidal adenoma is less common than thymic tongue ectopia.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If only 3 parathyroids are found and the left gland’s position is consistent with {{c1::superior parathyroid::which gland}}, the missing gland is most likely the {{c2::inferior parathyroid::missing gland}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Superior glands are relatively fixed; inferior glands wander more.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: When the inferior parathyroid is not found adjacent to the inferior thyroid pole, the next step is transcervical exploration/excision of the {{c1::cervical thymic tongue::most likely ectopic location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Cervical thymic tongue = superior extension of thymus into neck along its embryologic descent path from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch to the mediastinum.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An ectopic inferior parathyroid is found in the thymic tongue about {{c1::25%::approx %}} of the time.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Exploration of thymic tongue is high yield.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: PTH decreases serum phosphorus by {{c1::decreasing renal phosphate reabsorption::mechanism}}, causing {{c2::phosphaturia::physiologic effect}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: PTH dumps phosphate via the kidney.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On imaging, the {{c1::retromandibular vein::structure}} is typically just {{c2::medial::medial/lateral}} to the facial nerve and helps localize parotid masses.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Lhermitte sign::clinical sign}} is electric/shock-like sensations down the spine with neck flexion.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often transient after cervical cord irradiation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After H&N RT, risk of Lhermitte sign increases with cervical cord doses around/above {{c1::50::dose threshold}} Gy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Dose-dependent effect.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Osteoradionecrosis is more likely with pre-existing {{c1::dental disease::risk factor}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Dental optimization pre-RT matters.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Early ORN management focuses on {{c1::conservative measures::management approach}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Stepwise approach.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Late-stage ORN is managed with {{c1::microvascular free flap reconstruction::definitive management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Reserved for advanced disease.

Advance ORN
• Pathologic fracture
• Orocutaneous fistula
• Full-thickness bone necrosis
• Necrosis extending below inferior alveolar canal
• Skin involvement / chronic drainage
• Failure of conservative therapy

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After chemoradiotherapy, the most common cause of severe late dysphagia is {{c1::pharyngeal stricture requiring dilation::most common consequence}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Late functional complication.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ORN of the {{c1::maxilla}} is classically associated with irradiation for {{c2::nasopharyngeal carcinoma::primary}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: NPC fields often irradiate bilateral maxillary supply.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Post-RT fibrosis appears {{c1::4–12::timeframe}} months after therapy and progresses over {{c2::years::trajectory}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Delayed and progressive.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: FRIENDS causes of fistula: {{c1::Foreign body, Radiation, Inflammation, Epithelialization, Neoplasm, Distal obstruction, Steroids::mnemonic expansion}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Checklist for nonhealing fistula.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Radiation toxicities: acute <{{c1::120::cutoff}} days; late >{{c1::120::cutoff}} days.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Operational definition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ORN risk: {{c1::2%::risk}} at {{c2::60–70::dose range}} Gy; {{c3::9%::risk}} at >{{c4::70::dose}} Gy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Dose is major driver.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Continued tobacco use: second primary SCC risk {{c1::2–3%::risk}} per year (up to {{c2::25–30%::max cumulative}}).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Powerful cessation counseling stat.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An {{c1::extracapsular dissection}} (ECD/ECE), also known as {{c2::extracapsular parotidectomy}}, removes benign parotid tumors.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consider for superficial, solitary, ~4 cm, benign, mobile tumors.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Consider extracapsular dissection when tumors are {{c1::superficial lobe::location}}, {{c2::solitary::number}}, ~{{c3::4::size}} cm, {{c4::benign::path}}, and {{c5::mobile in two planes::exam finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Selection criteria for low morbidity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In structural rhinoplasty, the dorsal hump is reduced by {{c1::separating the ULCs from the septum and individually reducing bone and cartilage::mechanism}}, creating a(n) {{c2::open roof deformity::result}} that requires middle vault reconstruction

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Because the ULC–septum relationship is disrupted, the middle vault must be reconstructed to prevent inverted-V deformity and internal valve collapse. Reconstruction commonly uses spreader grafts, spreader flaps, and controlled osteotomies. Best suited for: large humps, twisted or asymmetric noses, thick skin, strong cartilage/bone, significant dorsal irregularity, and revision rhinoplasty cases where precise control and major structural change are required.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In dorsal preservation rhinoplasty, the dorsal roof is kept intact and the hump is eliminated by {{c1::subdorsal septal resection::maneuver}}, lowering the entire nasal pyramid via {{c2::push-down (small lowering) or let-down (larger lowering with maxillary wedge resection)::techniques}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Preserves native dorsal aesthetic lines, avoids open roof deformity, and better maintains internal nasal valve function. Best suited for straight noses, moderate humps, thin skin, and primary rhinoplasty with good baseline dorsal aesthetics. Technically demanding and less forgiving than structural techniques.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: FAMM flap = {{c1::Facial Artery Musculomucosal::name of flap}} flap composed of buccal mucosa + buccinator muscle, supplied by the facial artery

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Pedicled intraoral flap providing excellent like-for-like mucosal reconstruction for oral cavity and oropharyngeal defects. Does not require microvascular anastomosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Inferiorly-based FAMM uses {{c1::antegrade::flow direction}} facial artery flow → reconstructs {{c2::floor of mouth, tongue, lower alveolus, lower lip::target sites}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Orientation depends on desired arc of rotation and target defect. Inferiorly-based flap is ideal for lower oral cavity structures.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Superiorly-based FAMM uses {{c1::retrograde::flow direction}} facial artery flow → reconstructs {{c2::soft palate, hard palate, tonsillar fossa, upper alveolus::target sites}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Superiorly-based design allows excellent reach to oropharyngeal and palatal defects without free flap reconstruction.

When a FAMM flap is designed as a retrograde flap, the facial artery is divided proximally, and the flap survives by blood flowing backward through distal anastomoses.
  • angular artery
  • superior labial artery
  • infraorbital branches
  • contralateral facial system

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c3::Low- and intermediate}}-grade salivary gland tumors often behave more like {{c1::benign tumors::behavior}} → treatment is usually {{c2::surgical resection with adequate margins::treatment}} alone.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: “Don’t overtreat” principle: if completely resected with negative margins, management is often surgery alone and you typically do not need an elective neck dissection. Grading-driven outcomes data in mucoepidermoid carcinoma: Nance 2008.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: First bite syndrome is caused by injury to {{c1::sympathetic innervation::nerve type}} → {{c2::unopposed parasympathetic activity::mechanism}} with painful “first bite” parotid contractions.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classically occurs after parapharyngeal space / deep lobe parotid work where sympathetic fibers are disrupted. Presents as sharp pain at the start of meals that can improve as eating continues.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: First bite syndrome is most commonly seen after {{c1::deep lobe parotid tumor resections::typical setting}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Also described after parapharyngeal space surgery; deep lobe parotid is the classic association.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: During parotidectomy for malignancy, the tumor is close to the facial nerve but there is no gross invasion. Should you resect the facial nerve to “get a wider margin”? {{c1::No::yes/no}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The facial nerve is not sacrificed solely for margin. Nerve sacrifice is considered when there is direct invasion or non-salvageable encasement.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Many post-parotidectomy salivary fistulas resolve with {{c1::conservative management::initial management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Typical conservative measures: pressure dressing, aspiration if needed, antisialagogues, diet modification, wound care. If refractory, botulinum toxin injection may help by decreasing salivary production.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Salivary duct carcinoma::tumor}} has the highest rate of {{c2::cervical lymph node metastasis::metastasis pattern}} among salivary malignancies.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-grade aggressive tumor; often treated with aggressive multimodality therapy and careful nodal management.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Salivary duct carcinoma can be {{c1::androgen receptor positive::biomarker}} → sometimes allowing {{c1::androgen deprivation therapy::targeted therapy}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Asking about AR status can open systemic therapy options in advanced/recurrent disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On parotid biopsy, both {{c1::lymphoma::diagnosis}} and {{c1::Warthin tumor::diagnosis}} can show {{c2::abundant lymphocytes::path feature}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Warthin = oncocytic epithelium + lymphoid stroma; lymphoma = clonal malignant lymphoid population.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SCC unknown primary: {{c1::TORS tongue base mucosectomy (partial glossectomy) + palatine tonsillectomy::key procedures}} yield the greatest rate of identifying the primary site.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Micro-primaries often hide in tonsillar crypts or lingual tonsil; complete tonsillectomy and directed tongue base mucosectomy outperform random biopsies.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Palatine tonsillectomy detection rate is about {{c1::33%::detection rate}} and is ~10× higher than random tonsil biopsies.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Supports doing tonsillectomy rather than random tonsil biopsies.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma: {{c1::primary resection + elective neck treatment::surgical management}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Regional nodal failure risk is meaningful; elective neck management is recommended alongside definitive management.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SNUC: {{c1::trimodality therapy::treatment strategy}} tends to provide the best locoregional control outcomes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Trimodality commonly means surgery + radiation + chemotherapy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Spindle cell SCC is more common in the {{c1::true vocal cords::site}} and is thought to be more aggressive.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Also termed sarcomatoid carcinoma; behaves as an SCC variant clinically.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Neck dissection quality metric: at least {{c1::18::number}} lymph node(s) should be yielded to assess for occult disease in head & neck patients.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Node yield is used as a surrogate for dissection adequacy and staging reliability.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Supraclavicular flap arterial supply is based on the {{c1::supraclavicular artery::vessel}}, a branch of the {{c2::transverse cervical artery::parent vessel}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Skin paddle placement and pedicle width should protect the vascular axis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Classic supraclavicular artery course: over the {{c1::middle third of the clavicle::landmark}} toward the {{c1::ventral deltoid::direction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The arterial blood supply to the supraclavicular flap is based on the supraclavicular artery, which is a branch off of the transverse cervical artery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The anterior perforating vessel supply to the supraclavicular flap courses over the {{c1::medial third of the clavicle::landmark}} toward the {{c1::deltopectoral fossa::direction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Understanding both vascular supplies improves flap reliability.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On staging PET/CT for head & neck cancer, the most common incidental second malignancy is {{c1::thyroid cancer::site}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Always scrutinize the thyroid; focal uptake is more concerning than diffuse uptake.
If there is uptake in the thyroid, get an FNA. You don't necessarily need a fromal thyroid ultrasound

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For differentiated thyroid cancer size {{c1::>1 cm and <4 cm::size range}} with {{c2::no extrathyroidal extension::risk feature}} and {{c3::cN0::nodal status}}, the initial surgery can be {{c4::lobectomy or total thyroidectomy::extent of surgery}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Thyroid lobectomy alone may be sufficient for low-risk papillary and follicular carcinoma. Total thyroidectomy may be chosen to enable RAI or improve follow-up.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A reason to choose {{c1::total thyroidectomy::procedure}} is to facilitate {{c2::RAI therapy::reason}} and/or improve {{c3::follow-up surveillance::reason}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Molecular testing of indeterminate thyroid nodules helps differentiate {{c1::surgical management::pathway}} vs {{c1::observation/nonsurgical management::pathway}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Bethsda III and IV

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For differentiated thyroid carcinoma, RAI is {{c1::always indicated::indication}} in {{c2::ATA high-risk::risk group}} disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Best-survival thyroid cancer subtype: {{c1::follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma::specific histology}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For thyroid cancer size {{c1::>4 cm::size threshold}}, the initial surgical procedure should include {{c2::near-total or total thyroidectomy::extent of surgery}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If surgery is chosen for thyroid cancer size {{c1::<1 cm::size threshold}} with {{c2::no extrathyroidal extension::risk feature}} and {{c3::cN0::nodal status}}, the initial operation should be {{c4::thyroid lobectomy::procedure}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ACR TI-RADS: {{c1::TR3::level}} biopsy if >{{c2::2.5::size}} cm. {{c3::1-3}}% chance of malignancy

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: ACR TI-RADS: {{c1::TR4::level}} biopsy if >{{c2::1.5::size}} cm. {{c3::4-40}}% chance of malignancy

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: ACR TI-RADS: {{c1::TR5::level}} biopsy if >{{c2::1.0::size}} cm. {{c3::40-80}}% chance of malignancy

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: ACR TI-RADS: {{c1::TR1::level}} and {{c1::TR2::level}} require {{c2::no biopsy::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: ~0% chance of malignancy

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most predictive ultrasound feature of thyroid malignancy: {{c1::irregular margins::US finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Not really weighted as such on TI-RADS though

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bethesda {{c1::II::class}} is {{c2::benign::interpretation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: ~1-3% chance of malignancy

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bethesda {{c1::III and IV::classes}} are {{c2::indeterminate::interpretation}}.

fields.name: Extra
