fields.value:
Three four open the door (with genetic testing)
III = 5-15% chance of malignancy
IV = 15-30% chance of malignancy

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bethesda {{c1::V and VI::classes}} suggest {{c2::malignancy::interpretation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
V = 60-75% chance of malignancy
VI = 97-99% chance of malignancy

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In medullary thyroid cancer with {{c1::no RET mutation::genetics}}, risk of {{c2::pheochromocytoma::MEN association}} is {{c3::virtually zero::risk}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: MEN2A: medullary thyroid carcinoma + {{c1::pheochromocytoma (20–50%)::association}} + {{c2::primary hyperparathyroidism (5–20%)::association}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
MEN 2A = “2A = 2 Additional” 
Add 2 additional P's
The hyperparathyroidism is due to parathyroid hyperplasia

fields.name: Text
fields.value: MEN2B: medullary thyroid carcinoma + {{c1::pheochromocytoma (~50%)::association}} + {{c2::marfanoid habitus::phenotype}} + {{c3::mucosal/digestive neuromas::phenotype}}; thyroidectomy before age {{c4::1::age}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
MEN 2B = “B = Body Build” 
B extra cautious about the thyroid

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Known medullary thyroid cancer requires {{c1::at least total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central neck dissection::procedure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
If medullary thyroid cancer >1cm do ipsilateral II-V neck.
Consider prophylactic ipsilateral central and lateral neck when basal calcitonin >20pg/ml
Contralateral lateral neck if serum calcitonin >200pg/mL

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If final pathology shows {{c1::encapsulated follicular thyroid cancer::pathology}}, {{c2::observation::management}} is appropriate.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
No need for completion thyroidectomy when completely excised and encapsulated.

Kind of a misnomer since the definition of a follicular carcinoma is that it is not encapsulated

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In well-differentiated thyroid cancer, nodal metastases occur in about {{c1::25%::percent}} and most often involve the {{c2::central compartment::nodal basin}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Central neck lymph nodes do not change the prognostication of patients

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After RAI for DTC, relative risk of second primary malignancy is {{c1::2.7::relative risk}}; common sites {{c2::breast, colon, lung::sites}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For thyroid cancer size {{c1::<1 cm::size}}, extent of surgery {{c2::does not change recurrence or survival::outcome}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For thyroid cancer size {{c1::>1 cm::size}}, {{c2::total thyroidectomy::procedure}} lowers recurrence and improves survival.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For AUS (Bethesda III) nodules with {{c1::KRAS::mutation}}, malignancy risk ≈{{c2::33%::percent}}.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: If Bethesda {{c1::II::class}} with {{c2::KRAS::mutation}}, treat with {{c3::lobectomy::procedure}}.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: Papillary microcarcinoma can be {{c1::observed::management}} when {{c2::no unfavorable ultrasound features::criteria}} are present.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• High-risk location (posterior/dorsal surface, adjacent to RLN or trachea)
• Clinically evident cervical nodal disease
• Progressive growth on serial ultrasound
• Aggressive cytologic features
• High-risk patient factors (prior neck radiation, strong family history, poor surveillance compliance)

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Family history of thyroid cancer = {{c1::≥2 immediate family members::definition}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Unresectable thyroid cancer refractory to RAI → {{c1::external beam radiation::treatment}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Thyroid cancer
Highest malignancy risk by location: {{c1::isthmus::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
some reports 4x as likely to be a cancer
Keep in mind that the likelihood of any given nodule being a cancer is about 5-10%

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Thyroid nodule work up: after {{c1::two benign biopsies::criterion}}, malignancy risk becomes {{c2::negligible::risk level}} and the nodule can be {{c3::safely observed::management}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In well-differentiated thyroid cancer, the Delphian node is positive in about {{c1::20%::percent}} of cases.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Delphian (prelaryngeal) nodes drain isthmus and lateral lobes; positive node often predicts additional cervical nodal disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Thyroid cancer
Initial surgery should include {{c1::near-total or total thyroidectomy::extent}} when tumor is {{c2::>4 cm::size}}, {{c3::gross extrathyroidal extension::feature}}, or {{c4::clinically apparent nodal/distant disease::extent}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Total thyroidectomy is required; neck dissection is performed only when nodal disease is clinically present and is always therapeutic (not prophylactic) in the lateral neck.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Diameter of the facial nerve in the labyrinthine segment is {{c1::0.68mm}}

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Surgery for thyroiditis is associated with an increased risk of postoperative {{c1::hypocalcemia and hypoparathyroidism::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Inflammatory changes in thyroiditis increase surgical difficulty and risk of devascularizing or injuring the parathyroid glands, leading to transient or permanent hypoparathyroidism.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most important exclusionary criterion for patients being considered for endoscopic thyroidectomy is {{c1::thyroiditis::contraindication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Thyroiditis causes dense inflammatory planes around the gland, making endoscopic dissection difficult with poor visualization and higher risk of complications.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hyperplastic thyroid nodules are {{c1::polyclonal::clonality}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: whereas NIFTP is monoclonal

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In a patient with a thyroid nodule and hyperfunctioning gland after ultrasound the next test should be a {{c1::radioactive uptake and thyroid scan::test}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
uptake quantifies how much
Thyroid scan lays it over anatomy

Kind of like a PET-CT but for the thyroid

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A POD1 PTH {{c1::>10::threshold}} allows safe management with outpatient oral calcium supplementation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Early postoperative PTH is a strong predictor of hypocalcemia risk and helps guide discharge planning and supplementation strategy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Hypocalcemia
If patient is on PPI, elderly with achorlhydria, or s/p gastric bypass then it may be better to treat them with {{c1::calcium citrate}} since it does not require an acidic environment for absorption.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: You can normally give patients calcium carbonate (Tums) for hypocalcemia

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Approximately {{c1::25%::percentage}} of patients undergoing thyroidectomy for cancer experience a voice change lasting longer than 3 months post-op.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
It is about 1-5% for patient undergoing thyroidectomy for benign disease

Reflects temporary or permanent RLN dysfunction, laryngeal edema, or intubation-related effects; duration >3 months is clinically meaningful.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The majority of post-thyroidectomy neck hematomas occur within the first {{c1::8 hours::timeframe}} after surgery.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Highest-risk monitoring window; rapid recognition is critical due to airway compromise risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Absolute contraindications to TORS include the classic {{c1::“8 T’s”::mnemonic}}: teeth, transverse dimension of mandible, tori, tilt (neck extension), trismus, tumor factors, treatment (prior radiation), and tongue.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Other absolute/major contraindications often cited include: retropharyngeal carotid artery, midline base of tongue tumor, ICA encasement, T4b cancers, tumor extension to larynx, distant disease, and tumor involving mandible or hyoid (bleeding/exposure/oncologic feasibility concerns).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most commonly mutated gene in HNSCC is {{c1::TP53::gene}}, altered in >80% of tumors.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Common foundational mutation in HNSCC tumor biology; useful anchor fact.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For Zenker diverticulum, {{c1::endoscopic repair::approach}} generally has lower overall complication and morbidity rates.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Relative to open repair, endoscopic repair typically leads to earlier return to normal diet and shorter hospital discharge. Major drawback: inability to adequately expose the diverticulum occurs in ~4% of patients.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Compared with open repair, endoscopic Zenker repair has a {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} recurrence rate.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consider this tradeoff particularly in younger patients (lower periop morbidity vs higher long-term recurrence risk).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Benign vocal fold lesions that DO change mucosal wave include {{c1::cysts and fibrous masses::2 lesions}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Lesions that typically do NOT change mucosal wave: nodules, polyps, reactive vocal fold lesions. Preserved wave suggests more superficial pathology; decreased/absent wave suggests deeper lamina propria involvement.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Management of reactive vocal fold lesions: {{c1::do not surgically excise::management}}; can consider {{c2::steroid injection into the vocal folds::treatment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Focus on conservative management and addressing underlying phonotrauma/inflammation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vocal fold granulomas occur near the {{c1::vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage::location}} due to {{c2::intubation or chronic phonotrauma::etiology::2}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often associated with chronic coughing/voicing and LPR.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Treatment of vocal fold granuloma is primarily {{c1::conservative::management}}; options include surgical removal or {{c2::botulinum toxin injection into the TA–LCA complex::procedure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Botox reduces hyperfunctional closure forces contributing to granuloma persistence/recurrence.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vascular ectasias / venous lakes of the vocal folds are treated with {{c1::KTP laser::treatment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Targets vascular lesions with minimal mucosal injury.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Deep cervical fascia has {{c1::three::number of layers}} layers: {{c2::investing::layer 1}}, {{c2::pretracheal::layer 2}}, and {{c2::prevertebral::layer 3}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Investing = outer coat;
Pretracheal = strap muscles + visceral structures;
Prevertebral = vertebral column & deep neck muscles.
These layers create surgical compartments and deep neck spaces.

https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The superficial cervical fascia contains the {{c2::platysma::muscle}}, superficial veins, cutaneous nerves, fat, and lymphatics.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Cutaneous nerves: lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2–3), transverse cervical (C2–3), supraclavicular (C3–4). Lies just under skin; does not form deep neck spaces.

https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia envelops {{c2::SCM and trapezius::2 muscles}} and encloses the {{c3::parotid and submandibular glands::2 glands}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Forms roof of anterior/posterior triangles; contributes to parotid fascia → stylomandibular ligament.

https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia has {{c1::muscular::portion}} and {{c1::visceral::portion}} components.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Muscular portion wraps strap muscles; visceral portion encloses thyroid, trachea, esophagus, and pharynx.

https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The visceral portion of the pretracheal fascia extends from the {{c1::skull base::superior limit}} to the {{c1::mediastinum::inferior limit}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The visceral portion of the pretracheal fascia is also called the buccopharyngeal fascia. Explains spread of infection to mediastinum.
This is the retropharyngeal space
PBR ADPPA

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the {{c2::cervical vertebrae::bone}}, {{c3::deep neck and scalene muscles::muscles}}, and contains the {{c4::phrenic::nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Deep neck muscles include longus colli, longus capitis, splenius capitis/cervicis, levator scapulae; forms floor of posterior triangle.

https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The carotid sheath is formed by contributions from {{c1::all three layers of deep cervical fascia::source layers}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Contributing layers: investing, pretracheal, prevertebral. Contents: carotid artery, IJV, vagus nerve, deep cervical nodes.

https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The retropharyngeal space lies between the {{c1::visceral portion of the pretracheal (buccopharyngeal portion) fascia::anterior boundary}} and the {{c2::alar portion of the prevertebral fascia::posterior boundary}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Buccopharyngeal fascia = visceral portion of pretracheal fascia. Major deep neck infection space; pediatric nodes regress after ~5 years.

How you learn deep neck spaces in medical school is different than how you deal with them in ENT. Clasically you learn that the order is pharyngeal mucosa, buccopharyngeal fascia, retropharyngeal space, alar fascia, danger space, prevertebral fascia, prevertebral space, anterior spinal ligament.

In practice, the buccopharyngeal fascia is part of the visceral fascia which is a subsite of the pretracheal fascia. The alar fascia is a subsite of the prevertebral fascia

https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia forms the {{c1::roof::anatomic role}} of both the anterior and posterior cervical triangles.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Anterior triangle: between midline, mandible, anterior SCM.
Posterior triangle: between posterior SCM, trapezius, clavicle.
Roof = investing fascia + platysma/skin.


https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The superficial cervical fascia does {{c1::not::does/does not}} create deep neck spaces.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Deep neck spaces are defined by layers of deep cervical fascia, not superficial fascia.

https://www.earthslab.com/anatomy/deep-cervical-fascia-fascia-colli/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c2::Dorello’s canal::eponym}} transmits {{c1::abducens nerve (CN VI)::cranial nerve}} into the {{c3::cavernous sinus}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
CN VI is tethered here → vulnerable to ↑ICP, clival/petroclival lesions, and petrous apicitis (Gradenigo syndrome).

Boundaries of Dorello’s canal:
Superior = Gruber’s (petrosphenoidal) ligament;
Inferior = petrous apex of temporal bone;
Medial = clivus;
Lateral = petrous apex.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Reinke’s edema: first-line management is {{c1::smoking cessation::behavior change}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
AKA polypoid corditis
Smoking drives the inflammatory/edematous changes. Procedure options are adjuncts; counsel voice hygiene. If persistent/refractory after conservative measures, consider office-based or OR intervention (e.g., KTP laser or microflap depending on bulk and goals).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Reinke’s edema refractory to conservative management can be treated with {{c1::KTP laser::procedure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Recalcitrant = ongoing symptoms despite risk-factor modification and voice hygiene. KTP targets vascularity; microflap also considered.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Chronic cough chemoreceptors are {{c1::unmyelinated C-fiber nociceptors::fiber type}} that express {{c2::TRPV1 and TRPA1::2 receptors}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The chemo removes all of the myelin
Trip to VA
Chronic cough involves both chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors. Chemoreceptors = unmyelinated C fibers; mechanoreceptors = myelinated fibers responding to touch/stretch/airflow.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Chronic cough mechanoreceptors are {{c1::myelinated fibers::myelinated/unmyelinaated}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Chronic cough involves both chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors. Mechanoreceptors = myelinated fibers; chemoreceptors = unmyelinated C fibers (TRPV1/TRPA1).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ACE inhibitor cough is due to accumulation of {{c1::bradykinin (± substance P)::mediators}} normally metabolized by ACE.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Can present even after years of tolerance. Diagnostic maneuver = stop ACEi (switch to ARB).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After stopping an ACE inhibitor, cough typically resolves in {{c1::1–4::timeframe}} weeks but can persist up to 3 months.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: If persistent, reassess for UACS, asthma, reflux, neuropathic cough.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Upper airway cough syndrome is related to {{c1::sinonasal disease::etiology}} and is often the {{c2::most common::frequency}} cause of chronic cough.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Treat the nose and reassess.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Upper airway cough syndrome initial therapy: {{c1::intranasal steroids::medication}}; consider {{c2::1st-gen antihistamines::medication}} for anticholinergic effect.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: 1st gen antihistamines help via anticholinergic effect.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If spirometry is normal but cough-variant asthma is suspected, order a {{c1::methacholine challenge::test}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Helps diagnose variable airflow restriction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For suspected neuropathic/refractory chronic cough, first-line is {{c1::gabapentin or pregabalin::medication}} plus {{c1::speech therapy::therapy}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Neuromodulation + behavioral therapy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Strong predictors of dysphagia after anterior cervical spine surgery include {{c1::female sex, revision surgery, and multilevel surgery::risk factors::3}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful for counseling.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Inclusion body myositis is associated with {{c1::cricopharyngeus dysfunction::condition}} causing dysphagia.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often includes obstructing CP segment (CP bar), plus pharyngeal weakness and poor hyolaryngeal elevation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In inclusion body myositis with poor hyolaryngeal elevation, the {{c1::Mendelsohn maneuver::therapy}} can be used.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Targets hyolaryngeal elevation/UES opening.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For significant dysphagia from obstructing CP segment in inclusion body myositis, definitive treatment is {{c1::cricopharyngeal myotomy::procedure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Balloon dilation/CP Botox mixed; myotomy effective when obstruction dominates.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In unilateral vocal fold paralysis after cardiothoracic surgery, {{c1::injection laryngoplasty::procedure}} may reduce pneumonia risk.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Improves glottic closure and cough.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The hallmark of silent aspiration is loss of {{c1::laryngeal sensation::physiology}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High risk in neurologic disease, post-radiation sensory loss.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Parkinson-related dysphonia is best treated with {{c1::voice therapy focused on increasing loudness (e.g., LSVT LOUD)::therapy}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Deep brain stimulation can worsen speech; meds often don't help voice.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dysphonia guideline: perform laryngoscopy when dysphonia fails to resolve within {{c1::4::timeframe}} weeks.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Earlier if red flags or airway symptoms.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dysphonia guideline: {{c1::do not::do/do not}} routinely prescribe antibiotics for dysphonia.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Avoid unnecessary harm.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dysphonia guideline: {{c1::do not::do/do not}} obtain CT/MRI before visualizing the larynx.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Image later if indicated.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dysphonia guideline: before prescribing voice therapy, clinicians should {{c1::perform laryngoscopy and communicate/document results to the SLP::process}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Prevents treating blind.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A distinguishing laryngeal finding for {{c1::multiple system atrophy (MSA)::diagnosis}}  is {{c2::bilateral vocal fold paralysis::key finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Parkinson disease can have hypophonia/dysarthria, but true BVFP points toward MSA.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Tongue fasciculations::exam finding}} are associated with {{c2::ALS::diagnosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: LMN involvement; major neurologic red flag in dysarthria workup.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common infectious cause of esophagitis is {{c1::Candida esophagitis::diagnosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Independent risk factors: age, HIV status, corticosteroid use (dose dependent). Majority may lack classic immunosuppression.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In vocal fold atrophy, a good response to trial VFI predicts a {{c1::good::outcome}} response to long-term augmentation about 75% of the time.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Trial injection is a guide, not perfect predictor; persistent handicap may occur.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In vocal fold atrophy, a poor response to trial VFI predicts a {{c1::poor::outcome}} response to long-term augmentation about 55% of the time.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: ~45% with poor trial response may still benefit from long-term augmentation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In glottic insufficiency with dysphagia, vocal fold injection can improve dysphagia by increasing {{c1::peak expiratory flow and acceleration during cough::mechanism}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Better glottic closure → stronger cough → improved airway clearance.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Outcomes after medialization laryngoplasty for UVFP in patients >65 years are {{c1::similar::comparison}} to younger patients.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Do not withhold medialization based on age alone.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Compared with idiopathic subglottic stenosis, GPA-related stenosis has higher risk of {{c1::mechanical dilations::outcome}} and {{c2::tracheotomy::outcome}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: GPA behaves more aggressively for recurrence/airway compromise.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In idiopathic subglottic stenosis, endoscopic resection has the {{c1::lowest::relative}} voice handicap scores.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Open resection: better airway/QOL but worse long-term voice in many series.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Idiopathic subglottic stenosis: open approaches are {{c1::less likely::comparison}} to require subsequent surgeries but higher risk of persistent vocal change (especially when {{c2::cricoid::structure}} involved).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classic durability vs voice tradeoff.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cricotracheal resection lowers pitch because it removes the {{c1::cricothyroid muscle::structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Patients may have reduced pitch change and overall lower pitch.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Idiopathic subglottic stenosis: topical {{c1::mitomycin C::medication}} may increase duration between operations.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Use as counseling point; variable evidence.
Mitomycin C use can complicate resection surgery

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Inducible laryngeal obstruction (ILO) is the new term for {{c1::paradoxical vocal fold motion::old term}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Episodic inappropriate laryngeal closure; treated with breathing/SLP techniques.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Schatzki rule: symptoms usually appear when esophageal lumen is ~{{c1::13::mm}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Normal adult lumen is 20–30 mm.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Normal adult esophageal lumen diameter is {{c1::20–30::mm}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Compare with Schatzki threshold ~13 mm.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: in RRP. Papillomas on the {{c1::infraglottic surface::location}} often need multiple angiolytic laser treatments.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Not perpendicular to laser fiber → harder ablation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A common donor nerve for laryngeal reinnervation is the {{c1::ansa cervicalis::donor nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Proximity, size match to RLN, minimal morbidity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laryngeal amyloidosis: Most commonly {{c1::isolated to the larynx::distribution}}; systemic involvement occurs in {{c2::<20%::frequency}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: For isolated laryngeal amyloidosis, local therapy is typically appropriate (e.g., endoscopic debulking/laser as needed). Systemic disease is uncommon but important to screen for. Most common systemic manifestation to remember: nephrotic syndrome.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laryngeal amyloidosis (systemic): Most common systemic manifestation is {{c1::nephrotic syndrome::systemic manifestation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Systemic involvement in laryngeal amyloidosis is uncommon (<20%), but when present, renal involvement with nephrotic syndrome is the classic association to recall.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laryngocele: Contraindication to {{c1::scuba diving::activity}} until surgically repaired.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Laryngocele can expand with pressure changes; counsel patients to avoid scuba diving until repaired.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laryngocele risk association: Laryngocele is classically seen in {{c1::glass blowers and wind instrument players::association}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Think chronic increased intralaryngeal pressure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Muscle tension dysphonia: Laryngoscopic finding can include {{c1::anterior and posterior compression::laryngoscopic finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Symptoms often fluctuate and worsen with excess voice use (helps distinguish from fixed structural lesions; confirm with exam and treat with voice therapy/behavioral strategies).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Adductor laryngeal dystonia: Characterized by a strained and strangled voice quality with breaks, most pronounced during {{c1::vowel-heavy words::trigger}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classic elicitation task: counting 80–89 to bring out adductor breaks.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Abductor laryngeal dystonia: Presents with {{c1::breathy voice breaks::voice quality}} during consonant-heavy sentences with voiceless-to-voiced phonemes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Common trigger phonemes include f, h, k, p, s, sh, t, th (voiceless → voiced transitions).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Mixed laryngeal dystonia: Has elements of both {{c1::abductor and adductor laryngeal dystonia}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Expect both breathy (abductor) and strained (adductor) breaks depending on speech task.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vocal tremor: Characterized by shaky voice quality with regular oscillatory alterations in pitch and volume most pronounced with {{c1::sustained vowel phonation::task}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Different from dystonia (task-specific breaks); tremor is rhythmic and often brought out by sustained vowels.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Laryngeal dystonia history clue: Suggestive features include voice breaks, worsening {{c2::on the phone/under stress}}, and normal voice when {{c1::laughing/singing/whispering::history clue}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Diagnosis cannot be confirmed based solely on history; confirmation requires exam/phenomenology (history is supportive but not definitive).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Abductor laryngeal dystonia treatment: Best first-line therapy is botox into the {{c1::posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA)::target}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: PCA injection is technically harder than TA-LCA complex; dosing limited by dyspnea risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Botox for laryngeal dystonia: Voice outcomes are best for patients with {{c1::adductor laryngeal dystonia::subtype}}, with an estimated {{c2::90–95%::success rate}} success.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Abductor laryngeal dystonia has less consistent benefit, with success ~66–75% in reported series. Practical reasons include PCA injection being technically more challenging with an estimated miss rate ~1 in 8 (vs ~1 in 20 for TA-LCA injections), and dosing limitations due to dyspnea/airway obstruction risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ILO refractory therapy: ILO refractory to laryngeal control therapy/biofeedback can be treated with {{c1::botox injections::treatment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Dyspnea Severity Index is expected to improve post-injection; patients often require more than one injection; most common side effect is breathy voice.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Voice grading: GRBAS = {{c1::grade, roughness, breathiness, asthenia, strain::components}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Standard perceptual scale for dysphonia severity/quality characterization.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Posterior glottic stenosis (clinical pitfall): Can mimic {{c1::bilateral vocal fold paralysis::mimic}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Nerve is intact; limitation is from posterior glottic scar/ankylosis rather than RLN injury.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Posterior glottic stenosis risk factors: Risk factors include {{c1::prolonged/traumatic intubation, oversized endotracheal tube, diabetes mellitus, and longer duration of intubation::risk factors}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Core concept: posterior glottic mucosal pressure injury + poor wound healing → scar/stenosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bogdasarian & Olson staging (PGS): Stage I = {{c1::vocal process adhesion::Stage I}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Higher stages reflect increasing posterior commissure scarring and cricoarytenoid (CA) joint involvement.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bogdasarian & Olson staging (PGS): Stage II = posterior commissure stenosis with scarring in the {{c1::interarytenoid plane and internal surface of posterior cricoid lamina::Stage II description}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Stage II implies posterior commissure scar without CA joint ankylosis yet.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bogdasarian & Olson staging (PGS): Stage III = posterior commissure stenosis with {{c1::unilateral cricoarytenoid joint ankylosis::Stage III}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Joint fixation begins; impacts motion and drives management complexity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bogdasarian & Olson staging (PGS): Stage IV = posterior commissure stenosis with {{c1::bilateral cricoarytenoid joint ankylosis::Stage IV}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most severe; bilateral fixation severely compromises airway/voice.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: PGS management: “Low grade” (Bogdasarian–Olson stage I–II) can be treated with {{c1::steroid injection + endoscopic scar lysis with dilation::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Low grade = no CA joint ankylosis (adhesion/scar). “Advanced/high grade” (stage III–IV) involves CA joint ankylosis and/or severe posterior commissure stenosis and often needs airway-enlarging procedures.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: PGS management (advanced/recurrent): Advanced/high grade PGS (Bogdasarian–Olson stage III–IV) may require {{c1::cordotomy with or without arytenoidectomy, and/or endoscopic advancement flaps::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High grade typically implies CA joint ankylosis (unilateral or bilateral) and higher recurrence risk; airway gains often come with voice/aspiration tradeoffs.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Presbyphonia (aging changes): Aging causes {{c1::neuromuscular + connective tissue changes::category}} including decreased laryngeal nerve fiber density/TA atrophy, calcification of supporting hyaline cartilages, increased disorganized type I collagen, and decreased elastin/hyaluronic acid → increased vocal fold stiffness.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These changes variably reduce neuromuscular control and mucosal wave efficiency; symptoms and severity are patient-dependent.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Presbyphonia prevalence/treatment: Presbyphonia affects at least {{c1::30%::prevalence}} of older adults; first-line treatment is {{c2::voice therapy::treatment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Exam classically shows bowing with prominent vocal processes (spindle-shaped gap from atrophy).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Puberphonia: Also called {{c1::mutational falsetto / adolescent male transitional dysphonia / incomplete mutation / persistent falsetto::aka}}; first-line treatment is {{c2::behavioral voice therapy::treatment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Functional voice disorder around adolescent voice change; can persist into adulthood.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Tracheal resection capacity (adults): Resection and primary anastomosis can include up to {{c1::50%::fraction}} of tracheal length or {{c2::6::measurement}} cm with releasing procedures.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Release maneuvers increase mobility to reduce anastomotic tension; tension is the limiting factor.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Diabetes and obesity::risk factors}} are risk factors for adult subglottic stenosis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Predispose via wound healing/inflammation pathways; also consider prolonged intubation history, autoimmune causes, etc.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In-office flexible laser bronchoscopy contraindications: Contraindications include {{c1::glottic or tracheal stenosis::contraindication}} and vertical scar length >{{c2::1::measurement}} cm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Greater scar burden or airway narrowing typically needs OR-based approach and more controlled airway management.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Subglottic stenosis (endoscopic contraindications): Contraindications include {{c1::circumferential cicatricial scarring; abundant scar tissue >1 cm vertical; fibrotic scar in posterior commissure/interarytenoid; severe bacterial infection after tracheotomy; exposure of perichondrium/cartilage during CO2 excision; combined laryngotracheal stenosis; failure of previous endoscopic procedures; significant loss of cartilaginous framework::contraindications}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Core idea: high scar burden, multi-level disease, active infection, cartilage/perichondrium exposure, or failed prior endoscopic management predicts poor endoscopic outcomes and pushes toward open reconstruction strategies.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Swallow trigger: Tongue moving posteriorly to touch the {{c1::faucial arches::trigger point}} triggers the {{c2::pharyngeal phase::swallow phase}} of swallowing.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Oral phase transitions to pharyngeal phase once sensory trigger at anterior pillars/faucial arches is reached.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Primary muscle of the UES is the {{c1::cricopharyngeal (CP) muscle::muscle}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: CP forms functional high-pressure zone; relaxation + hyolaryngeal excursion enables bolus passage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: CP/UES has dual innervation from {{c1::CN IX via pharyngeal plexus + CN X (external branch SLN / RLN)::innervation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mixed plexus contributions explain variability in dysfunction patterns and surgical targeting.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cricopharyngeal dysfunction phase: Cricopharyngeal dysfunction is a disorder of the {{c1::esophageal phase::swallow phase}} of swallowing.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Even though CP sits at the pharyngoesophageal segment, the dysfunction is typically conceptualized as esophageal phase (UES opening/relaxation issue).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::7–22%::prevalence}} of adults over the age of 50 have a swallowing disorder.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: In 2001, yearly expenditure for an individual dependent on tube feeding was ~$30,000, and Medicare spent ~6% of its annual DME budget (~$670 million) on enteral feeding supplies alone.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::30%::percentage}} of individuals who localize swallowing dysfunction to the neck have a primary {{c2::esophageal::subsite}} etiology.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: “Feels stuck in the neck” does not exclude esophageal pathology.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nearly {{c1::25%::percentage}} of individuals with unilateral vocal cord immobility will aspirate thin liquids.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Supports early swallow evaluation/precautions in symptomatic patients.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Pooled saliva in the {{c1::pyriform sinuses::location}} suggests profound swallowing dysfunction and predicts aspiration.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield endoscopic red flag for impaired clearance.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After successful medialization laryngoplasty (± arytenoid adduction), advised waiting period before elective intubation is {{c1::6 months::timeframe}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Common counseling point for patients worried about future surgeries.
These patients can be intubated with a size 6 ETT after the waiting period

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Recommended endotracheal tube size after medialization is {{c1::6.0 or smaller::tube size}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: To avoid edema in a slightly narrowed glottis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Rate of stenosis from ETT is about {{c1::~3%::rate}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Helpful for counseling and risk framing.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Inhalation burn is associated with about {{c1::6%::rate}} risk of laryngotracheal stenosis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-risk group for airway surveillance.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For a trial vocal fold injection, preferred temporary material is {{c1::carboxymethylcellulose::material}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
ex Prolaryn
Trial injection generally correlates with permanent outcomes but is not perfect.
Lasts for 6-8 weeks and up to 3 months

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Carboxymethylcellulose typically lasts {{c1::6–8 weeks to 3 months::duration}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Appropriate window for a “trial” effect.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
{{c1::Fat::material (not CAHA)}} is a permanent autologous injectable;
 CaHa last for about {{c2::12 months::timeframe}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Quick durability hierarchy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Teflon fell out of favor for medialization due to late {{c1::granuloma formation::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classic board fact.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Injection augmentation is reasonable for glottic gaps up to {{c1::3::measurement}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Larger gaps tend to have poorer outcomes with injection alone → consider surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vocal fold cyst = {{c1::subepidermal epithelial-lined sacs within the lamina propria::definition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Typically unilateral; stroboscopy shows decreased/absent mucosal wave on the cyst side.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common cause of unilateral vocal fold immobility in adults is {{c1::iatrogenic::etiology}} (~46%).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Non-thyroid surgery accounts for ~two-thirds of iatrogenic cases (e.g., ACDF, CEA, cardiac surgery).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Mean time to recovery of vocal function after vocal fold paralysis is about {{c1::180::time}} days.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mobility is not required for function; ~90% recover vocal fold function; recovery not affected by age, sex, laterality, or injury site. Preliminary studies in animals and humans suggest early promise for nimodipine in acute UVFP.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Conus elasticus originates from the {{c1::upper border of the cricoid cartilage::origin}} and rises to the glottic aperture.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Memory hook: “conus = cricoid.”
Quadrangular Membrane (Supraglottis)

Located above the ventricle.

Attachments:

* Superior: lateral epiglottis
* Posterior: arytenoid cartilage

Free edges:

* Superior free edge → aryepiglottic fold
* Inferior free edge → vestibular ligament (forms the false vocal fold)

Function:

* Supports the supraglottic larynx
* Forms the framework of the false cords and aryepiglottic folds

Conus Elasticus (Glottis/Subglottis)

Located below the ventricle.

Attachments:

* Inferiorly: superior border of the cricoid cartilage
* Anteriorly: thyroid cartilage
* Posteriorly: vocal process of the arytenoid

Free superior edge:

* Vocal ligament (forms the true vocal fold)

Function:

* Supports the true vocal folds
* Forms the cricothyroid membrane anteriorly
* Provides the elastic recoil of the vocal folds

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Superiorly, thickened free edges of the conus elasticus form the {{c1::vocal ligaments::structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Links conus elasticus to layered vocal fold anatomy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Typical glottal cycle frequency is ~{{c1::100::rate}} Hz in men and ~{{c2::220::rate}} Hz in women.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: “Cycles per second” = Hz.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cog separates the {{c1::supratubal recess::space}} from the epitympanum.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Small but high-yield anatomic divider.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Intact ossicular chain provides about {{c3::27.5}} dB of gain.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Breakdown: ~25::TM/footplate dB from TM-to-stapes footplate area ratio + ~2.5 dB from ossicular lever ratio.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A {{c1::3}} dB change corresponds to a doubling/halving of {{c2::intensity::physical}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Rule of thumb: +3 dB ≈ 2× intensity (power).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A {{c1::10}} dB change corresponds to a doubling of {{c2::perceived loudness::perception}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Rule of thumb: +10 dB ≈ 2× loudness (subjective).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Occlusion effect}} = plugged sensation with own voice/chewing louder (more common with {{c2::ITC/CIC hearing aids::device type}} vs open-fit RIC).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: ITC = in-the-canal; CIC = completely-in-canal. Mechanism: trapped low-frequency bone-conducted sound in an occluded ear canal.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Squelch effect}} = binaural listening improves effective signal-to-noise ratio compared with one ear.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Central auditory processing phenomenon (binaural advantage in noise).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Stenger phenomenon: same tone to both ears at different loudness levels is perceived {{c1::only in the louder ear::key point}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful in suspected non-organic unilateral hearing loss.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: TM-to-stapes footplate area ratio (~{{c1::20:1::ratio}}) accounts for most {{c2::impedance matching::process}} from air to inner-ear fluid.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Major contributor to impedance matching vs lever ratio.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Frequency region of greatest energy concentration and optimal transmission is about {{c1::3–4::frequency band}} kHz.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield anchor when thinking about transmission and speech energy distribution.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For tympanometry in newborns to 6 months, preferred probe tone is {{c1::1000::Hz probe tone}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: For 6–9 months, consider using both 226 Hz and 1000 Hz probe tones if needed to clarify middle ear pathology (transitional physiology).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Type {{c1::As::tymp type}} tympanogram = shallow peak with normal ear canal volume/pressure → {{c2::hypocompliance::mechanics}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Seen with stiff middle ear systems (e.g., ossicular fixation) or TM changes (e.g., tympanosclerosis).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Type {{c1::Ad::tymp type}} tympanogram = normal ear canal volume/pressure with {{c2::hypercompliance::mechanics}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consistent with ossicular disarticulation (including post-stapedectomy) and TM atrophy; may suggest patulous ET in aural fullness complaints.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Poor low-frequency hearing rising to normal in the high frequencies can be seen with {{c1::middle ear pathology and endolymphatic hydrops/Ménière disease::associations}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Pattern-recognition clue; correlate with tymps and symptoms.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Two most powerful neurodiagnostic ABR values: wave {{c1::I–V interpeak latency::metric}} and interaural latency difference of wave {{c2::V::wave}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield for retrocochlear pathology screening.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ECochG has three major components: {{c1::cochlear microphonic (CM)::component}}, {{c2::summating potential (SP)::component}}, and {{c3::action potential (AP)::component}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Normal responses include all three.

Sum Sinner: SP is from the inner hair cells
Outer hair cells generate the cochlear microphonic 
Action potential is generated by the auditory nerve fibers

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ABR: Cochelar microphonic is generated by {{c1::outer hair cells::generator}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: CM (cochlear microphonic) is an alternating-current receptor potential that mirrors the acoustic stimulus waveform.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Summating potential is thought to be generated largely by {{c1::inner hair cells::generator}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
SUM Sinner

SP (summating potential) is a direct-current shift reflecting asymmetric hair-cell transduction during sustained stimulation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ECochG AP is generated by {{c1::CN VIII fibers nearest the cochlea::generator}} and corresponds to ABR wave {{c2::I::ABR wave}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: AP (action potential) is the compound action potential of the auditory nerve.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A pronounced {{c1::unilateral deficit::pattern}} is one common auditory processing disorder test-battery pattern.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: APD = auditory processing disorder (difficulty processing auditory information in the CNS despite normal peripheral hearing in many cases).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Best behavioral audiology modality by age: {{c2::<6 months}} = {{c1::behavioral observation audiometry::test}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Approx. developmental ageTestWhat the child does
0–6 moBOA — Behavioral Observation AudiometryExaminer observes reflexive/behavioral change to sound
6 mo–2.5 yrVRA — Visual Reinforcement AudiometryTurns toward sound → rewarded with visual stimulus
2.5–5 yrCPA — Conditioned Play AudiometryPerforms a game task when sound is heard
≥5 yrConventional audiometryRaises hand/pushes button when sound is heard

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ABR is least accurate at {{c1::low frequencies::frequency range}} and with {{c2::severe-to-profound hearing loss::severity}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Inherent uncertainty between ABR and behavioral thresholds may be as much as ~15::dB.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Diagnosing ANSD requires present {{c1::outer hair cell::anatomy criterion}} function plus {{c2::dys-synchronous auditory neural activity on ABR::criterion}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Sound enters the ear and the cochlea works (present OAEs) but the signal gets scrambled after that (inner hair cells so abnormal ABR)

Cochlear microphonic must be present
ANSD = auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder (intact cochlear OHC function with impaired neural synchrony/afferent transmission). Pure-tone thresholds don’t correlate with severity; hyperbilirubinemia/prematurity are risk factors but not sufficient.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common genetic etiology for ANSD is {{c1::OTOF (otoferlin) mutations::gene}}, causing an “auditory synaptopathy.”

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Otoferlin is expressed in presynaptic neurotransmitter vesicles.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Differential for a blue middle ear includes {{c1::glomus tumor, cholesterol granuloma, jugular bulb dehiscence, and aberrant carotid artery::differential}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Classic “blue ear” list.
Glomus: 
Cholesterol granuloma: 
Dehiscence of jugular bulb: 
Abberant internal carotid artery:

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In bilateral conductive hearing loss, unilateral vs bilateral BAHD can have similar outcomes on {{c1::speech in noise testing::testing condition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Bilateral BAHD improves localization, tonal detection, word recognition in quiet, and SRT, but speech-in-noise benefit is mixed and can be neutral or worse in some noise configurations.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Soft tissue complication rate after BAHD is ~{{c1::27%::rate}} in both adults and children.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Children are >3× as likely to lose the implant 13% children vs 4% adults, often due to head trauma risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c3::Bruns}} nystagmus (often from CPA tumors) = {{c1::low}}-frequency, {{c1::large}}-amplitude nystagmus when looking {{c1::ipsilaterally}} and {{c2::high}}-frequency, {{c2::low}}-amplitude nystagmus when looking {{c2::contralaterally}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Ipsilateral component relates to cerebellar dysfunction; contralateral component relates to ipsilateral vestibular loss.
Can be seen in CPA tumors

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A lesion in the CPA that is hyperintense on pre-gadolinium T1, hyperintense on T2, and drops signal on fat-suppressed sequences is most consistent with {{c1::lipoma::diagnosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Fat-suppression is the key discriminator; typically congenital and slow growing → often observed.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: At the brainstem, CN VII is {{c1::anterior::anterior/posterior}} and CN VIII is {{c1::posterior::anterior/posterior}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: In the IAC, mnemonic: “7 up, Coke down.”

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nonvestibular schwannomas account for {{c1::2–3%::frequency}} of CPA tumors; most common subtype is {{c2::trigeminal schwannoma::type}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often in NF2; trigeminal schwannoma can present with ipsilateral facial hypoesthesia and may be adjacent to/expand Meckel’s cave.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Facial schwannoma: if House–Brackmann I–III, initial management is {{c1::observation::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: If worse function: consider decompression (middle fossa or transmastoid depending on extent). If nonfunctional nerve: resection + cable graft (greater auricular or sural).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Meningioma is the {{c1::second::rank}} most common neoplasm of the CPA.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Treatment options include observation, radiation, and microsurgical resection (depending on growth/symptoms).
T1 w contrast

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A CPA lesion that is iso- or slightly hypointense to gray on T1, variable on T2, enhances with gadolinium, and has a broad dural base (“dural tail”) is most consistent with {{c1::meningioma::diagnosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Correlate with location/extra-axial signs; dural attachment is a key clue.
T1 w contrast

T2

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nonenhancing lesion that is T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, and often hyperintense on FLAIR = {{c1::epidermoid vs dermoid::diagnosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Epidermoid is an intracranial congenital cholesteatoma analog. Dermoid contains fat and adnexal components (often intrinsic high T1 from fat; may calcify on CT).
T1

T2

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Management of asymptomatic petrous apex cholesterol granuloma
{{c1::observation::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Imaging clue: classically bright on both T1 and T2; correlate with CT for expansile change/erosion.

symptoms include:
Unilateral hearing loss (conductive, mixed, or sensorineural)
tinnitus,
aural fullness,
vertigo or chronic disequilibrium,
deep temporal or retro-orbital headache.
Cranial nerve involvement from mass effect may occur, most classically CN VI causing horizontal diplopia; CN V involvement can cause facial numbness or pain.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: MRI: High signal on T1 and high signal on T2 in a petrous apex lesion is most consistent with {{c1::cholesterol granuloma::diagnosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Correlate with CT (expansile lesion with trabecular thinning and possible bony erosion depending on size/location).
T1

T2

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::conus elasticus::anatomic structure}} is the same thing as the cricothyroid membrane

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Quadrangular Membrane (Supraglottis)

Located above the ventricle.

Attachments:

* Superior: lateral epiglottis
* Posterior: arytenoid cartilage

Free edges:

* Superior free edge → aryepiglottic fold
* Inferior free edge → vestibular ligament (forms the false vocal fold)

Function:

* Supports the supraglottic larynx
* Forms the framework of the false cords and aryepiglottic folds

Conus Elasticus (Glottis/Subglottis)

Located below the ventricle.

Attachments:

* Inferiorly: superior border of the cricoid cartilage
* Anteriorly: thyroid cartilage
* Posteriorly: vocal process of the arytenoid

Free superior edge:

* Vocal ligament (forms the true vocal fold)

Function:

* Supports the true vocal folds
* Forms the cricothyroid membrane anteriorly
* Provides the elastic recoil of the vocal folds

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Aural irrigation complication rate is about {{c1::1 in 1,000::frequency}} episodes (significant enough to require ENT referral).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This is a practical counseling/risks number for cerumen irrigation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The pouch of von Troeltsch lies between the TM and the {{c1::anterior malleal fold::structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: In cholesteatoma with a labyrinthine fistula, if cochlear function is {{c1::nonfunctional (dead ear)::hearing status}}, you can remove matrix from the fistula and patch it;

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
if hearing is present, many leave matrix in place.

Key concept is balancing eradication vs iatrogenic SNHL/inner ear injury risk when peeling matrix off a fistula.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cost/outcomes literature shows that recurrence risk in single-stage cholesteatoma removal is {{c1::similar::better/same/worse}} compared with planned second-look surgery.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Important caveat is selection bias: surgeons tend to choose single-stage when they believe they can clear all disease. (Crowson et al., Laryngoscope 2016 — per your note.)

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Average hearing outcomes (PTA) are better with {{c1::canal wall up::canal wall up/canal wall down}} procedures (about 30 dB vs 45 dB).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: CWU tends to preserve canal anatomy and can have better audiometric outcomes, but disease control/recurrence considerations vary by case and technique.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: EAONO/JOS middle ear cholesteatoma staging: Stage I = {{c1::localized to the primary site::stage definition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This is the “confined” stage before multi-site involvement or complications.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: EAONO/JOS stage II cholesteatoma = involvement of {{c1::two or more sites::stage definition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Think “multi-compartment” disease without defined extra-/intracranial complication criteria.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: EAONO/JOS stage III cholesteatoma = extracranial complications/pathologic conditions (e.g., facial palsy, labyrinthine fistula/labyrinthitis, postauricular abscess/fistula, zygomatic/neck abscess, canal wall destruction).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: “Bad local behavior” but not intracranial.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: EAONO/JOS stage IV cholesteatoma = {{c1::intracranial complications::stage definition}} .

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The “IC” complication stage.
(e.g., meningitis, epidural/subdural/brain abscess, sinus thrombosis, brain herniation into mastoid cavity)

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Mastoidectomy can be considered for non-cholesteatomatous chronic otitis media when there is {{c1::failed tympanoplasty::indication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: “Dry ear goal” logic: persistent disease despite tympanoplasty may push toward mastoid work depending on pattern and surgeon judgment.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ideal cochlear implant insertion is into the {{c1::scala tympani::site}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Classic atraumatic insertion teaching point.
Sound has to pass through the tympanic membrane in a normal ear and the scala tympani in an implant ear

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cochlea (uncoiled) length is roughly {{c1::30–35::length}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful for electrode array length intuition and insertion depth discussions.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cochleostomy is made at the {{c1::anterior-inferior}} quadrant of the round window membrane.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Same as where you put a PE tube
Mastoid view orientation can feel “superior-lateral” depending on patient positioning.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Adult cochlear implant candidacy in the US often uses sentence recognition (e.g., AzBio) in best-aided condition: <{{c1::50%::cutoff}} open-set sentence recognition in quiet in the ear to be implanted and <{{c2::60%::cutoff}} in the contralateral ear.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Your note emphasizes sentence recognition (not just pure-tone thresholds).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After CI for SSD, CNC words and AzBio sentences in quiet can improve by {{c1::3 months::timepoint}} post-op; by {{c2::6 months::timepoint}}, scores may not improve much further vs 3 months (in the referenced cohort).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Practical counseling: early improvement plateau can happen; continued adaptation varies.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Long-term language trajectory after early simultaneous bilateral CI: children may perform similarly to normal hearing peers around {{c1::2 years::timepoint}} post-implant, but underperform again at {{c2::4–6 years::timeframe}} post-implant in some cohorts.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: From your cited Norwegian data: gap narrows in early years, then later expressive grammar/receptive vocabulary may lag; outcomes relate to speech recognition, age at activation, and maternal education.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Cogan syndrome}}: non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis + vestibulo-auditory dysfunction consistent with autoimmune vasculitis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Menière mimic; systemic findings can include fever, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, MSK symptoms. Anti–68 kDa antibody may be seen in autoimmune inner ear disease but is not diagnostic.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common cause of interstitial keratitis is {{c1::syphilis::etiology}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
SLE, TB, and herpes are other causes to consider.
If ear and vestibular symptms, think about Cogan syndrome

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If ABR shows {{c1::no response::ABR result}} (in congenital hearing loss), the patient is generally not amenable to amplification and will need a {{c2::cochlear implant::intervention}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield counseling/triage point.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Common genetic causes of congenital SNHL include {{c1::GJB2, SLC26A4, and CDH23::genes}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: GJB2 = potassium homeostasis (stria vascularis); SLC26A4 = ion transporter; CDH23 = hair cell tip links.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ETDQ-7 cutoff for ETD is {{c1::14.5::cut point}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful for clinic screening and pre/post intervention comparison.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After ET dilation, ETDQ-7 improves in ~{{c1::93.4% short-term and 91.5% long-term::improvement rates}}, but “normalized” in only ~{{c2::53.3% short-term and 58.9% long-term::normalization rates}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Tympanogram improvement seen in >50% and stable at 12 months.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ability to perform Valsalva improved from ~{{c1::13% baseline::baseline}} to {{c2::71% short-term and 81% long-term::follow-up}} after ET dilation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This was the greatest domain improvement in your cited study.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Three primary functions of the Eustachian tube: {{c1::ventilation/pressure equalization, clearance of secretions, and protection from sound/reflux::functions}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield conceptual triad.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::isthmus}} is the narrowest portion of the Eustachian tube and lies {{c2::just distal to the bony portion::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful landmark for ET anatomy and procedures.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Patulous ETD results from failure of the functional valve to close, most commonly due to a {{c1::concave}} defect

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The anterolateral wall is normally convex
A small concave defect limited to the ET orifice alone is common and not diagnostic of patulous ETD.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Comorbidities associated with patulous ETD include {{c1::allergy, rapid weight loss (often post–gastric bypass), LPR, and stress/anxiety::associations}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Weight loss is a classic precipitant.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: DDx of aural fullness includes {{c1::obstructive ETD, patulous ETD, TMD, SSCD, Ménière disease, and migraine::differential}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Helpful short list when evaluating isolated fullness.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Patulous ETD vs otic capsule dehiscence: patulous ETD features autophony of voice/breathing that improves when {{c1::supine or head-dependent::key feature}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Otic capsule dehiscence more often involves autophony of other bone-conducted sounds (e.g., footsteps, chewing, eye movement) and may include CHL, vertigo, and Tullio phenomenon.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Otic capsule dehiscence typically causes autophony of {{c1::voice plus other bone-conducted sounds (footsteps, chewing, eye movement)::features}}, often with CHL/vertigo/Tullio phenomenon.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Symptoms may also improve supine.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Common findings in patulous ETD include autophony and frequent {{c1::sniffing::clinical signs}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Patients often report hearing their own breathing.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Aural fullness that resolves after myringotomy is diagnostic of {{c1::obstructive ETD::interpretation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Functional test of middle ear ventilation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c2::Glasscock–Jackson}} classification applies to {{c1::jugulotympanic paragangliomas::scope}} and differs for glomus tympanicum vs glomus jugulare.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Separate staging systems depending on tumor origin.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hemifacial spasm usually starts in the {{c1::orbicularis oculi::initial muscle}} and then spreads to the rest of the face.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Tumors are an uncommon cause; most cases are vascular compression at the root exit zone (REZ) of the facial nerve.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Tumor-related hemifacial spasm often requires {{c1::tumor removal plus microvascular decompression at the REZ::treatment principle}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: REZ = root exit zone of the facial nerve. Both the mass effect and vascular compression contribute.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If a patient has no clear separation between the cochlea and vestibule (common cavity), consider a {{c1::straight electrode::CI choice}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Common cavity = no clear separation between cochlea and vestibule; straight electrode can facilitate lateral placement.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Incomplete partition type I → consider {{c1::straight or precurved modiolus-hugging array::CI choice}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reflects very rudimentary cochlear partition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Incomplete partition type II → consider {{c1::precurved modiolus-hugging array::CI choice}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: More developed than type I but still abnormal.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Mal de Débarquement syndrome::condition}} is characterized by persistent rocking/swaying/bobbing sensation after motion has stopped

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Rare neurologic condition; patients often describe feeling like they are still on a boat.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: To stop therapy for fungal malignant otitis externa (MOE), require {{c1::normalized ESR after ≥2 months of voriconazole OR a negative gallium scan::criteria}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Symptoms may improve earlier despite residual infection.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common organism in MOE is {{c1::Pseudomonas::organism}} (~65%).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Fungal (~7.8%) and S. aureus (~7.3%) are less common.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Underlying conditions in MOE: {{c1::~82% diabetes vs ~9% other immunosuppression::epidemiology}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Diabetes is the dominant risk factor.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common presenting symptom in MOE is {{c1::otalgia::symptom}}, followed by EAC edema and otorrhea.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Pain is usually severe and persistent.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most commonly involved cranial nerve in MOE is {{c1::CN VII::nerve}} (~27%).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Less commonly X (~4.6%), XII (~3.7%), IX (~3.2%).

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Necrotizing fungal otitis externa is commonly associated with {{c1::HIV::risk factor}}; most common organism is {{c2::Aspergillus fumigatus::organism}}.
Workup for suspected fungal NOE includes {{c3::deep culture/biopsy + CT temporal bone ± contrast MRI}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Not just HIV though. Immunosuppresion in general
Manage with systemic voriconazole and serial debridements
If patient is progressing despite voriconazole, make sure you check voriconazole serum levels to make sure they are high enough

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Key diagnostic clue (NOT PHYSICAL EXAM) for MOE is {{c1::nonresponsiveness to initial therapy::feature}}; ESR is elevated but fever/leukocytosis are often absent.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: ESR is useful for monitoring.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Initial imaging for MOE should be {{c1::PET-CT or PET-MRI plus MRI::imaging}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Historically, Technetium-99 scan were used to help with diagnosis.
In modern practice, get a PET CT or MR and follow the disease with a gallium scan

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Antibiotic duration for MOE is typically {{c1::4–6 weeks::duration}} (time for bone revascularization).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Longer courses are common in advanced disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In ill/advanced MOE, start {{c1::vancomycin plus cefepime/ceftazidime/meropenem::regimen}}; add {{c2::metronidazole::drug}} if intracranial abscess.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Broad coverage for severe disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If fungal MOE suspected (e.g., HIV/failure of standard therapy), treat with {{c1::amphotericin B (preferably liposomal), itraconazole, voriconazole, or caspofungin::options}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: No single best antifungal established.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In the middle ear, in ~70% of cases, the facial nerve runs {{c1::lateral to the plane of the annulus in the posterior EAC wall::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Key mastoidectomy safety landmark.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After surgery for medial canal fibrosis, long-term partial/complete restenosis can reach {{c1::~64%::rate}}, yet {{c2::~60%::patients}} still have favorable hearing outcomes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Short-term restenosis rates can be much lower.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Diagnostic criterion for Ménière disease includes {{c1::≥2 spontaneous vertigo episodes lasting 20 min to <12 hours::criterion}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Must be accompanied by audiologic features (not clozed here).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After cochlear implantation for Ménière disease, audiometric outcomes generally {{c1::improve::direction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: About 20% in some series also had labyrinthectomy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vestibular nerve section typically {{c1::does not::does/does not}} worsen hearing.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: But it is intradural with higher complication risk than labyrinthectomy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Endolymphatic sac shunt surgery is indicated in Ménière disease after failure of {{c1::medical management (diuretics + intratympanic injections)::indications}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Low risk of vestibular or hearing complications (relative to more ablative options).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Allergic disease prevalence is about {{c1::3× higher::association strength}} in patients with Ménière disease.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Treatment of allergy should be included in the treatment plan; animal models suggest antigen exposure can increase allergic markers and contribute to hydrops.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Evidence that {{c1::diuretics::medication}} improve Ménière disease is {{c2::weak/limited::evidence strength}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Commonly used anyway in practice.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Endolymphatic sac {{c1::shunting and decompression::procedures}} are reported to be equally effective for Ménière disease.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful when counseling on endolymphatic sac surgery options.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cochlear implantation in Ménière patients s/p {{c1::labyrinthectomy::prior surgery}} can improve audiometric outcomes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Systematic review/meta-analysis (Villavisanis et al., Laryngoscope 2021).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Can a patient with Ménière disease and nonserviceable hearing undergo combined cochlear implantation and labyrinthectomy? {{c1::yes::yes/no}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consider for refractory vertigo with nonserviceable hearing or when planned.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Migraine diagnosis requires ≥{{c1::5::number}} attacks lasting 4–72 h, with ≥2 (unilateral, pulsating, moderate/severe, worse with activity) and ≥1 of (n/v, photo+phonophobia).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: ICHD-3 framing; not better accounted for by another diagnosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide)::mediator}} is released during migraine and can drive pain, vasodilation, and plasma extravasation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Can contribute to sensory hypersensitivity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vestibular migraine can cause “peripheral” symptoms (aural pressure, tinnitus, subjective hearing loss).  audiometry is typically {{c1::normal::normal/abnormal}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This often leads to misdiagnosis as Ménière disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vestibular migraine criteria: ≥{{c1::5::number}} episodes of vestibular symptoms lasting 5 min to 72 h + migraine history + ≥{{c2::50%::proportion}} of episodes with a migraine feature.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Migraine features include migraine-type headache, photophobia/phonophobia, or visual aura; exclude other vestibular/ICHD diagnoses.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Probable vestibular migraine: ≥{{c1::5::number}} episodes (5 min to 72 h) with only {{c2::one of migraine history OR migraine features during episodes::criterion}} fulfilled.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Exclude other vestibular/ICHD diagnoses.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Granular myringitis: {{c1::chronic, painless otorrhea + pruritus + granulation on the TM with no OM::presentation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Can rarely progress to medial canal fibrosis; treat with antibiotic/steroid drops and dilute vinegar irrigation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bullous myringitis: {{c1::painful vesicles on the TM::exam, pain yes/no}} and may have AOM; often viral.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Generally avoid antibiotics/steroids; occasional myringotomy for refractory cases; obtain an audiogram.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs) are sensitive for noise-induced hearing loss because they assess sound up to {{c1::16 kHz::frequency}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful early outer hair cell injury marker.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: With ossicular discontinuity (even after ossiculoplasty), patients commonly have a persistent {{c1::high-frequency air–bone gap::audiogram pattern}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Helpful for preoperative counseling.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An air–bone gap >{{c1::30::threshold}} dB suggests a(n) {{c2::ossiculoplasty::procedure}} may be required.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Rule-of-thumb threshold.
30dB air bone gab will cause the Rinne to flip with 512Hz
10-15dB gap causes a 256Hz to flip

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In otosclerosis, quality of life is often most improved by successful {{c1::stapes surgery::intervention}} (vs hearing aids).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Many patients prefer fewer external devices if surgery is successful.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Acoustic reflexes are typically {{c1::absent::reflex}} in otosclerosis, helping differentiate it from SSCD.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Preserved reflexes favor SSCD over stapes fixation.
Absentsclerosis

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The stapes footplate derives from the {{c1::otic capsule::embryology}}, while the stapes superstructure derives from the {{c2::branchial arches::embryology}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield embryology split.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Congenital stapes footplate fixation is detectable around age {{c1::3::age}}, whereas juvenile otosclerosis is often not detectable until around age {{c2::21::age}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Helps differentiate pediatric vs young adult conductive hearing loss.

Congenital stapes fixation: The stapes superstructure is derived from the 2nd branchial arch (Reichert cartilage), while the footplate has contributions from both the 2nd arch and otic capsule. Abnormal development of the footplate–oval window interface/annular ligament can leave the footplate fixed to the otic capsule, causing congenital conductive hearing loss.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Management of Otitis media 2-3 weeks after otosclerosis surgery is {{c1::IV antibiotics::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Post-stapes OM can risk inner ear complications.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Stapedectomy (otosclerosis) pre-op/intra-op check: verify {{c1::all ossicles are mobile::exam}} to consider {{c2::tympanosclerosis/myringosclerosis::alternate CHL cause}} as contributing/primary cause of CHL.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Clinical pearl: conductive loss isn't always stapes fixation alone. If malleus/incus mobility is limited or TM/ossicular chain is stiff from tympano-/myringosclerosis, a stapes procedure may not fix the ABG (or may only partially help). This is why you confirm mobility of each ossicle (malleus, incus, stapes) and the TM/annulus mechanics during evaluation/at surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Otosclerosis supportive findings: {{c1::type As tympanogram::tympanogram type}}, {{c1::absent::absent/present}} acoustic reflexes, and {{c1::good/excellent word recognition::speech testing}} in quiet.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Packaged “triad+” for quick recall: (1) type As (stiff system), (2) absent stapedial reflexes, (3) preserved WRS in quiet. (Carhart notch at ~2 kHz is another classic association.)

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common cause of persistent/recurrent {{c1::conductive hearing loss::type of loss}} after {{c2::stapedectomy/stapedotomy::procedure}} is {{c3::resorptive osteitis of the incus::most common cause}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Think “incus problem” first (erosion/osteitis at the long process where the prosthesis attaches). Other reported causes of post-stapes persistent CHL to consider: otosclerotic obliteration of the round window (~23%), displaced prosthesis onto a fragment of the footplate (~23%), prosthesis abutting the bony margin of the oval window rather than centered in the fenestration (~18%), and neo-osteogenesis in the oval window (~14%).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Patulous Eustachian tube symptoms: {{c1::autophony::symptom}} and {{c2::pulsatile tinnitus::symptom}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: History clues: often after recent weight loss or deconditioning. Exam clue: TM can move with respiration (breathing-synchronous excursion).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Patulous Eustachian tube risk factors include {{c1::recent weight loss::risk factor}} or {{c2::deconditioning::risk factor}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mechanism is functional “over-opening” of the ET (often related to peritubal fat loss). Pair with symptoms (autophony, breathing-synchronous sensation) and TM movement with respiration.

fields.name: Text
