fields.value: Patulous Eustachian tube: physical exam can show TM {{c1::movement with respiration::exam finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This is a helpful differentiator vs obstructive ET dysfunction (which is more about retraction from negative pressure without breathing-synchronous excursion).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Patulous Eustachian tube: limited treatments include {{c1::estrogen nasal drops::treatment}}, {{c2::stopping nasal decongestants::behavior change}}, and {{c3::bulking the nasopharyngeal ET opening::procedure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Can also place a tympanostomy tube to add weight to the TM
Management is often frustrating. Focus on addressing precipitating factors (weight loss, decongestants), and recognize that procedural options exist but outcomes vary.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If a patient presents with {{c1::bilateral perichondritis::presentation}}, work them up for {{c2::relapsing polychondritis::diagnosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Red flag: bilateral auricular chondritis/perichondritis should trigger systemic thinking (cartilage inflammation elsewhere: nose, laryngotracheal, joints, eyes).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Relapsing polychondritis vs infectious auricular chondritis: relapsing polychondritis {{c1::spares the lobule::key finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Resparesing
The lobule has no cartilage, so cartilage-specific inflammation tends to spare it. Infectious chondritis often does not spare the lobule and should be treated with antipseudomonal antibiotics when suspected.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Preauricular pits/sinuses: can be {{c1::autosomal dominant with variable expression::inheritance}} and are bilateral in {{c2::~25–50%::frequency}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Association pearl: preauricular sinuses are uncommonly associated with syndromes (e.g., branchio-oto-renal syndrome).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Preauricular sinus/pit: if {{c1::acutely infected::scenario}}, treat immediately with {{c2::I&D + antibiotics::acute management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Definitive excision is typically for recurrent infection and is best done after the infection has cleared.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Preauricular sinus/pit: indication for definitive removal is {{c1::recurrent infection::indication}}, and excision should be done after infection is {{c2::cleared::timing}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Workflow: I&D/abx now if infected → let inflammation settle → definitive excision to reduce recurrence.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Stenger test principle (pseudohypoacusis): when the same tone is presented to both ears simultaneously, the patient perceives it in the ear with the {{c1::louder stimulus::Stenger principle}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Used when unilateral nonorganic hearing loss is suspected: the patient may “not respond” because hearing the tone in the ‘bad’ ear would reveal they can hear it.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common cause of pulsatile tinnitus is {{c1::venous abnormalities::etiology category}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Examples: sigmoid sinus wall dehiscence, sigmoid sinus diverticulum, transverse sinus stenosis. Also consider idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) due to venous sinus stenosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) can cause pulsatile tinnitus via {{c1::venous sinus stenosis::mechanism}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Clinical tie-in: look for headache/visual symptoms/papilledema risk factors; consider neuro/ophtho involvement and appropriate imaging/workup.

IDK why they call it idiopathic if there is venous sinus stenosis but whatever

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For suspected dural AV fistula as a cause of pulsatile tinnitus, {{c1::digital subtraction angiography (DSA)::imaging}} is the gold standard (invasive).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Pearl: MRI/MRA and CTA can miss flow dynamics for some DAVFs; DSA is the definitive diagnostic and characterization study when suspicion remains high.

AV fistulas are most common in the sigmoid and/or transverse sinuses

fields.name: Text
fields.value: CROS and BAHD can restore the {{c1::head shadow effect}} (routing sound to the better ear)

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: do not restore binaural summation/squelch because true binaural input is still absent.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Reparative granuloma}} after stapes surgery: presents with vertig, otalgia, and tinnitus with a {{c2::reddish mass/hue in the middle ear space::otoscopic finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Rare complication after stapedectomy/stapedotomy (reported incidence on the order of 0.07–0.1%). Consider in early postop deterioration with inflammatory-appearing middle ear findings.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Sulodexide is sometimes used for chronic idiopathic {{c2::subjective tinnitus}}; common side effects include {{c1::GI disturbance::side effect}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Evidence note: studied in at least one randomized controlled trial setting for subjective tinnitus; keep expectations modest and weigh risks/benefits.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If SSNHL patient cannot undergo MRI for retrocochlear evaluation, obtain a(n) {{c1::ABR::alternative test}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: ABR can suggest retrocochlear pathology (e.g., abnormal wave V / interwave latencies vs contralateral ear), but it is less sensitive than MRI for vestibular schwannoma, especially small intracanalicular tumors.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: ABR evidence of retrocochlear pathology includes abnormal {{c1::wave V::ABR wave}} and abnormal {{c2::interwave latencies::ABR parameter}} relative to the opposite ear.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Counseling: ABR is not as sensitive as MRI for vestibular schwannoma; CT with contrast is not recommended to rule out retrocochlear pathology in SSNHL.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::MRI}} is indicated for all SSNHL patients to evaluate retrocochlear pathology, even if hearing improves with steroids.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Pearl: steroid response does not exclude vestibular schwannoma; imaging is still recommended.
You do not need MR for bells palsy

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Gentamicin}} is the most vestibulotoxic aminoglycoside and often affects vestibular function before auditory function.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
SGT KAN
Pearl: aminoglycoside ototoxicity can present delayed (months after exposure) and is often irreversible; risk increases with renal dysfunction/high levels.

Mechanism summary: accumulate in endolymph/perilymph (related to plasma levels/renal clearance) and damage hair cells (often OHCs first) and vestibular structures.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Steroids for vestibular neuritis should be started within {{c1::24–72 hours::timeframe}} of symptom onset.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Typical regimen example: oral prednisolone 50–60 mg daily for 5 days, then taper over the next 5 days (varies by protocol). Vestibular neuritis often affects the superior vestibular nerve distribution.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vestibular neuritis: most commonly involves the {{c1::superior vestibular nerve::which nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Innervation details: superior vestibular nerve supplies the utricle, superior semicircular canal, and lateral semicircular canal. Mnemonic: “LSU is superior” = Lateral + Superior canals + Utricle.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vestibular paroxysmia diagnostic criteria include: ≥{{c1::10 attacks::number}} of vertigo, duration <{{c2::1 minute::duration}}, stereotyped episodes, {{c3::response to carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine::treatment response}}, and not better explained by another diagnosis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• Compression of the vestibular portion of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) by a looping vessel (most often AICA)
 • Analogous to trigeminal neuralgia — but for balance
Can consider neurovascular decompression in refractory cases


Extra pattern recognition: seconds-long stimulus-triggered vertigo can reflect increased vestibular afferent activity in disorders like BPPV, superior canal dehiscence syndrome (SCDS), or vestibular paroxysmia.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vertigo duration pattern: {{c1::seconds-long stimulus-triggered::pattern}} suggests disorders like BPPV/SCDS/vestibular paroxysmia, whereas {{c2::prolonged spontaneous spinning::pattern}} suggests disorders like Ménière/perilymph fistula/vestibular neuritis/IMIED/vestibular migraine.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful high-yield sorting tool for dizzy patients: seconds + triggered = “burst” problems (BPPV/SCDS/VP). Prolonged + spontaneous = asymmetric vestibular firing problems (Ménière, neuritis, etc.).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Immune-mediated inner ear disease (IMIED): hearing loss/vestibular symptoms evolve over {{c1::weeks to months::time course}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
(vs hours-days in SSNHL)

Associated systemic diseases include Cogan syndrome, relapsing polychondritis, Behçet, Susac (and less commonly sarcoid, PAN, GPA, SLE, RA, Sjögren). Workup pearls: rule out syphilis; ask about eye symptoms. Typical steroid approach taught: ~60 mg/day for ~1 month, then taper to maintenance; consider stopping around ~3 months depending on course/plan.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Vestibular migraine: vertigo occurs in about {{c1::~25%::frequency}} of patients with migraine.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Remember: vestibular migraine is a very common cause of episodic vertigo overall. Interictal central ocular motor abnormalities can occur even between attacks (e.g., gaze-evoked nystagmus).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c3::Bilateral vestibular hypofunction}}: hallmark symptoms are {{c1::oscillopsia::symptom}} and {{c1::unstable gait::symptom}} without true spinning vertigo.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most common cause is aminoglycoside ototoxicity. Patients rely heavily on vision and proprioception for balance; management includes stopping vestibular suppressants and vestibular physical therapy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common cause of bilateral vestibular hypofunction is {{c1::aminoglycoside ototoxicity::most common cause}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Other causes include genetic (COCH), IMIED, meningitis, vestibular atelectasis, NF2, chemotherapy, superficial siderosis, CANVAS, and B12/folate deficiency.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Definite bilateral vestibulopathy requires symptoms of chronic vestibular syndrome (unsteadiness ± oscillopsia with movement; worse in dark/uneven ground; no symptoms at rest) plus bilaterally reduced angular VOR function (e.g., vHIT gain <{{c1::0.6::vHIT cutoff}} or caloric sum SPV <{{c2::6 deg/s::caloric cutoff}} or rotary chair gain <{{c3::0.1::rotary chair cutoff}}).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These criteria help distinguish bilateral vestibular loss from episodic vertigo disorders: patients usually do not have spinning vertigo; instead they have chronic imbalance and movement-induced blurred vision.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SSNHL: published spontaneous (no treatment) recovery rates are ~{{c1::47–63%::recovery range}} (including complete + partial/good recovery).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Definitions vary: some classic frameworks define complete recovery as PTA <10 dB or equal to the uninvolved ear; good recovery as a PTA <40 dB or >50% improvement from initial audiogram (depends on the study/criteria used).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SSNHL prognostic factor: associated {{c1::vertigo/imbalance::symptom}} tends to portend a {{c2::lower recovery rate::prognosis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Clinical pearl: vestibular symptoms suggest more extensive labyrinthine involvement and often correlate with worse outcomes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SSNHL follow-up: obtain repeat audiometry at end of treatment and again by at least {{c1::6 months::timepoint}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reason: the “final” hearing threshold may not be stable immediately after treatment; long-term follow-up helps document ultimate recovery and guides rehab options.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Typical oral steroid regimen for SSNHL: prednisone {{c1::1 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg)::dose}} for {{c2::7–10 days::duration}}, then taper over {{c3::5–12 days::taper duration}} (e.g., decrease by 10 mg/day).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Regimens vary; the key is early initiation and adequate dose. Many protocols cap at 60 mg/day and use a short taper.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In SSNHL, prevalence of CPA tumors on MRI is ~{{c1::2.7–10.2%::range}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Pearl: even when there seems to be a viral trigger or hearing improves, retrocochlear evaluation (ideally MRI) is still recommended.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Intratympanic (IT) steroids as salvage after systemic steroids for SSNHL show hearing improvement rates around {{c1::~48.5%::IT salvage improvement}} in some analyses (vs ~15% systemic and ~17% placebo in one cited comparison).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Timing pearl: many trials start IT within ~7 days of completing systemic steroids (varies). Some meta-analyses suggest dexamethasone may outperform methylprednisolone for IT use. One RCT comparing IT alone vs IT+systemic showed no difference by Siegel criteria.

Siegel criteria (SSNHL outcomes): Complete = final PTA ≤25 dB. Partial = ≥15 dB PTA improvement with final PTA 25–45 dB. Slight = ≥15 dB improvement with final PTA >45 dB. None = <15 dB PTA improvement.

Text
fields.value: Approximately {{c1::90%::percent}} of scalp hair is in the anagen (growth) phase, which lasts {{c2::3–10}} years.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Anagen is the active growth phase of the hair cycle. Its duration determines maximum hair length and varies by individual and body site.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Approximately {{c1::5–15%::percent}} of scalp hair is in the telogen (resting) phase.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Telogen hairs are shed at the end of the resting phase. Increased synchronization of follicles entering telogen results in telogen effluvium.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After stopping minoxidil, any hair regrowth achieved is typically lost within {{c1::3–4::months}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Minoxidil prolongs anagen and increases follicle size. Discontinuation allows follicles to revert to baseline cycling and miniaturization.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Follicular unit grafts consist of naturally occurring groups of {{c1::1–4::number}} terminal hairs with an associated sebaceous gland.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Follicular unit transplantation preserves native hair groupings and produces the most natural-appearing hair restoration results; it is the gold standard technique.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Androgenetic alopecia is mediated by {{c1::5-alpha reductase::enzyme}} activity and can be treated with {{c2::finasteride::medication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which miniaturizes susceptible follicles. Finasteride reduces DHT levels.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve branches into the {{c1::frontal, lacrimal, and nasociliary::3 branches}} nerves.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These are the three primary sensory branches of V1 supplying the forehead, scalp, orbit, and upper nasal structures.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The nasociliary nerve provides sensory innervation to the {{c1::cornea, iris, ciliary body, and conjunctiva::ocular structures}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This shared innervation explains the severe pain associated with corneal injury or intraocular inflammation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The terminal branch of the {{c3::nasociliary}} nerve is the {{c1::anterior ethmoidal}} nerve, which supplies the {{c4::medial nasal ala::location of sensory input}} via the {{c2::external nasal}} nerve.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
CN V → V1 (ophthalmic) → nasociliary nerve → anterior ethmoidal nerve → external nasal nerve.
Medial nasal ala sensation is V1-derived, an important distinction from lateral nasal ala sensation.
If you want to numb up the nose in an awake patient, do a V2 block at the infraorbital foramen and an injection of the lateral sidewall of the nose near the junction o fthe nasal bones and the upper lateral cartilages

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Sensation to the lateral nasal ala is supplied by the {{c1::infraorbital nerve}}, a branch of the maxillary (V2) nerve.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This distinction is important for local anesthesia and reconstructive planning.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For optimal cosmetic outcomes with an auricular prosthesis, the {{c1::tragus}} should be preserved if possible.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Preserving the tragus maintains natural auricular contour and improves prosthesis camouflage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A normal Schirmer test is {{c1::>10–15}} mm over 5 minutes; values {{c2::<5::mm}} indicate severe dry eye.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Significant dry eye increases the risk of exposure keratopathy after eyelid surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Active Graves ophthalmopathy is a contraindication to blepharoplasty unless it has been stable for at least {{c1::1 year::timeframe}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Operating during the active inflammatory phase increases the risk of worsening exposure, edema, and ocular complications.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most commonly injured extraocular muscle during blepharoplasty is the {{c1::inferior oblique}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The inferior oblique lies near the inferior orbital fat pads, making it vulnerable during lower eyelid surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ideal upper eyelid crease height is {{c1::8–11::mm}} in women and {{c2::6–9::mm}} in men.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Crease height varies with sex, ethnicity, and aesthetic goals.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Botulinum toxin type A has an onset of {{c1::2–5::days}}, whereas type B begins in approximately {{c2::24::hours}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Type B has a faster onset but tends to have more autonomic side effects and shorter duration.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A coronal brow lift minimizes visible scarring but tends to {{c1::elevate::effect}} the hairline.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Best suited for patients with a low hairline who can tolerate posterior hairline movement.
Not often a good option in facial feminization surgery

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A pretrichial brow lift is ideal for patients with a {{c1::high}} forehead and a good hairline.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This approach allows brow elevation without further increasing forehead height.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Isotretinoin should be discontinued for {{c1::6::months}} prior to dermabrasion.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Isotretinoin impairs wound healing and increases the risk of hypertrophic scarring.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The strongest risk factor for post-facelift skin flap necrosis is {{c1::smoking}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Approximately 80% of patients with postoperative skin necrosis smoke at least one pack per day. Other risk factors include diabetes, radiation, thin flaps, and excessive tension.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The ogee line is an {{c1::S-shaped::shape}} contour of the midface best visualized on the {{c2::three-quarter}} view.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: It represents the transition from malar convexity to submalar concavity and is a marker of youthful facial contour.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The ideal alar-to-lobule ratio is {{c1::1:1}}, measured on lateral profile view.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This proportion helps guide rhinoplasty planning and tip refinement.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Using the {{c2::Goode::eponyn}} method deal nasal tip projection is {{c1::60%::percent}} of nasal length from nasion to the tip-defining point.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often assessed using the Goode method.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The distance from nasion to subnasale should be {{c1::43%::percent}} of the nasion-to-menton distance.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Used to assess vertical facial balance.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ideal bony nasal width is {{c1::75–80%::percent}} of the alar base width.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Over-narrowing risks both aesthetic imbalance and nasal airway compromise.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The medial brow begins on a vertical line through the {{c1::medial canthus::landmark}} aligned with the nasal-alar junction.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This landmark is used in aesthetic facial analysis and brow lift planning.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The lower eyelid margin should rest at the {{c1::inferior limbus}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Inferior scleral show suggests lid laxity or malposition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Interpupillary distance should equal the distance from the {{c1::nasion}} to the {{c1::upper lip vermilion}} (other facial landmarks).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classic facial proportion guideline for aesthetic assessment.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Facial nerve injuries {{c1::medial::location}} to the {{c2::lateral canthus}} typically do not require exploration.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High arborization and spontaneous recovery rates make surgical repair unnecessary in most cases.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common cause of bilateral facial paralysis is {{c1::Lyme disease}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Facial paralysis is stage II Lyme
Always consider Lyme disease in patients presenting with bilateral facial weakness.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On nerve excitability testing, a side-to-side difference of {{c1::3.5::mA}} indicates significant weakness.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This test assesses the minimum current needed to elicit a muscle response.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Wallerian degeneration first occurs in Sunderland grade {{c1::II}} nerve injuries.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Grade I (neuropraxia) does not undergo Wallerian degeneration.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Sunderland grade II injuries preserve the {{c1::endoneurium}} and do {{c2::not::yes/no}} result in synkinesis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Axons regenerate within intact endoneurial tubes, maintaining correct muscle reinnervation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Complete nerve transection (Sunderland grade V) carries a risk of {{c1::neuroma}} formation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These injuries require surgical repair to optimize recovery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Do columellar struts influence nasal resistance?
{{c1::no::yes/no}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
They are structural tip support grafts rather than airway-support grafts.
They are helpful for adding nasal projection and locking in the rotation you want for the tip

fields.name: Text
fields.value: External nasal valve collapse due to over-resected lower lateral cartilages is treated with {{c1::alar batten grafts}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Alar batten grafts provide lateral wall support and restore valve competence.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The internal nasal valve accounts for at least {{c1::50%::percent}} of total nasal airway resistance.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Explains why small anatomic changes at the internal valve can cause major obstruction and why valve support is central to functional septorhinoplasty.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An auto-spreader graft involves separation of the {{c1::septum and upper lateral cartilage}}, followed by medial infolding of the {{c1::upper lateral cartilage}} with suture stabilization.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Uses native cartilage rather than harvested grafts to widen the internal nasal valve after dorsal hump reduction.

Autospreader grafts (spreader flaps) use the folded upper lateral cartilage to reconstruct the middle vault, preserving native anatomy and avoiding cartilage harvest. They provide subtle internal nasal valve widening and smooth dorsal lines, making them ideal for primary rhinoplasty with dorsal hump reduction and thin-skinned patients.
Traditional spreader grafts use separate cartilage grafts and offer greater strength, precision, and asymmetry control, making them preferred for significant valve collapse, crooked noses, trauma, or revision cases.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Linear transposition flaps have a tendency toward {{c1::trapdoor deformity::complication}} due to underlying scar formation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Wide undermining and tension-free, everted closure reduce circumferential scar contraction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A melolabial transposition flap should be designed slightly {{c1::wider than the height of the lip defect::design principle}} to avoid contraction.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Over-narrow designs risk postoperative distortion and lip tightness.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The ideal width-to-length ratio for fusiform excision of a lesion is {{c1::1:3::ratio}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Helps avoid dog-ears while allowing primary closure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Can you perform nerve grafting for facial paralysis on patients with Mobius syndrome?
{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Facial nerve absence precludes nerve grafting; reanimation relies on regional muscle transfer.
Primary dynamic procedures for facial asymmetry in Möbius syndrome include temporalis muscle sling and masseter muscle transposition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In otoplasty, the {{c1::Mustardé::suture}} recreates the antihelical fold. It is made up of horizontal matttress sutures placed {{c2::2mm}} apart and involves a {{c3::16mm}} distance across the estimated antihelical fold with a {{c4::1cm}} bite width

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Uses horizontal mattress sutures across the estimated antihelical fold to create antihelical definition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In otoplasty, the {{c1::Furnas::suture}} technique tacks the concha to the mastoid periosteum.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reduces conchal prominence by setback rather than fold creation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Management of a pollybeak deformity is revision rhinoplasty with resection of the {{c1::anterior caudal septal angle cartilage::structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Targets excess supratip fullness from cartilage or soft-tissue bulk.

A true pollybeak deformity is caused by excess projection of the anterior caudal septal angle, making the dorsum appear more prominent than the tip and creating supratip fullness. Because this is a structural cartilage problem rather than soft-tissue edema, definitive management requires revision rhinoplasty with resection of the anterior caudal septal angle cartilage to restore proper dorsal–tip height relationships.



https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Pollybeak deformity results from {{c1::under-resection of the dorsal hump, over-resection of the supratip, or inadequate tip support::3 causes}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Memory line: dorsum too high, supratip too low, or tip too weak.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Methods to decrease nasal projection include {{c1::complete strip procedure, full transfixion incision, and septal reduction::3 procedures}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Each reduces structural support contributing to tip projection.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Methods to increase nasal projection include {{c1::lateral crural steal, shield grafting, interdomal sutures, tongue-in-groove, and columellar strut grafting::5 procedures}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Improve projection by enhancing tip support and/or rotation.
https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
The {{c1::delivery approach::endonasal approach}} is the most versatile endonasal technique for nasal tip surgery.
Uses {{c2::marginal}} and {{c2::intercartilaginous}} incisions connected to a full transfixion incision.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The delivery approach is a closed (endonasal) rhinoplasty technique in which the lower lateral cartilages (LLCs) are delivered outside the nostril through intranasal incisions to allow direct modification—without a transcolumellar incision.

Uses marginal and intercartilaginous incisions connected to a full transfixion incision.




https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::retrograde}} approach for endonasal rhinoplasty uses a(n) {{c2::intercartilaginous}} incision(s) and does not violate the soft tissue triangles.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Preservation of soft tissue triangles reduces risk of tip ischemia and contour deformity.

Retrograde dissection is helpful in cases where the surgeon is having difficulty following the caudal margin of the intermediate and lateral crus. This is not unusual in cases where there is buckling of the intermediate crus or domes. Retrograde dissection may not be the approach of choice for secondary rhinoplasty when the lateral crura has been excised or previously resected. However, the retrograde approach can be extremely helpful in secondary rhinoplasty cases in which the primary surgery was performed via an external approach, when the medial crura dissection is hindered by excessive scarring.

https://www.rhinoplastyarchive.com/articles/rhinoplasty-fundamentals/anatomy-incisions-approaches-open-closed-rhinoplasty

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Tissue expanders should be placed in the {{c1::subgaleal::anatomic plane}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Provides predictable expansion and improved vascularity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Wound tensile strength is approximately {{c1::3%}} at week 1, {{c2::50%}} by week 5, and {{c3::80%}} at 3–6 months.

fields.value: Segmental resection is indicated for ameloblastoma with {{c1::multiloculated disease and bone thinning or erosion::indications}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reflects aggressive local behavior and high recurrence risk.

fields.value: The post-styloid parapharyngeal space contains cranial nerves {{c1::IX, X, XI, and XII::4 cranial nerves}}.

fields.name: Extra

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ototoxicity in long-term pediatric cancer survivors treated with platinum-based chemotherapy or head/brain radiation is {{c1::50%::percent}} and primarily affects {{c2::high frequencies::frequency range}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Cisplatin and cranial irradiation cause dose-dependent cochlear hair cell injury with early high-frequency loss preceding speech-frequency involvement.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In children with meningitis steroids reduce the risk of severe hearing loss for {{c1::H. influenzae::organism}} infection; steroids must be given {{c2::with the first dose of antibiotics::timing}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Do aggressive open surgical approaches show improved survival outcomes in patients with acute invasive fungal sinusitis (AIFS)? {{c1::no::yes/no}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Evidence favors early diagnosis

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most frequent intracranial complication of acute otitis media is {{c1::meningitis::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Occurs in 5–15% of cases; followed by epidural abscess (3–8%)

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In children {{c1::6–24 months::age range}} with unilateral or bilateral acute otitis media and severe symptoms

fields.name: Extra

fields.name: Text

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lifestyle changes shown to reduce the risk of acute otitis media include {{c1::exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months::protective factor}}, {{c2::pneumococcal and influenza vaccination::vaccines}}, and avoidance of {{c3::cigarette}} exposure

fields.name: Text
fields.value:

{{c1::Children under 2, treat immediately

fields.value: The primary arterial supply to the adenoid is the {{c1::pharyngeal branch of the internal maxillary artery::vessel}}.

fields.name: Extra

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In children {{c1::≥4 years old::age}} tympanostomy tubes provide the most reliable short-term resolution of {{c2::hearing loss from OME::condition}} while adenoidectomy reduces the need for {{c3::repeat surgery::outcome}}

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In children over {{c1::4 years old::age}} adenoidectomy performed with the first set of PE tubes reduces the risk of needing a second set by {{c2::39%::percent}}.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Persistent velopharyngeal insufficiency lasting {{c1::>6 months::timeframe}} after adenoidectomy warrants evaluation for {{c2::22q11 microdeletion::genetic condition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Consider syndromic causes when VPI does not resolve spontaneously.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Post-operative medical therapy for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis includes {{c1::steroids, oral antihistamines, and nasal saline::3 things}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Does not need antifungals

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis is a subtype of {{c1::CRSwNP::disease category}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Represents a local type I hypersensitivity response rather than a systemic allergic process.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cromolyn is a {{c1::mast cell stabilizer::drug class}} that must be taken {{c2::prophylactically::timing}} and may require dosing up to {{c3::four times per day::frequency}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most effective when started before allergen exposure; limited utility for acute symptom relief.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: There is no evidence that allergen immunotherapy reduces {{c2::nasal polyp size::CRSwNP outcome}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Immunotherapy addresses allergic sensitization, not established polypoid disease.
, though it may improve symptoms of allergic rhinitis

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Having {{c1::two atopic parents::risk factor}} confers a {{c2::47%::percent}} likelihood of a child developing atopic disease.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Asthma and allergic rhinitis are strongly linked; asthma increases the likelihood of allergic rhinitis by ~4–6×.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Can you continue leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast) during intradermal allergy testing? {{c1::yes::yes/no}}

fields.name: Extra

antihistamines, topical steroids, and beta blockers must be discontinued.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
in contact dermatitis
Assesses delayed (T-cell–mediated) hypersensitivity rather than IgE-mediated allergy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Alpha-gal allergy is caused by IgE sensitization to {{c1::galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose::carbohydrate}} following {{c2::lone star tick::bug}} bites.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Leads to delayed reactions to mammalian meat; management is strict avoidance and epinephrine prescription; immunotherapy is not used.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Both sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) and subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) are effective, but SLIT has a {{c1::lower risk of anaphylaxis::safety profile}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Efficacy is comparable; safety and administration differ.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Allergy immunotherapy typically lasts {{c1::3–5 years::duration}}, with improvement beginning around {{c2::12 weeks::timeframe}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: When skin testing is used, therapy commonly begins at dilution #4.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Fel d 1::allergen}} corresponds to {{c2::cat::source}} allergy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Major cat dander allergen with low cross-reactivity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Mus m 1::allergen}} corresponds to {{c2::mouse::source}} allergy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Important in occupational and laboratory exposure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Der f and Der p::allergens}} correspond to {{c2::dust mite::source}} allergy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most common dust mite species tested; major indoor allergen.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Bla g 1 and Bla g 2::allergens}} correspond to {{c2::cockroach::source}} allergy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Cockroach sensitization is associated with pediatric asthma.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Pollen–food syndrome cross-reactivity: {{c1::ragweed::pollen}} → {{c2::melon::food}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Oral allergy symptoms after ingestion of raw foods.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Pollen–food syndrome cross-reactivity: {{c1::birch::pollen}} → {{c2::apple::food}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Heat denaturation often reduces symptoms.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Latex allergy is associated with cross-reactivity to {{c1::banana, avocado, and kiwi::foods}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Association is not reversible; food allergy does not imply latex allergy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A positive skin test is defined as a wheal {{c1::≥3 mm larger than the positive control::criterion}}, with histamine being {{c2::≥7 mm larger than saline::control comparison}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Ensures adequate histamine responsiveness and test validity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If a {{c1::flash response::reaction}} occurs during allergy testing, testing should be {{c2::stopped for the day::management and repeated later.}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Prevents systemic reactions and false-positive interpretation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::perilymphatic duct::structure}} runs within the {{c2::cochlear aqueduct::canal}} and connects the scala tympani to the {{c3::subarachnoid space::space}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Explains potential CSF–perilymph communication.
The perilymphatic duct is essentially the same thing as the cochlear aqueduct

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ethmoturbinal development gives rise to the {{c1::agger nasi and uncinate process::first}}, {{c2::middle turbinate::second}}, {{c3::superior turbinate::third}}, and {{c4::supreme turbinate::fourth/fifth}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
IMPORTANTE themoturbinals do no line up perfectly with the sinus lamellae
Ethmoturbinals arise from the lateral nasal wall at 9–10 weeks’ gestation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The sphenoid sinus ostium is located {{c1::11 mm}} inferior to the skull base, {{c2::~7 cm}} from the anterior nasal spine, and at a {{c3::30°}} angle from the nasal floor.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Also ~1.5–2 cm above the choanal roof and ~2/3 of the distance from choana to skull base.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In ~{{c1::20%::percent}} of patients, the uncinate process attaches to the skull base or middle turbinate, causing the frontal sinus to drain {{c2::lateral::medial/lateral}} to the uncinate.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Key anatomic variant for frontal sinus surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most spontaneous recovery in SSNHL occurs within the first {{c1::2 weeks::timeframe}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Recovery after 4–6 weeks is uncommon, supporting early initiation of therapy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Overall recovery rates for SSNHL with treatment are approximately {{c1::60–80%::percent}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Recovery typically includes complete, partial, or slight recovery by Siegel or similar criteria.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Systemic steroid treatment alone for SSNHL results in recovery rates of approximately {{c1::50–70%::percent}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Oral steroids remain first-line therapy when not contraindicated.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Intratympanic steroid therapy alone for SSNHL achieves recovery rates of approximately {{c1::45–65%::percent}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often used when systemic steroids are contraindicated or as salvage therapy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Combined systemic and intratympanic steroid therapy yields recovery rates up to {{c1::70–85%::percent}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Highest benefit seen in moderate–severe losses treated early.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Steroid treatment provides an absolute recovery benefit of approximately {{c1::10–30%::percent}} over natural history in SSNHL.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Benefit is greatest when therapy is started early.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SSNHL treatment is most effective when initiated within {{c1::2 weeks::timeframe}} of symptom onset.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Delayed treatment (>4–6 weeks) is associated with markedly reduced recovery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: House–Brackmann grading hinges primarily on {{c1::facial symmetry at rest}} and {{c1::eye closure completeness}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most board questions can be answered by asking two questions: (1) symmetric at rest? (2) complete eye closure?

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The transition from House–Brackmann Grade {{c2::III}} to {{c2::IV}} is defined by {{c1::loss of complete eye closure}} and {{c1::asymmetry at rest}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This is the single most commonly tested breakpoint on exams.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most common complication of frenotomy is {{c1::bleeding::complication}} (≈3–5%).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Bleeding is usually minor and self-limited; major complications are rare.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In children (not infants), a {{c1::speech-language pathology evaluation::evaluation}} should be completed before considering frenulectomy for speech difficulties.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Speech issues are rarely due solely to tongue tie; evaluation helps avoid unnecessary surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Indications for frenulectomy vary by age: Infants – {{c1::feeding difficulty (poor latch)::indication}}; Children – {{c2::phonation/articulation (rare)::indication}}; Adolescents – {{c3::functional or cosmetic issues::indication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: True speech indications are uncommon outside infancy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If a child can articulate /t d n l s/ sounds, a frenulectomy is {{c1::unlikely to improve speech::clinical implication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Adequate production of these sounds indicates sufficient tongue mobility despite a tongue tie.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: AERD is technically a subtype of {{c1::CRSwNP::disease category}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classically associated with asthma and NSAID sensitivity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Typical AERD patient: {{c1::women::sex}} with onset at {{c2::30–40 years::age range}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Prevalence is higher among patients with both asthma and CRSwNP.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Among leukotriene-targeting therapies, {{c1::zileuton::drug}} is more effective for AERD than montelukast or zafirlukast.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
AERD = aspirin exacerbated respiratory disease
Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase; monitor LFTs due to hepatotoxicity risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In AERD patients with disease recalcitrant to ESS, consider {{c1::aspirin desensitization::therapy}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Patients with AERD have higher recurrence rates and worse QOL after ESS compared with other CRS patients. Aspirin desensitization improves polyp size and recurrence, nasal symptoms and smell, reduces systemic steroid use, acute rhinosinusitis episodes, and the need for revision surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: PPD is positive in {{c1::30–60%::percentage}} of atypical mycobacterial infections but does not indicate tuberculosis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: PPD lacks specificity in this setting.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The gold standard test to rule out tuberculosis when considering atypical mycobacteria is the {{c1::Quantiferon Gold assay::test}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Definitive management with the highest cure rate is surgical excision (~96%) but carries a facial nerve palsy risk (~14%). I&D alone has ~34% cure rate and is associated with poor cosmetic outcomes and fistula formation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH) most commonly occurs in {{c1::older men::demographic}} at the {{c2::posterior nasal septum::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Can cause olfactory cleft widening and may mimic nasal polyps.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The only risk factors associated with complications from paranasal sinus mucosal cysts are {{c1::size >20 mm::risk factor}} and {{c2::bilateral cysts::risk factor}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Both increase the likelihood of sinus outflow obstruction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Inverted papilloma most commonly arises from the {{c1::maxillary sinus::site}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Malignant transformation risk is 5–15% (SCC ex-inverted papilloma).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Definitive surgical management of sinonasal papillomas requires dissection to the {{c1::subperiosteal::surgical principle}} plane.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Applies to inverted, exophytic, and oncocytic papillomas to reduce recurrence.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Second branchial cleft anomalies course from the {{c1::tonsillar pillar::origin}} to the {{c2::anterior border of the SCM::termination}}, passing between the {{c3::ICA and ECA::vascular relationship}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most common branchial cleft anomaly; ~10% are bilateral.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Fourth branchial cleft anomalies originate from the {{c1::pyriform sinus apex::origin}} and course near the {{c2::recurrent laryngeal nerve::nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: May contain ectopic thyroid, parathyroid, or thymic tissue.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In children under 8 years with fourth branchial cleft anomalies, {{c1::endoscopic cauterization of the pyriform sinus opening::management}} is preferred.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Observation alone fails ~89% of the time; endoscopic and open approaches have similar success, but endoscopic management has lower morbidity in younger children.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Third or fourth branchial cleft anomalies often present as {{c1::recurrent infections of the left thyroid lobe::presentation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often due to a pyriform sinus fistula tract extending into the left thyroid lobe, resulting in suppurative thyroiditis. CT often shows left thyroid lobe involvement; diagnosis is confirmed with direct laryngoscopy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: First branchial cleft anomalies are usually intimately related to the {{c1::facial nerve::nerve}} and require a {{c2::parotidectomy approach::surgical approach}} for safe excision.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The tract may run deep or lateral to the facial nerve; careful nerve dissection is required.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After button battery ingestion, significant histologic damage can occur within {{c1::2 hours::timeframe}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Honey or sucralfate may be given within 12 hours of suspected ingestion to reduce injury severity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If no esophageal perforation is present after button battery ingestion, irrigate the esophagus with {{c1::50–150 mL of 0.25% sterile acetic acid::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Document battery orientation intraoperatively: the anode side is at higher risk of tissue damage. Image reference: https://accutronwatchpage.com/batcon.jpg

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If endoscopy reveals a tracheoesophageal fistula after button battery ingestion, initial management can be {{c1::observation::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Spontaneous closure is not uncommon. Make patient NPO with gastrostomy tube feeding and PPI therapy; consider surgical closure if not resolved by ~70 days.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On radiographs, most coin-like objects in the esophagus lie with their long axis {{c1::Transverse::orientation}}, .

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
whereas in the trachea they appear A–P (rod-like)
Example of coin in the esophagus

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On Zargar classification, injuries graded {{c1::0–IIa::grade range}} are considered low-grade caustic injuries.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Grade 0: normal; I: edema/hyperemia; IIa: friability, erosions, superficial ulcerations. References:

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Zargar grade {{c1::IIb or higher::grade threshold}} is associated with an increased risk of {{c2::esophageal stricture::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-grade injuries involve deep or circumferential ulceration and necrosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Bleach::substance}} is the most commonly ingested household caustic but rarely causes severe injury due to its {{c2::near-neutral pH::property}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Despite frequent ingestion, significant esophageal injury is uncommon.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: There is evidence to support {{c1::IV steroid therapy::treatment}} in patients with Zargar {{c2::Grade IIb::grade}} caustic injuries.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Steroids may reduce inflammation and stricture formation in selected patients.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Central compartment atopic disease::disease}} is characterized by central nasal cavity opacification with peripheral sinus clearing on CT.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Endoscopy often reveals polypoid swelling of the middle turbinates or septum; disease is closely related to allergic sensitization.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nearly {{c1::~50%::percentage}} of patients with central compartment atopic disease have {{c2::asthma::associated condition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Associated with allergy and minimal sinus involvement. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7185061/

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Gamma Knife radiosurgery is contraindicated for acoustic neuromas larger than {{c1::3 cm::size}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Larger tumors may swell post-treatment causing obstructive hydrocephalus; inferior tumor spread may not be adequately treated by the collimator helmet.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common cause of traumatic CSF leaks is {{c1::endoscopic sinus surgery::etiology}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Systematic review (Sharma et al., 2015) found traumatic causes most common overall.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Following nasal endoscopic CSF leak repair, the most common site of failure is the {{c1::sphenoid sinus::site}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Second most common site is the ethmoid roof/cribriform plate (Psaltis et al.).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Unilateral choanal atresia is generally managed with {{c1::supportive care::management}} initially.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: If the child is stable, surgical repair can usually be delayed until ~1 year of age; management differs significantly from bilateral choanal atresia.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The presence of {{c1::scutal erosion::imaging finding}} on CT distinguishes acquired from congenital cholesteatoma.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Scutal erosion is present in acquired and absent in congenital disease, aiding surgical planning and counseling.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The muscle most affected by aging changes in the midface is the {{c1::orbicularis oculi::muscle}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Orbicularis laxity contributes to lower lid elongation and midface descent.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Telogen effluvium::process}} commonly occurs after hair transplantation in the first few weeks post-op.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Shedding is expected and temporary.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After post–hair transplant telogen effluvium, hair typically regrows by {{c1::~3 months::timeframe}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Patients should be counseled preoperatively to reduce anxiety.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Minoxidil works by increasing {{c1::hair shaft diameter::effect}} and the percentage of follicles in the {{c2::anagen phase::hair cycle}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Does not create new follicles.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The frontal branch of the facial nerve runs on the {{c1::undersurface of the temporoparietal fascia::anatomic plane}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Key plane during temporal dissection and brow procedures.
If you are using the SCALP mnemonic. TPF corresponds to the A (aponeurosis).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A negative vector eye occurs when the {{c1::orbital rim lies posterior to the anterior corneal convexity::definition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Treat with restoration of midface volume; blepharoplasty alone will not correct this.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Botulinum toxin–induced ptosis can be treated with {{c1::apraclonidine (Iopidine)::medication}} eye drops.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Alpha-2 agonist → stimulates Müller muscle contraction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: On EMG, fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves first appear at approximately {{c1::3 weeks::timepoint}} after facial nerve injury.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Indicates denervation.
When you think of EMG, think of 3 weeks

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cross-facial nerve grafting using the {{c1::sural nerve::donor nerve}} is most effective within {{c2::6 months::timeframe}} of injury.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Variable results; avoid in severe peripheral neuropathy (e.g., diabetes).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Superiorly::Superiorly/inferiorly}} based local flaps are more prone to trapdoor deformity .

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Facial lymphatic drainage is predominantly inferior.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For nasal tip defects <5 mm and superficial, consider {{c1::secondary intention::repair}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Part of practical nasal tip reconstruction algorithm.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nasal tip defects 5–10 mm are commonly repaired with a {{c1::bilobed flap::reconstruction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Good color and texture match.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nasal tip defects >15–20 mm or with exposed cartilage often require a {{c1::paramedian forehead flap::reconstruction}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Gold standard for large or deep defects.
plus cartilage graft.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In nasal ala reconstruction, involvement of the {{c1::alar rim::subunit}} mandates a {{c2::cartilage graft::requirement}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Prevents notching and external valve collapse.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A small full-thickness alar defect can be repaired with an {{c1::auricular composite graft::reconstruction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Best for limited defects.
Small = <1cm

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If not closed primarily, a ≤2 cm helical rim defect is classically repaired using an {{c1::Antia–Buch flap::technique}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Preserves contour and ear height.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nxl1AgQNRI8

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nasal defects >{{c1::1.5 cm::size threshold}} are often best repaired with a {{c2::paramedian forehead flap::reconstruction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Bilobed flaps best for nasal tip <1.5 cm and ≥5 mm from alar rim; FTSG on tip best for <1 cm.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Melolabial flaps::flap}} are best indicated for defects limited to the {{c2::lateral alar subunit::subunit}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Excellent color and texture match; not ideal for nasal tip or medial alar rim defects.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Prominent ear deformity is associated with abnormally distal insertion of the {{c1::antitragicus}} muscle.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Contributes to increased conchal–mastoid angle.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: During lateral osteotomies in rhinoplasty, the osteotomy should not extend superior to the {{c1::medial canthus::landmark}} to avoid {{c2::rocker deformity::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Rocker deformity occurs when bone inferior to the osteotomy sinks relative to bone superior to the cut.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, rhytidectomy is associated with increased risk of {{c1::postoperative hemorrhage::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Cutis laxa affects elastic fibers but not collagen synthesis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ipratropium bromide works by {{c1::blocking muscarinic receptors::mechanism}}, producing a localized anticholinergic effect.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Especially helpful for rhinorrhea.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Dermatographism::condition}} is an absolute contraindication to allergy skin testing.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Causes false-positive wheal responses.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The levator palpebrae superioris muscle is suspended by the {{c1::Whitnall ligament::structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Acts as a functional pulley.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Inferior turbinate size grading ranges from Grade 0–4 based on percent nasal airway obstruction.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Grade 0: absent; Grade 1: <25%; Grade 2: 25–50%; Grade 3: 50–75%; Grade 4: >75% obstruction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c2::Godtfredsen}} syndrome involves palsies of cranial nerves {{c1::VI and XII::cranial nerves}} most commonly related to a mass of the clivus

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most commonly metastatic tumor to the clivus; second most common is nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c2::Vernet}} syndrome involves cranial nerves {{c1::IX, X, and XI::cranial nerves}} most commonly due to a lesion at the jugular forement.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Dysphagia, dysphonia, posterior tongue taste loss, neck weakness.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The cricothyroid muscle is innervated by the {{c1::external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve::nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Injury affects pitch control.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In the Pittsburgh staging system, EAC carcinoma with facial nerve paralysis is classified as {{c1::T4::stage}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: T4 also includes invasion of cochlea, petrous apex, dura, or brain.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Salvage surgery for free flap failure is most successful in {{c1::venous compromise::failure type}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Arterial thrombosis has poorer salvage rates.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A radial forearm free flap can be harvested with the {{c1::antebrachial cutaneous nerves::sensory nerves}} for sensory reinnervation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Allows sensate reconstruction in selected cases.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An anterolateral thigh flap can be harvested with the {{c1::lateral femoral cutaneous nerve::sensory nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Used when sensate reconstruction is desired.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A lateral arm flap may be harvested with the {{c1::posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm::sensory nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Option for sensate flap design.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The uncinate process usually attaches to the {{c1::lamina paparycea}} and results in frontal sinus drainage {{c2::medial::medial/lateral}} to the uncinate

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Occurs in 80% of patients

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For ear avulsions, a {{c1::≥1–2 cm::measurement}} well-perfused skin bridge is generally sufficient for primary closure if tissue is not crushed and shows active bleeding.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Viability depends on skin perfusion rather than cartilage continuity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For ear avulsions, posterior auricular skin bridges are more reliable due to supply from the {{c1::posterior auricular artery::artery}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Posterior skin has more dependable vascularity than anterior auricular skin.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For ear avulsions, skin bridges {{c1::<5 mm::measurement}} have a high risk of necrosis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: For ear avulsions, skin bridges <5 mm are generally considered nonviable for primary closure without microsurgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For ear avulsions, skin bridges {{c1::5–10 mm::measurement}} are {{c2::borderline::viability}} and require case-dependent judgment.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Assessment depends on perfusion, bleeding, degree of crush injury, and patient factors.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Two::number}} fixation points allow a plate to function as a {{c2::tension band::mechanism}}, resisting distraction forces only.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Does not control rotational forces.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Two::number}} fixation points do NOT provide {{c2::rotational stability::mechanical property}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Rotation remains the primary failure mode.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Four::number}}  fixation points should be the minimum goal for stable plate fixation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
two on each side of the fracture
Provides both axial and rotational stability to each fragment.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Five to six::number}}  fixation points per side may be desirable when {{c2::bridging bony defects or poor healing conditions::indications}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Used for comminution, bone loss, or compromised healing environments.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::frontal sinus::structure}} is more resistant to fracture than any other facial bone.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Typically requires high-energy trauma.
The most common frontal sinus fractures involve a combination of the anterior and posterior tables with or without frontal recess involvement (about 2/3).
Isolated anterior table fractures account for only approximately 1/3.
Isolated posterior table fractures are extremely uncommon (< 1%).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Frontal sinus fracture evaluation must assess the {{c1::anterior table, frontal sinus outflow tract, and posterior table/dura::3 key components}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These three anatomic factors determine management algorithms.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Frontal sinus outflow tract obstruction increases the risk of {{c1::chronic sinusitis and mucocele formation::complications}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Risk of mucocele formation is low in mild or moderately displaced anterior table fractures. Radiographic severity of outflow tract obstruction does not predict long-term patency.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nonoperative management of frontal sinus fractures includes {{c1::nasal steroids at 1 week::timing}} and {{c2::sinus irrigations at 3 weeks::timing}} post-injury.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Medical therapy aims to preserve sinus drainage and aeration.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: CT surveillance after frontal sinus fracture should be performed at {{c1::6 weeks}} and {{c1::12 months}} to assess sinus aeration.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Persistent sinus opacification on surveillance imaging should prompt consideration of FESS.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Posterior table fracture with CSF leak requires {{c1::skull base precautions for 5–7 days::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Persistent CSF leak after observation requires endonasal repair.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Severe posterior table fractures require {{c1::cranialization::procedure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Includes ≥4 mm displacement, severe comminution, dural disruption, or persistent CSF leak.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Risk of meningitis within 90 days after posterior table fracture is {{c1::~1%::risk}}, higher in patients with CSF leak.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Patients should be counseled on warning signs and need for follow-up.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Secondary camouflage::term}} refers to implant placement for residual contour deformity after frontal sinus fracture observation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Delayed cosmetic correction after fracture healing.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::Schaefer–Fuhrman classification::system}} is used to grade laryngeal injury severity.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Guides operative versus nonoperative management.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Schaefer–Fuhrman {{c2::Group I}} is defined by {{c1::minor endolaryngeal hematoma without fracture::definition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
No structural instability.
StageKey Injury FeaturesGeneral Treatment Recommendations
Stage IMinor endolaryngeal hematoma or laceration; no fracture; normal airwayObservation, humidified oxygen, voice rest, anti-reflux therapy; short course steroids often used
Stage IIMore severe edema/hematoma; nondisplaced laryngeal fracture; minor mucosal disruption without exposed cartilageClose airway observation; steroids; anti-reflux therapy; antibiotics if mucosal injury; typically non-operative
Stage IIIMassive edema; mucosal tears with exposed cartilage; displaced fractures; vocal cord immobilitySecure airway (often tracheostomy); operative exploration; ORIF of fractures; mucosal repair
Stage IVSame as Stage III plus severe disruption of anterior larynx, unstable fractures, or multiple fracture linesImmediate airway control (tracheostomy); urgent surgical reconstruction
Stage VComplete laryngotracheal separationEmergent airway control and immediate surgical repair

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Schaefer–Fuhrman {{c2::Group II}} includes {{c1::edema, hematoma, minor mucosal disruption without exposed cartilage, and nondisplaced fractures::features}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Usually managed nonoperatively with close observation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Schaefer–Fuhrman {{c2::Group III}} includes {{c1::exposed cartilage, displaced fractures, vocal fold immobility, or massive edema::features}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Key differentiator from lower grades is exposed cartilage
Often requires operative intervention.

Life-threatening injury requiring emergent management.
