fields.name: Text
fields.value:
For laryngeal injuries
Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended if there are {{c1::mucosal injuries::indication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
These injuries are considered contaminated.
Grade II or higher

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The strongest predictor of poor outcome in laryngeal trauma is {{c1::treatment delay >72 hours::factor}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Early intervention improves airway and voice outcomes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::thyroid cartilage::structure}} is the most commonly fractured laryngeal framework element.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Due to its anterior location and rigidity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Exposed cartilage::finding}} is an indication for surgical exploration or endolaryngeal repair in laryngeal trauma.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
High risk of infection and scarring if untreated.
Exposed cartilage is grade III or higher

fields.name: Text
fields.value: For {{c1::minimally displaced condylar fractures::indication}}, management with MMF for {{c2::2 weeks::timeframe}} followed by {{c3::bands/elastics::next step}} is appropriate.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This staged approach is only appropriate for minimally displaced condylar fractures; displacement, malocclusion, or instability may require alternative management.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Compared with arch bars, {{c1::IMF screws::device}} provide more comfort, better oral hygiene, and shorter application time.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Consider dentition, periodontal status, and fracture pattern when choosing fixation.
You need arch bars if patient is edentulous or has comminuted/multiple fractures

fields.name: Text
fields.value: During {{c1::anterior mandible exposure::approach}}, identify and protect the {{c2::mental nerve::structure}} as it exits {{c3::inferior to and between the first and second premolars::landmark}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Critical step to prevent lower lip and chin numbness.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Normal maximal interincisal opening (MIO) is {{c1::40–50 mm::range}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reduced MIO suggests condylar injury, trismus, or mechanical obstruction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bilateral condylar or subcondylar fractures cause a symmetric {{c1::anterior open bite::finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Results from bilateral loss of posterior vertical height.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Horizontal unfavorable mandible fractures (often at the {{c1::angle::location}}) relate to pull from the {{c2::masseter, medial pterygoid, and temporalis::muscle group}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Favorability predicts displacement and fixation strategy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Nonmobile, nondisplaced, or incomplete mandible fractures can be treated with a {{c1::soft diet for 4 weeks::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often no surgery or IMF required; pediatric cases may differ.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Load-bearing::type}} fixation removes functional load from the mandible.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Used for comminuted fractures, atrophic mandibles, or segmental defects.
Recon plates with locking screws

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Load-sharing::type}}  fixation provides stability without absolute rigidity.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Appropriate for most mandible fracture patterns.
Ex Champy plates, compression plates, lag screws, non locking miniplates

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Comminuted mandible fractures should be treated with {{c1::locking reconstruction plates::hardware}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Locking plates maintain strength without precise plate-to-bone contouring.

Edentulous patients also need recon plates

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In addition to a plate along the inferior aspect of the fracture line, mandible fixation often requires a {{c1::tension band::principle}} at the superior border.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Prevents fracture gapping during mastication.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Can you use the Champy technique for an angle fracture in a comminuted fracture?
{{c1::No}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
he Champy technique requires a non-comminuted angle fracture; inferior border comminution prevents effective compressive forces.

Need recon plates with fracture simplification or MMF for comminuted angle fractures

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In pediatric mandible fractures, the most common fracture site is the {{c1::condyle::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Unlike adults, the jaw may deviate away from the fracture due to hematoma formation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If one mandible fracture is dentate and one is non-dentate, treat the {{c1::dentate fracture::priority}} first.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The dentate segment is most important for restoring occlusion.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Class I occlusion: the mesiobuccal cusp of the maxillary first molar sits in the {{c1::mesiobuccal groove::landmark}} of the mandibular first molar.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Baseline for assessing occlusion after reduction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Class II occlusion: the maxillary first molar mesiobuccal cusp is {{c1::anterior::direction}} to the mandibular first molar groove.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Angle classification.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Class III occlusion: the maxillary first molar mesiobuccal cusp is {{c1::posterior::direction}} to the mandibular first molar groove.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Angle classification.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Parasymphyseal fracture fixation using {{c1::lag screws alone::technique}} carries a risk of {{c2::bone shearing during screw placement::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Infection, malocclusion, and mental nerve injury are risks across fixation methods—not unique to lag screws.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Norwood classification describes androgenetic alopecia. {{c1::Norwood III::stage}} represents the first clinically significant hair loss.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Norwood I = no significant recession; Norwood II = mild symmetric bitemporal recession; Norwood III = deep temporal recessions; III Vertex = early crown thinning; IV = frontal + vertex bald spot with bridge; V = enlarged frontal + vertex with thinning bridge; VI = merged frontal/vertex loss; VII = severe horseshoe pattern. Progression is not always linear.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Donor hair for transplantation is typically harvested from the {{c1::occipital horseshoe zone::donor site}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The occipital and posterior temporal scalp is relatively androgen-resistant, allowing transplanted follicles to maintain growth.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The SMAS is continuous with the {{c1::temporoparietal fascia::superiorly}} and the {{c1::platysma::inferiorly}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The temporoparietal fascia is also continuous with the galea aponeurotica, which is critical for facelift dissection planes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hyperactivity of the {{c1::depressor septi nasi::muscle}} causes a smiling (plunging tip) deformity.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Findings include nasal tip depression, shortened upper lip, and a transverse mid-philtral crease. Management includes botulinum toxin (temporary) or surgical resection (permanent).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Marionette lines are caused by the {{c1::depressor anguli oris::muscle}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Downward pull of the oral commissure contributes to an aged or sad appearance and is a common botulinum toxin target.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c2::Hering’s}} law of equal innervation explains postoperative {{c1::contralateral lid ptosis::finding}} after ptosis repair.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Manual elevation of the more ptotic lid may unmask subclinical ptosis on the opposite side due to shared innervation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A chemical brow lift is performed by injecting botulinum toxin into the {{c1::glabella and crow’s feet::injection sites}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Weakening brow depressors allows unopposed frontalis action, resulting in brow elevation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Forehead botulinum toxin injections should not extend lateral to the {{c1::midpupillary line::landmark}} to avoid ptosis.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
In practice you can see where the corrugator ends laterally by having the patient furrow their brow
Lateral spread may weaken the levator palpebrae superioris, causing upper eyelid ptosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Senile chin deformity results from weakening of the {{c1::mentalis and depressor labii inferioris::muscles}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Loss of muscular support causes inferior displacement of the chin soft tissue pad.
Aka witches chin deformity
You can get this deformity if you dont sew the muscle back together when you do a mandible ORIF

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Chin augmentation assessment includes {{c1::horizontal, vertical, and transverse::3 dimensions}} of the mentum.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Normal occlusion + weak chin = microgenia; normal occlusion + strong chin = macrogenia. Chin implants should be at least partially subperiosteal; bone resorption risk increases with subperiosteal placement.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dermal necrosis after facelift should be managed with {{c1::conservative debridement::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Includes gentle debridement, peroxide cleansing, and topical antibiotic ointment.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Facial nerve paralysis has a worse prognosis in {{c1::Ramsay Hunt syndrome::etiology}} than in idiopathic Bell palsy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: VZV-related neuritis causes more severe nerve injury and lower rates of full recovery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bone derived from {{c1::intramembranous ossification::bone type}} resorbs less than endochondral bone.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Cranial bone resorbs less than rib or scapula. Bone resorbs less than cartilage overall.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lower lip defects involving {{c1::<1/3::defect size}} of the lower lip without commissure involvement can be closed primarily.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Appropriate when tension-free closure preserves oral competence.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lower lip defects involving {{c1::1/4–1/2::defect size}} without commissure involvement can be reconstructed with an {{c2::Abbe flap::flap}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The Abbe (lip-switch) flap is a staged cross-lip flap based on the labial artery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lower lip defects involving {{c1::1/4–1/2::defect size}} with commissure involvement can be reconstructed with an {{c2::Estlander flap::flap}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The Estlander flap crosses the oral commissure and is preferred when commissure involvement is present.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lower lip defects involving {{c1::1/2–2/3::defect size}} can be reconstructed with a {{c2::Karapandzic flap::flap}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: An innervated circumoral advancement flap preserving neurovascular supply and oral competence.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Lower lip defects involving {{c1::>2/3::defect size}} require reconstruction with large local or free flaps.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Options include Gillies fan flap, Bernard-Burrow flap, Fujimori gate flap, or free tissue transfer.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The Abbe flap is also known as a {{c1::lip-switch flap::name}} and is ideal for reconstruction of the {{c2::philtrum::subunit}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Commonly used for central upper lip and philtral defects with preservation of orbicularis oris continuity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Early-stage trapdoor deformities can be treated with {{c1::Kenalog mixed with 5-FU::injection therapy}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mature trapdoor deformities require Z-plasty revision to redirect contractile vectors.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Open rhinoplasty combines {{c1::marginal, transfixion, and transcolumellar::3 incisions}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The transcolumellar incision connects bilateral marginal incisions for exposure of nasal tip structures.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In rhinoplasty, a {{c1::transcartilaginous}} incision passes through the lateral crus to remove a cephalic strip.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
It is an endonasal technique. Used for tip volume reduction while preserving cartilage support.
the intracartilaginous incision in the image below is the same thing as a trancartilaginous incision

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An intercartilaginous incision is made between the {{c1::upper and lower lateral cartilages::borders}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Provides access to the upper two-thirds of the nasal vault; combined with marginal incisions allows delivery of lower lateral cartilages.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In rhinoplasty {{c1::transfixion}} incision crosses the membranous septum just below the caudal septum.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Allows bilateral septal access during septoplasty or rhinoplasty.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Calvarial bone grafts are typically harvested from the {{c1::parietal}} bone

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Remain at least 1.5 cm lateral to the sagittal suture and at least 1 cm posterior to the coronal suture to reduce dural or sinus injury risk.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Endoscopic {{c1::transsphenoidal::surgical approach}} management of {{c2::petrous apex cholesterol granulomas}} is associated with low morbidity and a lower risk of recurrence compared with transotic approaches.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Endoscopic transsphenoidal approaches avoid otic capsule violation and hearing loss risk seen with transotic or infralabyrinthine routes. Best suited for medially located petrous apex lesions with sphenoid sinus access.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) can improve lower airway symptoms in asthma through the {{c1::unified airway theory::concept}}, even without measurable improvement in pulmonary function tests.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The unified airway theory proposes that upper and lower airway inflammation are linked; improving sinonasal inflammation can reduce bronchial inflammation, asthma symptoms, and exacerbations despite unchanged spirometry.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Steroid-eluting sinus implants reduce postoperative surgical interventions by {{c1::31::percent}}, lysis of adhesions by {{c2::51::percent}}, and oral steroid use by {{c3::40::percent}} compared with controls.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Based on Han et al. meta-analysis. Most implants are FDA-approved for intraoperative use after FESS; only one is approved for in-office placement. No proven benefit beyond 6 months.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: At 6 weeks post-ESS, the ethmoid sinus microbiota most closely resembles the {{c1::anterior nasal cavity::site}} and {{c2::pretreatment sinus::site}} microbial profiles.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The microbiota colonizing the ethmoid at 6 weeks postoperatively from ESS were most similar to anterior nasal cavity and pretreatment sinus microbial profiles, suggesting these sites may serve as sources for postoperative bacterial repopulation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The bitter taste receptor {{c1::T2R38::receptor}} is the first genetic polymorphism identified with a potential role in the etiology of chronic rhinosinusitis independent of systemic disease.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: T2R38 activation enhances innate immune responses in the upper airway, including nitric oxide production and pathogen defense.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After maximal medical therapy for CRS, {{c1::38::percent}}% of patients achieve sustained symptomatic relief.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: About half of patients remain symptomatic with radiographic disease; among initially asymptomatic patients, relapse is common over time.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Among CRS patients initially asymptomatic after maximal medical therapy, {{c1::43::percent}}% relapse symptomatically within 3–23 months, and {{c2::20::percent}}% eventually undergo surgery.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Illustrates the chronic and relapsing nature of CRS despite initial response to medical therapy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Only about {{c1::20::percent}}% of patients with CRSwNP achieve complete disease control at 3–5 years after FESS.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Supports the concept of CRSwNP as a chronic inflammatory disease rather than a surgically curable condition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In patients with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy does {{c1::not consistently improve::effect}} chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Although CRS is common in CVID, immunoglobulin replacement primarily reduces systemic and lower respiratory infections and does not reliably improve sinonasal disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most nasal polyps are {{c1::edematous eosinophilic::histologic subtype}} in nature.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Three main histologic subtypes exist: fibroinflammatory, edematous eosinophilic (most common), and glandular (least common).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hyposmia and anosmia in CRSwNP result from {{c1::mechanical obstruction of the olfactory cleft and direct inflammatory injury from eosinophil-derived toxins::2}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mechanical blockage limits odorant access, while toxic cationic proteins released by eosinophils directly damage the olfactory neuroepithelium.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In {{c3::CRSsNP}}, {{c1::low-dose macrolide::therapy}} treatment for {{c2::24}} weeks is associated with improved clinical outcomes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Benefit is thought to be immunomodulatory rather than antimicrobial.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Sensation of the auricle is supplied by the {{c1::great auricular nerve (C2–C3), auriculotemporal nerve (V3), lesser occipital nerve (C2), sensory branch of the facial nerve (CNVII) and auricular branch of the vagus nerve (CN X)::five nerves}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Great auricular: posterior surface + inferior/anterior auricle including lobule. Auriculotemporal (V3): anterior and superior auricle + tragus. Lesser occipital: superior posterior auricle. Auricular branch of vagus (Arnold nerve): concha + EAC → cough reflex.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::anterior vestibular artery::artery}} supplies most of the utricle, the superior and horizontal semicircular canals, and a small portion of the saccule.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Typically arises from the labyrinthine artery; infarction may cause selective vestibular deficits.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Donaldson’s line is an imaginary line drawn posteriorly through the plane of the {{c1::horizontal semicircular canal::landmark}}, along which the {{c2::endolymphatic sac::structure}} is usually found.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Key surgical landmark for endolymphatic sac decompression or shunt procedures; the sac is typically on or just inferior to this line.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The tympanic nerve (Jacobson’s nerve) branches from {{c1::CN IX::nerve}} in the jugular foramen and re-enters the temporal bone via the {{c2::inferior tympanic canaliculus::pathway}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Travels with the inferior tympanic artery (branch of ascending pharyngeal artery) and contributes to the tympanic plexus and internal carotid plexus.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Among surgical approaches for CPA tumors, the {{c1::middle cranial fossa::approach}} carries the highest risk of facial nerve injury.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reflects extensive facial nerve exposure within the IAC during hearing-preservation surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common patterns of cholesteatoma spread involve the {{c1::posterior epitympanum::location}}, {{c2::posterior mesotympanum::location}}, and {{c3::anterior epitympanum::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reflects ventilation pathways and common sites of retraction pocket formation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Cochlear implantation may proceed in the setting of otitis media with saline irrigation, topical {{c1::ofloxacin::antibiotic}}, and postoperative {{c2::ceftriaxone::antibiotic}}, without placement of tympanostomy tubes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Active infection can be managed intraoperatively; tubes increase meningitis risk and are avoided.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common complication of cochlear implantation in children is {{c1::flap infection::complication}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Meticulous soft tissue handling and postoperative wound care are essential in pediatrics.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After cochlear implantation, acute otitis media occurring >{{c1::2 months::timeframe}} post-op without inner ear malformation is treated with {{c2::oral antibiotics::therapy}}; serous effusions do not require treatment.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: IV antibiotics are reserved for early post-op infections or patients with inner ear malformations.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hemifacial spasm following cochlear implantation most commonly results from stimulation of the {{c1::labyrinthine segment::facial nerve segment}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Likely due to current spread near the proximal facial nerve within the IAC.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The Jahrsdoerfer scale is a {{c1::10-point::score}} CT-based system used to predict candidacy for {{c2::atresiaplasty::procedure}} in congenital aural atresia.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Stapes present = 2 points. ≥7 good candidate; 6 borderline; ≤5 poor (consider bone-conduction devices).

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most useful laboratory marker for monitoring malignant otitis externa is {{c1::CRP::lab}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Gallium scans track treatment response; CT best assesses bone erosion. Oral ciprofloxacin may be used as monotherapy in selected patients.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In the absence of congenital ossicular abnormalities, the most common site of perilymphatic fistula is {{c1::anterior to the anterior crus of the stapes::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Other described sites include anteroinferior and anterosuperior to the anterior crus.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c2::Cochleosaccular dysgenesis}} ({{c3::Scheibe aplasia::aka}}) is a malformation of the {{c1::membranous pars inferior::anatomic region}} and is the most common temporal bone dysplasia associated with congenital profound SNHL.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Radiographic imaging is typically normal; findings include absent or abnormal organ of Corti, cochlear duct collapse, and stria vascularis degeneration. It has normal semicircular canals.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c3::Alexander aplasia}} is absence of the {{c1::cochlear aqueduct::structure}}, causing preferential dysfunction of the {{c2::basal turn::cochlear region}} with preservation of low-frequency hearing.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Classically presents as high-frequency SNHL with relative apical preservation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Common cavity deformity results from arrest of otic capsule development at {{c1::4–5 weeks::gestational age}}, producing a single cavity formed by the {{c2::cochlea and vestibule::2 structures}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Associated with severe congenital SNHL and vestibular dysfunction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A {{c2::floating stapes footplate}} refers to {{c1::loss of fixation of the footplate to the annular ligament with mobility as a unit within the oval window::definition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Distinct from a depressed footplate, which is displaced medially into the vestibule and increases risk of SNHL.

Why it matters (high-yield)

  • Increases risk of:
    • Perilymph gusher
    • Inner ear trauma
    • SNHL
  • Often forces a change in surgical plan

Common management options (conceptual)

  • Abort the case and stage
  • Stabilize the footplate (e.g., soft tissue, laser technique)
  • Convert to a controlled stapedectomy if safe
  • Seal oval window carefully to prevent leak

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If the malleus becomes hypermobile during stapedectomy, management is to {{c1::abort the procedure and reoperate in 4–6 months::management}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Allows stabilization of ossicular mechanics before definitive stapes surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Aminoglycoside sensitivity is caused by a mitochondrial mutation in the {{c1::A1555G::gene}} locus.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This mutation affects mitochondrial 12S rRNA, increasing susceptibility to profound hearing loss even with low-dose aminoglycoside exposure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The primary advantage of {{c1::round window plugging::procedure}} for SSCD is {{c2::avoidance of a more invasive approach::advantage}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
it is otherwise a poor approach
Studies show poor improvement in vestibular symptoms, increased air–bone gaps, and no consistent objective vestibular benefit. Avoiding postauricular incision or middle fossa craniotomy is the only demonstrated advantage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Surgical repair of SSCD has an overall success rate of {{c1::~94%::percent}}, with no clear difference between {{c2::middle cranial fossa and transmastoid::2}} approaches.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Repair techniques include plugging, resurfacing, capping, and plugging + resurfacing. Older pooled data found ~94% overall success without a statistically significant difference among techniques, although the literature is heterogeneous and individual studies have suggested less durable results with resurfacing alone. 
https://otosurgeryatlas.stanford.edu/otologic-surgery-atlas/vestibular-surgery/superior-semicircular-canal-dehiscence/#

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After transmastoid canal plugging for SSCD, general {{c1::disequilibrium::symptom}} may persist postoperatively.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Autophony, ear fullness, pulsatile tinnitus, and sound- or pressure-induced vertigo usually improve or resolve. Persistent disequilibrium is an important counseling point; vestibular PT and migraine management help compensation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SSCD classically presents with a {{c1::low-frequency air–bone gap::air conduction}}, {{c2::supranormal thresholds::bone conduction}}, and {{c3::present::absent/present}} acoustic reflexes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Presence of acoustic reflexes helps distinguish SSCD from otosclerosis, which often abolishes reflexes despite a similar audiogram.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::SSCD::disease}} can be evaluated with {{c2::oVEMP::test}}, which remains sensitive even in patients with severe–profound SNHL.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: VEMPs bypass the cochlear nerve. oVEMP reflects utricular stimulation via the superior vestibular nerve; responses are reduced in conductive hearing loss.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: SSCD is associated with an SP/AP ratio on ECoG {{c1::elevated  >0.4}} and {{c2::abnormally low cVEMP thresholds ≤70-75 dB}} on VEMP.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: oVEMP may be more sensitive, but cVEMP is more commonly used clinically. Gold standard diagnosis remains high-resolution temporal bone CT.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Facial nerve paralysis with {{c1::>90% degeneration::ENOG threshold}} following temporal bone fracture indicates need for surgical exploration.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Timing and degree of degeneration guide operative decision-making for facial nerve decompression.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common site of facial nerve injury in temporal bone fractures is the {{c1::perigeniculate ganglion region::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This segment is anatomically vulnerable due to its bony canal configuration.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Temporal bone malignancy most commonly presents with {{c1::chronic otorrhea with EAC polyp formation::presentation}}, with or without {{c2::facial nerve paresis::finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Workup requires imaging and biopsy; presentation often mimics chronic infection.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The extratemporal facial nerve begins development at {{c1::6 weeks::gestational age}}, with terminal branches present by {{c2::8 weeks::gestational age}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical branches are identifiable by the end of week 8.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: CO₂ laser use at {{c1::low::low/high}} power produces more pathologic artifact

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Higher power allows faster cutting with less thermal spread into specimen margins.
whereas higher power (~3 W) reduces artifact.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Traumatic tympanic membrane perforations should be observed for at least {{c1::6 months::timeframe}}, as {{c2::80–94%::percent}} heal spontaneously.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Early surgical intervention is rarely required unless complications develop.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::retroauricular::approach}} tympanoplasty is favored for {{c2::anterior::location}} perforations

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Provides improved exposure and allows circumferential canalplasty.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In Wullstein Type {{c1::III::classification}} tympanoplasty, the graft is placed directly onto the {{c2::stapes head::structure}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Creates a columella effect; Types I–III are most common in modern practice.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Ossicular discontinuity with an {{c1::intact tympanic membrane::condition}} produces greater conductive hearing loss (~{{c2::60 dB::level}}) than when the membrane is absent.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Loss of acoustic coupling allows direct sound transmission to the oval and round windows.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A {{c1::smaller middle ear volume::anatomic feature}} is associated with worse conductive hearing loss for identical tympanic membrane perforations.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Acoustic impedance increases as middle ear volume decreases.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Lateral graft::procedure}} tympanoplasty is typically reserved for {{c2::near-total, total, or marginal perforations::3 indications}} or failed medial grafts.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Advantages: exposure and graft take. Disadvantages: prolonged healing, blunting, graft lateralization, epithelial cysts. Prevent blunting by preserving the tympanomeatal angle and avoiding graft placement directly on bone.
https://otosurgeryatlas.stanford.edu/otologic-surgery-atlas/tympanoplasty/lateral-graft-tympanoplasty/

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
What anatomic landmark separates condylar from subcondylar fractures?
{{c1::Sigmoid notch}}

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Auricular hematoma is caused by separation of the {{c1::perichondrium}} from the underlying cartilage.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This disrupts the cartilage blood supply and predisposes to cauliflower ear if untreated.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In auricular hematoma, fibroneocartilage begins to form {{c1::7–10::timeframe}} days after injury.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Delayed treatment becomes less effective once fibrocartilage forms.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Is there a difference in outcome between incision and drainage compared to needle aspiration for auricular hematoma? {{c1::No}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Incision and drainage is no more successful than needle aspiration when used alone; recurrence is common without compression to re-oppose the perichondrium.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Markowitz NOE fracture Type I is defined by the medial canthal tendon remaining attached to {{c1::a single central bone fragment::definition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Because the MCT remains attached, Type I fractures can often be managed with bony reduction alone. On axial CT, look for rotation and lateralization of the Y-shaped bone fragment containing the lacrimal fossa.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Markowitz NOE fracture Type II is defined by {{c1::comminution with an intact bone segment at the MCT insertion::definition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The MCT is still attached to bone, allowing for bony reduction rather than transnasal fixation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Markowitz NOE fracture Type III occurs when fractures extend into the bone fragment where the {{c1::medial canthal tendon::key structure}} inserts, potentially resulting in avulsion.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Type III fractures typically require transnasal wiring to restore medial canthal position.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most specific radiologic sign predicting enophthalmos after orbital floor fracture is a {{c1::rounded inferior rectus muscle::CT finding}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reflects loss of normal muscle tethering and increased orbital volume.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: During medial orbital wall fracture ORIF, what vascular injury should you be concerned about? {{c1::Posterior ethmoid artery}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The posterior ethmoid artery runs near the optic canal; cautery or thermal injury can transmit damage to the optic nerve and cause permanent vision loss.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Bleph 
{{c1::Ectropion::complication}} is more commonly associated with {{c2::transcutaneous incisions::approach}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Subciliary incisions carry a particularly high risk and have fallen out of favor.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Entropion::complication}} is more commonly associated with the {{c2::transconjunctival approach::approach}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Despite this risk, transconjunctival incisions have a lower ectropion rate than subciliary approaches.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most orbital floor blowout fractures occur medial to the {{c1::infraorbital nerve::anatomic landmark}} and inferior orbital fissure.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: A medial strut extending posteriorly from the nasomaxillary buttress is often preserved.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Changes in visual acuity alone are a {{c1::poor predictor::diagnostic value}} of ocular injury in orbital trauma.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: More sensitive indicators include pain, diplopia, photopsias, scotomata, and floaters. Any of these findings warrants immediate ophthalmology consultation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Non-ballistic foreign bodies penetrating from the {{c1::eye or nose into the brain::trajectory}} may require antibiotic therapy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These injuries carry a high risk of intracranial infection.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In penetrating neck trauma, stable patients should undergo {{c1::CTA}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This reflects the modern no-zone approach. Unstable patients should be taken directly to the OR.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Otic capsule sparing temporal bone fractures are most commonly associated with {{c1::conductive or mixed::type of HL}} hearing loss.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Usually due to temporoparietal blows. Facial paralysis occurs in ~6–13%.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Otic capsule disrupting temporal bone fractures are more likely to cause {{c1::sensorineural::type of HL}} hearing loss.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often due to occipital blows. Facial paralysis occurs in ~30–66% and CSF leaks are more common.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Approximately {{c1::~90%}} of patients with delayed-onset facial paralysis after temporal bone fracture will have complete spontaneous recovery.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Delayed-onset facial paralysis generally does not require surgical intervention.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In temporal bone fractures with immediate-onset facial paralysis, approximately {{c1::50%}} have facial nerve transection.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Despite this, 40–75% of patients with immediate-onset palsy still achieve complete recovery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If facial nerve function is not documented in the ED after temporal bone fracture, the patient should be considered to have {{c1::immediate-onset facial paralysis}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This classification affects prognosis and management decisions.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: CSF fistulas occur in approximately {{c1::17%}} of temporal bone fractures.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most CSF leaks resolve spontaneously within one week.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The risk of meningitis with a CSF leak lasting more than 7 days after temporal bone fracture is approximately {{c1::55–88%}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Persistent leaks >7–10 days should be surgically repaired.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The vessel most likely responsible for a retropharyngeal hematoma after nondisplaced cervical spine injury is the {{c1::vertebral artery}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This injury may cause stroke but usually does not initially present with respiratory symptoms.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Permanent central incisors: {{c1::8}} (maxillary right), {{c1::9}} (maxillary left), {{c1::24}} (mandibular left), {{c1::25}} (mandibular right).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield dental numbering for trauma documentation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A root fracture presents with a {{c1::slightly mobile crown}} and requires splinting for {{c1::4}} weeks.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: If pulp necrosis develops, root canal therapy is required.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An {{c1::alveolar fracture}} presents with segment mobility of multiple teeth.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Management includes repositioning and stabilization with arch bars or wires for 4 weeks.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A(n) {{c2::avulsed}} permanent tooth should be {{c1::replanted immediately}} if possible.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: If immediate reimplantation is not possible, store in milk or Hank’s solution and give amoxicillin.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Isolated zygomatic arch fractures are treated with {{c1::closed reduction}} using the {{c1::Keen or Gillies::2}} approach.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Fixation is often unnecessary in isolated arch injuries.

Gillies


Keen

fields.name: Text
fields.value: After suspected ZMC fracture, reassessment for malar depression should occur within {{c1::5–7}} days.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Waiting longer risks bony fusion and inability to reduce the fracture.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most commonly injured nerve in a zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture is the {{c1::infraorbital nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Infraorbital anesthesia or dysesthesia occurs in ~25% of cases.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Primary goals of ZMC fracture repair include restoration of {{c1::malar projection and facial width}} and {{c1::normal orbital volume}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Goals should be achieved while minimizing operative morbidity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: CPAP compliance is defined as use for ≥{{c1::4}} hours per night on at least {{c1::5}} days per week.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Common insurer and sleep lab definition.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: During DISE, {{c1::propofol::med}} causes greater tongue base and oropharyngeal obstruction than {{c1::dexmedetomidine::med}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Dexmedetomidine better preserves airway tone but may prolong the procedure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An Epworth Sleepiness Scale score greater than {{c1::10}} suggests excessive daytime sleepiness.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Seen in roughly one-third of adults.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A recognized complication of maxillomandibular advancement is {{c1::inferior alveolar nerve hypoesthesia}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Occurs in approximately 12.5% of patients.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Narcolepsy is diagnosed by MSLT showing ≥{{c1::2}} sleep-onset REM periods and a mean sleep latency ≤{{c1::8}} minutes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Type 1 requires cataplexy or low CSF hypocretin-1.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is defined by obesity with an awake PaCO₂ greater than {{c1::45}} mm Hg.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: BMI ≥30 kg/m²; PaCO₂ often increases further during sleep.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Approximately {{c1::31%}} of patients with obstructive sleep apnea have a coexistent sleep disorder.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Common comorbidities include PLMD, insomnia, and circadian rhythm disorders.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Approximately {{c1::one third}} of patients do not benefit from oral appliance therapy for OSA.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: CPAP is generally more efficacious, but oral appliances may have superior adherence in selected patients.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Mandibular advancement >{{c1::50%}} of maximum protrusion is associated with greater efficacy of oral appliance therapy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Greater advancement increases risk of TMJ pain and dental complications.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Complete response to OSA treatment (AHI <5/hr) is achieved in nearly {{c1::twice as many}} patients treated with CPAP compared to oral appliances.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Representative studies show ~34–75% response with CPAP vs ~19–43% with oral appliances.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A  Level {{c1::1}} sleep study is performed in a sleep laboratory and measures {{c1::≥7}} physiologic parameters.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Attended PSG including EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG, airflow, respiratory effort, and oxygen saturation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::N2::stage}} sleep is characterized by sleep spindles and K complexes

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Represents stable non-REM sleep.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Obstructive apnea is defined as a ≥{{c1::90%}} drop in airflow lasting ≥{{c1::10}} seconds with continued respiratory effort.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Airflow is typically measured using a thermistor signal.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An arousal is defined as an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting ≥{{c1::3}} seconds after ≥{{c1::10}} seconds of stable sleep.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: During REM sleep, a concurrent submental EMG increase ≥1 second is required.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Kleine–Levin syndrome is a form of {{c1::recurrent hypersomnia}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Typically begins in adolescent males; episodes last days–weeks with sleep up to 18–20 hours/day.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Core body temperature is lowest at approximately {{c1::4–5 AM::time of day}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reflects circadian rhythm physiology.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The first REM period typically occurs {{c1::~90 minutes}} after sleep onset.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: REM periods lengthen as the night progresses.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: N1 sleep is characterized by {{c1::theta waves}}, while N3 sleep shows {{c1::delta waves}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Awake EEG demonstrates alpha and beta activity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The proportion of slow-wave (N3) sleep {{c1::decreases}} with age.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Older adults spend more time in lighter sleep stages.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Kuhn frontal cell Type {{c2::I}} is defined as {{c1::a single cell superior to the agger nasi}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most common frontal cell type.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Kuhn frontal cell Type {{c2::II}} consists of {{c1::a tier of two or more cells above the agger nasi}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: May contribute to frontal recess obstruction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Kuhn frontal cell Type {{c2::III}} is a {{c1::single cell extending from the agger nasi into the frontal sinus}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Not super well visualized in the image below
Can significantly narrow frontal sinus drainage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Kuhn frontal cell Type {{c2::IV}} is defined as {{c1::an isolated cell entirely within the frontal sinus}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often mistaken for a frontal sinus septation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A skull base CSF leak is considered small when the defect measures {{c1::2–10}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Typically low-flow leaks.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A skull base CSF leak is considered midsize when the defect measures {{c1::11–20}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: May require multilayer repair depending on flow.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A skull base CSF leak is considered large when the defect measures >{{c1::20}} mm.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Large or high-flow leaks benefit from vascularized flap reconstruction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Mucosal grafts should be placed as an {{c1::onlay::onlay/underlay}} during CSF leak repair.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Underlay placement of mucosa risks mucocele formation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::Cotton test}} is used to evaluate candidacy for submucosal implantation in empty nose syndrome.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Symptom improvement with temporary cotton placement predicts benefit from implants.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common cause of 30-day readmission after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery is {{c1::epistaxis::cause}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: 30-day readmission rates: epistaxis 2.1%, hyponatremia 1.5%, CSF leak 0.9%.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Kadish::staging system}} stage is used to stage esthesioneuroblastoma.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Kadish staging describes anatomic extent of disease and guides prognosis and management.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Hyams::grading system - NOT STAGING SYSTEM}} grade is used to assess esthesioneuroblastoma tumor differentiation and prognosis..

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Hyams grade correlates with tumor differentiation and prognosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Kadish stage {{c1::A::stage}} esthesioneuroblastoma is confined to the {{c2::nasal cavity::extent}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Lowest stage with best prognosis.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Kadish stage {{c1::B::stage}} esthesioneuroblastoma involves the nasal cavity and {{c2::paranasal sinuses::extent}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: No extension beyond the sinonasal cavity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Kadish stage {{c1::C::stage}} esthesioneuroblastoma extends beyond the nasal cavity or sinuses.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Includes orbit, skull base, intracranial space, nasopharynx, or pterygopalatine fossa.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Modified Kadish stage {{c1::D::stage}} indicates {{c2::cervical nodal or distant metastases::extent}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Represents advanced disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The greatest reduction in proptosis for thyroid eye disease is achieved with combined {{c1::transpalpebral floor/lateral wall}} and {{c2::endoscopic medial wall::approach}} decompression.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Overall severe complication rate is ~0.12%.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Patient has fibrous dysplasia of the nasal cavity but no obstructive or compressive symptoms.
Should you treat it? {{c1::No}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Only treat if symptomatic
Radiation therapy is contraindicated.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Supra-agger nasi cells displace the frontal recess {{c1::medially::direction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Important landmark during frontal recess dissection.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Suprabullar cells displace the frontal recess {{c1::anteriorly::direction}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: May obscure the frontal sinus drainage pathway.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: α2-agonists used in ESS (e.g., xylometazoline, clonidine, dexmedetomidine) have been associated with {{c1::loss of smell::adverse effect}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Reported in ~14.7% of patients.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The long-term failure rate of endoscopic sinus surgery is approximately {{c1::5–15%::range}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Based on long-term outcome studies in CRS.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The most common cause of failed primary frontal sinus surgery is retained {{c1::agger nasi or frontal bulla remnants::cause}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Residual agger nasi is seen in ~79% of revision cases.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The nasoseptal flap is supplied by the {{c1::posterior septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery::vessel}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The artery runs submucosally along the posterior nasal septum.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: During endoscopic sinus surgery, the most common sites of iatrogenic CSF leak are the {{c1::cribriform plate}} and {{c1::posterior ethmoid roof::2 locations}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: During endoscopic skull base surgery, the sphenoid sinus is the most common site.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Fungal ball most commonly affects {{c1::women aged 50–60::demographic}} and often involves the {{c2::maxillary sinus::location}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Up to 32% of patients are asymptomatic.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Fungal balls are associated with prior {{c1::endodontic surgery::risk factor}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Zinc oxide–containing root-filling materials promote Aspergillus fumigatus growth.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Radiographic findings with the highest positive predictive value for acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis include {{c1::osseous erosion}}, facial soft-tissue thickening, and extrasinus involvement.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These findings often indicate late, irreversible disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis is analogous to {{c1::allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis}} but occurs in the sinuses.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Higher risk of orbital complications and cranial neuropathies, especially with expansile sphenoid disease.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Allergen immunotherapy promotes a shift from {{c1::Th2}} to {{c1::Th1}} predominance and increases {{c2::IL-10::immunology stuff}} and {{c2::IgG4::immunology stuff}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Allergen-specific IgE initially rises, then declines over time.

fields.value: The {{c1::vestibule}} houses the {{c3::otoltih}} organs which are the {{c2::saccule and utricle::2}} They detect {{c4::linear acceleration}} relative to gravity

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• Detect linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity.
  • Utricle: primarily senses horizontal motion (forward/backward, side-to-side).
  • Saccule: primarily senses vertical motion (up/down).
  • Contain hair cells embedded in a gelatinous layer topped by otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals).
  • Otolith input is important for balance, posture, spatial orientation, and perception of self-motion.

Extra 1
fields.value:
The Iter chordae anterius and Iter chordae posterius are the tiny bony canal openings through which the chorda tympani nerve enters and exits the middle ear.
  • Posterior iter (iter chordae posterius)
    • Entry point of the chorda tympani into the middle ear
    • Located near the posterior canaliculus off the facial canal, close to the mastoid segment of CN VII
  • Anterior iter (iter chordae anterius)
    • Exit point of the chorda tympani from the middle ear
    • Opens into the petrotympanic fissure toward the infratemporal fossa

fields.name: Image
Question Mask
Extra 1
fields.value:
The Pöschl view is:
Parallel to the plane of the superior semicircular canal
Roughly 45° oblique to standard sagittal/coronal planes
This gives you an “en face” or long-axis look at the canal.
You can see:
the arcuate shape of the canal
the bony roof over the canal
whether there is a true dehiscence
Conceptually:
You are slicing along the loop of the canal.

fields.name: Header
fields.value: Stenver

fields.name: Image
Question Mask
Extra 1
fields.value:
Perpendicular to the plane of the superior semicircular canal
Orthogonal to the Pöschl plane
This produces a cross-sectional view of the canal.
Conceptually:
You are slicing across the loop of the canal.
This helps:
confirm a suspected defect seen on Pöschl
reduce false positives from partial-volume averaging
A simple mental model:
Pöschl = “hot dog” cut (long axis)
Stenvers = “hamburger” cut (cross section)

fields.name: Answer Mask
Original Mask
Text
fields.value: The Head Impulse Test (HIT) assesses the {{c1::angular vestibulo-ocular reflex (aVOR)}} by having the examiner deliver a small, rapid, unpredictable head thrust while the patient maintains fixation on a target.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Normal
Abnormal


Purpose
  • Bedside assessment of the angular vestibulo-ocular reflex (aVOR)
  • Most sensitive for detecting moderate-to-severe vestibular hypofunction
How to Perform
  1. Patient fixes gaze on examiner's nose.
  2. Examiner turns the patient's head ~10–20° off center.
  3. Deliver a rapid, low-amplitude, unpredictable thrust back toward center.
  4. Observe whether the eyes stay on target or require a corrective saccade.
Interpretation
  • Normal: Eyes remain on target.
  • Abnormal: Catch-up saccade indicates deficient aVOR on the side toward which the head was rotated.
Clinical Pearl
  • Standard bedside HIT is qualitative.
  • vHIT (video HIT) uses high-speed cameras to quantify VOR gain and detect both overt and covert saccades.
  • Horizontal canal function is easiest to assess clinically, but vHIT can test all six semicircular canals.
Why it Works
When the head turns right, a normal right horizontal canal increases firing and drives compensatory eye movement leftward. If the right vestibular apparatus is impaired, the eyes move with the head and must "catch up" with a corrective saccade.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Dynamic Visual Acuity (DVA) testing evaluates the functional integrity of the {{c1::vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)::reflex}} by comparing visual acuity during head movement to visual acuity with the head still.


A > {{c2::2::#}} line difference between still and dynamic inticates abnormal result

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Purpose
  • Functional assessment of the VOR.
  • Measures the patient's ability to maintain clear vision during head movement.
How to Perform
  1. Measure baseline (static) visual acuity.
  2. Oscillate the patient's head horizontally at ~2 Hz.
  3. Repeat visual acuity testing during head movement.
  4. Compare static and dynamic scores.
Interpretation
  • Normal: ≤2-line decrease in visual acuity.
  • Abnormal: >2-line decrease.
  • Greater losses generally indicate poorer VOR function. Clinically >4 line decrease is more specific.
Clinical Relevance
  • Particularly useful in bilateral vestibular hypofunction (BVH).
  • Correlates with the patient's real-world complaint of blurred vision while walking or moving the head.
  • Provides a functional measure of vestibular impairment that complements physiologic tests such as calorics, rotary chair, and vHIT.
Limitation
  • DVA does not localize the lesion or identify which vestibular structure is impaired; it simply demonstrates impaired gaze stabilization during motion.
High-Yield Pearl
Think of DVA as asking: "Can the patient keep the world clear while moving?" Whereas HIT/vHIT ask: "Is the VOR working?" DVA measures the real-world consequence of VOR failure.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Rotary chair testing evaluates the {{c1::angular vestibulo-ocular reflex (aVOR)::reflex}} by measuring eye movements in response to controlled rotational stimuli. It tests the {{c2::horizontal}} SCC(s). {{c3::It tests in the low,medium, and high}} frequency(s).

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Normal

Abnormal showing low gain, normal symmetry, and phase lead (bilateral vestibular hypofunction)

Abnormal showing low gain, asymmetry, and phase lead in the low frequencies (stable unilateral vestibular loss)


Purpose
  • Quantitative assessment of the horizontal angular VOR.
  • Particularly useful for diagnosing and characterizing bilateral vestibular hypofunction (BVH).
How It Works
  • The patient sits in a motorized chair within a dark enclosure.
  • Eye movements are recorded with video or electro-oculography.
  • The chair rotates in a controlled sinusoidal or stepwise fashion.
  • The VOR response is measured across multiple frequencies.
Key Parameters
  • Gain = Eye velocity ÷ Head velocity
    • Normal ≈ 1
    • Reduced in vestibular hypofunction
  • Phase
    • Timing relationship between eye and head movement
    • BVH often causes phase lead
  • Symmetry
    • Assesses differences between rightward and leftward responses
Clinical Pearl
  • Calorics test the horizontal canals at an extremely low frequency (~0.003 Hz).
  • Rotary chair tests frequencies closer to everyday head movements (~0.01–1 Hz).
  • Because it stimulates both ears simultaneously, rotary chair is excellent for bilateral loss but less useful for identifying which ear is affected.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Caloric testing evaluates the {{c1::horizontal semicircular canal and superior vestibular nerve::anatomy}}.

The patient is positioned with the horizontal canal approximately {{c2::30° above horizontal::positioning}} to maximize stimulation.

It assesses vestibular function at an {{c3::extremely low frequency (~0.003 Hz)::frequency(s)}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Purpose
  • Assesses unilateral vestibular function.
  • Primarily evaluates the horizontal semicircular canal and superior vestibular nerve.
  • One of the few vestibular tests that can stimulate each ear independently.
How It Works
  1. Patient lies supine with head elevated 30°.
  2. Warm and cool air or water are delivered into each ear canal.
  3. Temperature differences create endolymph movement within the horizontal canal.
  4. Resulting nystagmus is recorded and quantified.
Normal Responses
  • Warm irrigation: nystagmus beats toward the irrigated ear.
  • Cool irrigation: nystagmus beats away from the irrigated ear.
Mnemonic
  • COWS
    • Cold → fast phase Opposite
    • Warm → fast phase Same
Clinical Interpretation
  • Unilateral weakness: Reduced response from one ear compared with the other.
  • Bilateral weakness: Reduced responses from both ears.
  • Directional preponderance: Stronger nystagmus in one direction regardless of stimulated ear (less localizing).
Frequency Spectrum of Vestibular Testing
TestApproximate Frequency
Calorics~0.003 Hz
Rotary Chair~0.01–1 Hz
vHIT~2–7 Hz
Clinical Pearl
A patient may have absent caloric responses but normal vHIT, because the tests evaluate different portions of the vestibular frequency spectrum. This pattern can be seen in disorders such as Ménière's disease and some compensated vestibular lesions.
High-Yield Pearl
Calorics do not mimic normal head movement. Instead, they create an artificial thermal stimulus that allows each labyrinth to be tested independently, which is why they remain valuable for detecting unilateral vestibular deficits.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
The video Head Impulse Test (vHIT) evaluates the {{c1::angular vestibulo-ocular reflex (aVOR)::reflex}}.

It provides a {{c6::quantitative::quantatative/qualitataive}} measurement.

It tests {{c7::all six::#}} semicircular canal(s)

It evaluates vestibular function in {{c8::high (~2–7 Hz)}} frequency(s)

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Purpose
  • Quantitative assessment of the angular VOR.
  • Detects semicircular canal dysfunction.
  • Evaluates all six canals individually.
How It Works
  1. Patient wears high-speed video goggles.
  2. Patient fixates on a stationary target.
  3. Examiner delivers small, rapid, unpredictable head impulses.
  4. Software measures head velocity, eye velocity, VOR gain, and corrective saccades.
What Is Measured?
  • VOR Gain
    • Eye velocity ÷ head velocity
    • Normal ≈ 0.8–1.0 depending on canal and system
  • Corrective Saccades
    • Overt: Occur after the head movement and can often be seen clinically.
    • Covert: Occur during the head movement and are usually invisible without vHIT.
Canals Tested
  • Horizontal canals
  • Right anterior–left posterior (RALP) pair
  • Left anterior–right posterior (LARP) pair
Advantages
  • Fast (<10 minutes)
  • Canal-specific
  • Physiologic stimulus
  • Detects covert saccades
  • Useful in both unilateral and bilateral vestibular hypofunction

fields.value: {{c1::30–70}}% of RLNs demonstrate extralaryngeal branching, with {{c2::bifurcation::type of branching}} accounting for the large majority. If a {{c2::bifurcation}} occurs, the {{c3::anterior::anterior/posterior}} branch is typically the motor branch.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Photo below is a little misleading. The branching usually occurs within 1cm of the entry point
The branching discussed above refers to the nerve fibers that enter the larynx. There are other extralaryngeal branches off of the RLN that innervate the esophagus and trachea, especially on the left side.

Remember that the RLN is part of the vagus nerve that forms form the 6th branchial arch. In addition to controlling the vocal cords, the vagus nerve helps with volitional swallow so it makes sense that it also innervates the esophagus.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The RLN typically courses {{c1::posteriorly}} to the inferior thyroid artery

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• The RLN is usually posterior to the ITA but can also be anterior to it or between ITA branches
  • More predictable on the patient's left side. More variability on the right side

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Most commonly, the RLN runs {{c1::posterior/deep::relationship}} to Berry's ligament.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Can also
* Run between fibers or branches of the ligament.
* Rarely run anterior/superficial to part of the ligament.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: RLN normally sits {{c1::posteriormedial}} to the tubercle of Zuckerkandl.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::Cernea}} classification is used to the describe the path of the {{c2::external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve}} as it enters the larynx

fields.name: Extra

Type 1: Crosses the superior thyroid vessels >1 cm above the superior pole → lowest risk, ~40–60%
Type 2a: Crosses the vessels <1 cm above the superior pole → intermediate risk, ~20–30% - more common with large goiters
Type 2b: Crosses the vessels at or below the superior pole → highest risk during superior pole dissection, ~10–25%

fields.value:
What flap dis?
{{c1::Rieger flap
}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• AKA dorsal nasal flap
  • Rotation flap recruiting skin from the glabella and upper nasal dorsum
  • Best for: medium (~1.5–2.5 cm) defects of the distal dorsum, supratip, and nasal tip
  • Advantages: single stage, excellent color/texture match, reliable random-pattern blood supply
  • Limitations: requires adequate glabellar laxity; may cause tip elevation or alar distortion in large defects
  • Not ideal for: large (>2.5–3 cm), full-thickness, or major alar defects (consider paramedian forehead flap)

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
What flap is this?
{{c1::Note Flap}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The note flap described by Walike and Larrabee is an
angular transposition flap that, when designed, looks like
a musical eighth note.5 This flap allows one to close a
circular defect with a triangular transposition flap that
maximizes the use of surrounding tissue (Fig. 8-3).6 The
flap is designed by first drawing a tangent on either side
of the circle parallel to relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs).
The tangent should have the length of 1.5 times the
diameter of the circular defect. At the end of the tangent
line, a 50° to 60° angled flap is designed, with the second
side of the flap having a length approximately equal to
the diameter of the circle.6 The flap is transposed into
the defect, and the distal tip of the flap is trimmed so that
there is no wound closure tension. As with rectangular
and parabolic transposition flaps, the greatest wound
closure tension is at the closure of the donor site. In the
case of the note flap, the greatest wound closure tension
is approximately perpendicular to the tangent line created
when the flap is designed. The surface area of the note
flap is designed so that it is 25% less than the area of the
defect; thus clinical judgment is required when this flap
is used. The flap is recommended primarily for small
(2 cm or less) skin defects. Because the pivotal arc of the
note flap is approximately 45°, a minimal standing cutaneous
deformity develops that may not require excision.
Standing cutaneous deformities of larger flaps will require
subsequent surgical revision unless the deformities are
removed at the time of flap transfer. I use the note flap
primarily for defects on the cheek, temple, and lateral
nasal sidewall. However, it may be used everywhere on
the head and neck, including the lip.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Note flap design: tangent {{c1::parallel}} to RSTLs with length {{c1::1.5×}} defect diameter → flap angle {{c1::50–60°}} → second limb {{c1::~1×}} defect diameter.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value: Dorsal nasal flap (Rieger flap): modified {{c1::rotation}} recruiting redundant skin from the {{c1::glabella}} → repairs defects of the {{c1::nasal tip, dorsum, and sidewall}} up to {{c1::~2.5 cm}} → axial blood supply from a branch of the {{c1::angular artery}} with pedicle centered near the {{c1::medial canthus}} → major disadvantage is {{c1::cephalic displacement of the nostril margin and nasal tip}}.

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value:
What flap is this?
{{c1::Bilobe}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• Type: Double transposition flap.
  • Uses: Small-to-moderate defects of the distal/lower third of the nose, particularly the nasal tip and ala; typically defects ≤1.5 cm.
  • Design: Two sequential lobes. The first lobe is approximately the size of the defect; the second is smaller and helps close the first-lobe donor site. The Zitelli modification uses a total rotation arc of ~90–110°, with ~45–50° between each lobe.
  • Disadvantages: Trapdoor/pincushion deformity, standing cutaneous deformity, relatively long scars, and alar retraction/elevation from excessive tension.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bilobed flap: {{c1::double transposition::type}} flap → used for {{c1::small-to-moderate distal nasal defects, especially the tip and ala::locations}} typically {{c1::≤1.5::size}} cm→ first lobe is {{c1::~equal}} to defect size, second lobe is {{c1::smaller}}; Zitelli design uses a {{c1::~90–110° total rotation arc (~45–50° per lobe::rotation)}} → disadvantages include {{c1::trapdoor/pincushion deformity, standing cutaneous deformity, long scars, and alar retraction/elevation from excessive tension}}.

fields.value: Hearing aids produce clinically meaningful tinnitus improvement in approximately {{c1::~2/3::proportion}} of patients with hearing loss

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• “Clinically meaningful” should mean a patient-perceived meaningful reduction in tinnitus burden, commonly operationalized using a TFI reduction of about ≥13 points.
  • The original TFI validation proposed 13 points as the threshold for meaningful change.
  • Benefit is primarily decreased bothersomeness/functional impact, not necessarily elimination of tinnitus.
  • Dedicated tinnitus masker/sound-generator features have not consistently outperformed amplification alone.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI) score >{{c1::65}} indicates high/severe tinnitus impact.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• 25 items, scored 0–100; higher = worse tinnitus-related functional impact.
  • There are proposed severity categories, although they're not as universally standardized as the scale itself.
  • A large 1,114-patient study proposed four grades: low, lower-moderate, upper-moderate, and high, with >65 = high severity.
  • The literature also contains alternative grading systems, so I would not memorize rigid “mild/moderate/severe” cutoffs as though they're universally accepted.
  • Meaningful improvement: traditionally ↓ ≥13 points.
  • Newer 2025 anchor-based data estimated an MCID closer to ~9 points, suggesting the exact threshold depends somewhat on baseline severity and follow-up interval.
For boards/clinical use, I'd remember TFI 0–100; >65 = high impact; ~13-point decrease = traditional clinically meaningful improvement.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A clinically meaningful improvement in the Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI) is a decrease of ≥{{c1::18 points}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
DHI is a 25-item (0–100) patient-reported measure of dizziness-related handicap. Yes = 4, Sometimes = 2, No = 0. Higher scores = greater handicap. Common severity classification: 0–30 mild, 31–60 moderate, 61–100 severe. Subscales are physical, functional, and emotional.

Score >60 correlates with high specificity to presence of comorbid functional or psychitric conditions
Score <30 correlates to abscence of comorbid condition

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Unlike a modified radical/CWD mastoidectomy, a radical mastoidectomy sacrifices the {{c1::TM and ossicular hearing mechanism}} and exteriorizes the {{c1::middle ear + mastoid}} into a common cavity.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The defining idea is sacrifice of the conductive hearing apparatus for maximal disease eradication.
  • Posterior canal wall is removed.
  • TM is removed/not reconstructed.
  • Malleus/incus are removed; middle-ear contents are cleared as required for disease.
  • Middle ear, attic, and mastoid become a single exteriorized cavity.
  • Wide meatoplasty allows surveillance and cleaning.

fields.value:
Pulsatile tinnitus
High-pitched/“pulsing” PT + pulsatile bruit + no change with ipsilateral jugular compression → consider {{c1::arterial causes}} First line work up after exam {{c3::CTA}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Examples:
  • Carotid atherosclerotic stenosis
  • Carotid dissection
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia
  • Tortuous ICA
  • Aberrant ICA
  • Aneurysm
Pearl: Sudden-onset PT + neck pain/headache or neurologic symptoms → consider carotid dissection.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Pulsatile tinnitus
Objective PT/bruit without typical venous features should raise concern for an {{c1::AV shunting lesion, particularly a dAVF}}. If genuinely concerned this is the dx, work up after exam with {{c2::neurovascular eval +/- DSA}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
• Can't miss dx

  • Bruit is basically the breakpoint for considering an AVM. Could be arterial but you wont know until you get imaging.

  • dAVF = dural arteriio venous fistula is the important AV shunt in isolated PT.
  • AVM: artery → nidus → vein.
  • dAVF: meningeal artery → dural vein/sinus without a nidus.
  • dAVF may present with PT alone.
  • Dangerous dAVFs have cortical venous reflux, which increases risk of intracranial hemorrhage.
  • AVM becomes more suspicious with associated seizure, focal neurologic symptoms, or intracranial hemorrhage.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Pulsatile tinnitus
PT that changes/disappears with {{c1::ipsilateral jugular compression or head position}} suggests a {{c2::venous source}}. First line work up after exam {{c3::CTA}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Think along the venous pathway:
Transverse sinus → sigmoid sinus → jugular bulb
Examples:
  • Venous sinus stenosis
  • Sigmoid sinus diverticulum
  • Sigmoid sinus dehiscence
  • High-riding/dehiscent jugular bulb
  • Jugular bulb diverticulum
  • Enlarged emissary veins
Pearl: Dehiscence may allow otherwise normal venous flow to become audible because bone no longer insulates the middle/inner ear from vascular sound.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Pulsatile tinnitus
PT + {{c1::headache, visual symptoms and/or papilledema}} → consider {{c2::idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)}}. After exam work up with {{c3::MRI/MRV + eye exam}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Extra:
Classic association: younger woman with elevated BMI.
Ask about:
  • Headache
  • Transient visual obscurations
  • Diplopia
  • Other visual changes
PT in IIH is strongly associated with transverse venous sinus stenosis.
Evaluation may include:
  • Ophthalmologic exam for papilledema
  • MRI/MRV
  • LP with opening pressure when appropriate

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Pulsatile tinnitus
PT + a {{c1::red/purple pulsatile retrotympanic mass}} → consider {{c2::paraganglioma or a vascular anomaly}}. Work up after exam with {{c3::CT temporal bone}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Differential:
  • Glomus tympanicum
  • Glomus jugulare
  • High/dehiscent jugular bulb
  • Aberrant ICA
Pearl: Don't assume a vascular-appearing middle-ear mass is a tumor—an aberrant ICA can mimic one.
High-resolution CT temporal bone is particularly useful for defining the bony/vascular anatomy.

fields.value:
Attic retraction
Tos {{c1::I}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Tos/Poulsen — pars flaccida:
I = toward malleus neck, air space remains
II = contacts malleus neck, no air space
III = extends beyond malleus, fundus/full extent visible, limited scutal erosion
IV = severe scutal/outer attic wall erosion

  • Can I see the fundus? If you can't see the bottom of the pocket, you can't exclude retained keratin deeper in the attic.
  • Is it self-cleaning, or is it retaining keratin/debris? Retained keratin is the major red flag for cholesteatoma.
  • Is there scutal/bony erosion? Erosion suggests more advanced/destructive disease.
  • Is it progressing? A stable shallow pocket is very different from one getting deeper over serial exams.
  • Are the ossicles involved / is there conductive hearing loss?

    • There is a new classification system that adds additional categories
    https://drive.google.com/file/d/17XHUEyEC7LzsQDsVXPwDqp9Wo526fz9x/view?usp=sharing

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Sade {{c1::I}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Sade classification — pars tensa retraction
  • I: Mild retraction
  • II: TM contacts incus/stapes
  • III: TM contacts promontory
  • IV: TM adherent to promontory → adhesive otitis
Clinical significance
  • Ossicular contact matters: chronic retraction can erode the long process of the incus → ossicular discontinuity and CHL, even without cholesteatoma.
  • III → IV: distinguishes promontory contact from actual adhesion; IV represents established adhesive middle-ear disease.
  • The grade alone does not determine treatment. More important are hearing loss, ossicular erosion, keratin trapping/cholesteatoma, ability to completely visualize the pocket, and progression over time.
