Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The {{c1::lateral process of the malleus}} produces the malleolar prominence and marks the inferior boundary of the pars flaccida.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Projects laterally from the upper manubrium. Anterior + posterior malleolar folds extend from this region. Pars flaccida / Prussak's space lie superior to it. Useful otoscopic and cholesteatoma landmark.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The {{c1::manubrium (handle) of the malleus}} is embedded in the TM and terminates inferiorly at the {{c2::umbo}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: On otoscopy, the visible malleus can be followed: Lateral process → manubrium → umbo. The manubrium provides mechanical coupling between the TM and ossicular chain.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The {{c1::head of the malleus}} lies in the epitympanum and articulates with the {{c2::body of the incus}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Together they form the incudomalleolar joint. The malleus head and incus body make up much of the ossicular content of the attic.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The {{c1::tensor tympani}} inserts onto the {{c2::malleus near the upper manubrium/neck}} anteriorly.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Tensor tympani → malleus. Stapedius → stapes. Tensor tympani travels through the semicanal for tensor tympani and turns around the cochleariform process before inserting on the malleus.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The {{c1::short}} process of the incus points {{c2::posteriorly}},

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
while the long process projects inferiorly toward the stapes.
Incus orientation: Body = epitympanum; Short process = posterior; Long process = inferior; Lenticular process = distal tip toward stapes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The short process of the incus sits in the {{c1::fossa incudis::specific}} and is stabilized by the {{c2::posterior incudal ligament}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: High-yield surgical landmark. Short process → posterior → fossa incudis. The fossa incudis is on the posterior epitympanic wall and helps orient you during mastoid/attic surgery.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The portion of the ossicular chain particularly prone to erosion from chronic otitis/cholesteatoma is the {{c1::long process of the incus}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: A common operative finding is: Malleus intact → long process of incus eroded → stapes remains. This vulnerability is related to its relatively tenuous blood supply and exposed position.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The {{c1::lenticular process}} is located at the distal end of the long process of the incus and articulates with the {{c2::stapes head}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Chain: Incus long process → lenticular process → incudostapedial joint → stapes head. The lenticular process is a distinct anatomical structure, not simply another name for the end of the long process.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

From lateral to medial, the stapes consists of the {{c1::head → neck → anterior/posterior crura → footplate}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Head → articulates with lenticular process; Neck → stapedius insertion; Anterior + posterior crura → surround obturator foramen; Footplate → oval window.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The stapedius tendon emerges from the {{c1::pyramidal eminence}} and inserts onto the {{c2::neck of the stapes}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Useful visual chain: Pyramidal eminence → stapedius tendon → stapes neck. This is an excellent orientation landmark in the posterior mesotympanum.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The stapes has {{c1::anterior and posterior crura}}, which connect the head/neck region to the footplate and surround the {{c2::obturator foramen}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: They are asymmetric: Anterior crus → generally thinner/straighter; Posterior crus → generally thicker/more curved. This can help orient an isolated stapes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The stapes footplate occupies the {{c1::oval window}} and is attached to its margin by the {{c2::annular ligament}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The medial surface of the footplate interfaces with the vestibule/perilymph. Important relationship: Tympanic facial nerve → immediately superior to the oval window/stapes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Ossicles

The ossicular chain runs: malleus {{c1::head}} → incus {{c1::body}} → incus {{c1::long process}} → {{c1::lenticular process}} → stapes {{c1::head}} → stapes {{c1::footplate}} → oval window.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Two joints: Incudomalleolar joint = malleus head ↔ incus body; Incudostapedial joint = lenticular process ↔ stapes head. Two muscles: Tensor tympani → malleus; Stapedius → stapes. Useful posterior landmarks: Short process of incus → fossa incudis; Stapedius tendon → pyramidal eminence.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
The air-bone gap in SSCD results from {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} air-conduction sensitivity + {{c2::increased::
increased/decreased}} bone-conduction sensitivity.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Why does a third window cause both?
Air conduction:
Stapes motion normally creates a pressure difference across the cochlear partition. The dehiscence provides an additional low-impedance outlet for inner-ear fluid displacement → some acoustic energy is shunted toward the third window → less pressure difference across the cochlear partition → less basilar-membrane motion → worse AC thresholds.
Bone conduction:
Skull vibration moves the otic capsule. The third window provides an additional compliant outlet for inner-ear fluid movement → greater differential fluid motion/pressure across the cochlear partition → greater basilar-membrane motion → better BC thresholds, sometimes <0 dB HL.
Key point: the cochlear nerve is not more sensitive. The third window changes the mechanics upstream of hair-cell/cochlear-nerve activation.
Clinical consequence:
↓ AC + ↑ BC → low-frequency ABG despite a normal middle ear.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Dx based on this audiogram
{{c1::Superior semicircular canal dehiscense}}

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Dx based on this vemp
{{c1::Bilateral superior semicircular canal dehiscense}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
How to read this cVEMP:
  • Identify the reproducible P1–N1 waveform at each stimulus intensity.
  • Threshold = lowest stimulus intensity that still produces a reproducible P1–N1 response.
  • Left: response persists to ~65 dB nHL
  • Right: response persists to ~75 dB nHL
  • These are abnormally low cVEMP thresholds → increased sound sensitivity of the vestibular system → third-window physiology.
Why in SSCD?
The dehiscence creates a low-impedance third window → sound produces greater vestibular fluid displacement → the otolith/VEMP pathway can be activated at lower sound intensities.
Key pattern:
SSCD → ↓ cVEMP threshold + ↑ oVEMP amplitude
Exact abnormal thresholds depend on the lab/stimulus protocol.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: cVEMP cut off values for SSCD differ from lab to lab but are generally {{c1::≤70–75}} dB

fields.value: The {{c1::bony}} labyrinth contains {{c2::peri}}lymph

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The membranous labyrinth is suspended within the bony labyrinth. Perilymph occupies the space between them.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::membranous}} labyrinth contains {{c2::endo}}lymph

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The membranous labyrinth includes the cochlear duct, utricle, saccule, and semicircular ducts.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In the cochlea the  scala {{c1::vestibuli}} and scala {{c1::tympani}} contain {{c2::peri}}lymph

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: These are spaces of the bony labyrinth and communicate with one another at the **helicotrema**.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In the cochlea the scala {{c1::media (cochlear duct)}} contains {{c2::endo}}lymph

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The scala media is part of the **membranous labyrinth**.

Superior → inferior:
Scala vestibuli — perilymph
Scala media — endolymph
Scala tympani — perilymph

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the {{c1::helicotrema}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The helicotrema is located at the **cochlear apex** and connects the two perilymph-filled scalae.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::helicotrema}} is located at the apex of the cochlea.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: It is where the **scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate**.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::oval}} window communicates with the scala {{c2::vestibuli}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The **stapes footplate** occupies the oval window. Stapes displacement therefore introduces pressure/volume displacement into the perilymph of the scala vestibuli.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::round}} window communicates with the scala {{c2::tympani}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The round-window membrane acts as the compliant pressure-release boundary of the normal inner ear.

Normal mechanical pathway:
Stapes → oval window → scala vestibuli → cochlear partition → scala tympani → round window

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Reissner}} membrane separates the scala {{c2::vestibuli}} from the scala {{c2::media}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Therefore, it separates:
perilymph (scala vestibuli) from endolymph (scala media).

Also called the vestibular membrane.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The {{c1::basilar}} membrane separates the scala {{c2::media}} from the scala {{c2::tympani}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Therefore, it separates:
endolymph (scala media) from perilymph (scala tympani).

The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The membranous labyrinth forms a connected {{c1::endo}}lymphatic system.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The **semicircular ducts, utricle, saccule, and cochlear duct** are components of the membranous labyrinth and contain endolymph.

Membranous structure → endolymph inside
Boney structure → perilymph inside

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Each bony semicircular {{c1::canal}} contains {{c2::peri}}lymph surrounding a membranous semicircular {{c1::duct}}, which contains {{c2::endo}}lymph

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Don't use canal and duct interchangeably when thinking about the fluid anatomy.

Bony canal → perilymph → membranous duct → endolymph

In SSCD, the defect is in the bone over the superior semicircular canal.

Text
fields.value: Movement of the {{c1::basilar}} membrane creates shearing motion between the organ of Corti and tectorial membrane, resulting in stereocilia deflection.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Sound → pressure difference across cochlear partition → basilar membrane displacement → relative motion within the organ of Corti → stereocilia deflection.

This is the mechanical step that converts the cochlear traveling wave into hair-cell stimulation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Deflection toward the {{c1::tallest}} stereocilia opens hair-cell mechanotransduction channels and causes depolarization.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Tip links connect adjacent stereocilia.

Deflection toward tallest → ↑ tip-link tension → MET channels open.
Deflection away → MET channels close → hyperpolarization.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Opening cochlear hair-cell mechanotransduction channels causes {{c1::K+::ion}} influx from endolymph, resulting in depolarization.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
This is unusual compared with conventional neurons.

Endolymph has high K+ and an approximately +80 mV endocochlear potential, creating a large electrochemical driving force for K+ to enter the hair cell through its apical MET channels.

This is how mechanical stereocilia deflection becomes an electrical receptor potential.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hair-cell depolarization opens {{c1::voltage-gated Ca²⁺}} channels, causing {{c2::glutamate::neurotransmitter}} release onto {{c3::spiral}} ganglion afferents.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Full sequence:

Stereocilia deflection → MET channels → K+ influx → depolarization → Ca²⁺ influx → glutamate → spiral ganglion → cochlear nerve

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The stria vascularis generates the approximately {{c1::+80}}  mV endocochlear potential.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The stria vascularis maintains the unusual ionic/electrical environment of scala-media endolymph.

Together, high endolymphatic K+ + positive endocochlear potential provide the electrochemical driving force for K+ influx during hair-cell mechanotransduction.

Think of it as the battery powering cochlear transduction.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Outer hair-cell electromotility is mediated by {{c1::prestin::protein}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Changes in OHC membrane potential cause prestin-mediated changes in cell length.

This feeds mechanical energy back into the organ of Corti/basilar membrane—the cochlear amplifier.

Consequences:
• increased sensitivity to quiet sounds
• sharper frequency tuning
• nonlinear compression

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Otoacoustic emissions primarily assess {{c1::outer}} hair-cell function.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
OHC electromotility generates mechanical energy that can propagate backward:

cochlea → ossicular chain/TM → ear canal

It can then be detected with a microphone as an OAE.

Therefore present OAEs indicate functioning OHC/cochlear-amplifier mechanics, not necessarily intact neural transmission.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Deiters}} cells aka outer phalangeal cells, support the {{c2::outer}} hair cells and contribute to the reticular lamina via their phalangeal processes.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: There are typically ~3 rows, corresponding to the 3 rows of outer hair cells. Deiters cells support the base of OHCs, and their long phalangeal processes extend apically to form part of the structural lattice of the reticular lamina.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The inner and outer {{c1::pillar}} cells form the {{c2::tunnel of Corti}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Pillar cells form a rigid structural framework between the inner and outer hair-cell regions.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: From medial → lateral, the major supporting structures/cells of the organ of Corti are: inner hair cell → {{c1::pillar cells}} → outer hair cells + {{c2::Deiters cells}} → {{c3::Hensen cells}} → {{c4::Claudius cells}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Inner phalangeal cells support IHCs. Deiters cells support OHCs. Pillar cells form the tunnel of Corti. Hensen and Claudius cells form the progressively more lateral supporting epithelium. Boettcher cells lie beneath Claudius cells, especially in the basal turn; recognize the name, but this is relatively low-yield.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The cochlear duct (scala media) communicates with the {{c1::saccule}} via the {{c2::ductus reuniens}}, thereby connecting cochlear endolymph to the endolymphatic duct/sac system.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Cochlear duct → ductus reuniens → saccule → saccular duct → endolymphatic duct → endolymphatic sac
The utricle similarly communicates with the endolymphatic duct via the utricular duct.
The endolymphatic duct/sac participates in endolymph volume and ionic homeostasis; this is not simply passive bulk “drainage.”

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Preferred surgical management of symptomatic SSCD is {{c1::superior semicircular canal plugging::procedure}}, performed through either a {{c2::middle cranial fossa or transmastoid::2}} approach.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Goal: eliminate the pathologic third-window physiology.
Plugging
  • Occludes the superior canal on either side of/around the dehiscence.
  • Prevents abnormal fluid motion through the affected canal.
  • Most commonly used strategy for durable third-window elimination.
  • Tradeoff: intentionally reduces function of that superior canal → postoperative vestibular hypofunction/disequilibrium can occur.
Resurfacing/capping
  • Attempts to restore a rigid boundary over the dehiscence while preserving canal patency/function.
  • Attractive theoretically because it may preserve superior-canal function.
  • However, resurfacing alone has historically had concern for persistent/recurrent third-window physiology; evidence comparing techniques is heterogeneous.
Approach ≠ repair technique
  • MCF = direct superior visualization; requires craniotomy.
  • Transmastoid = avoids craniotomy; feasibility depends on anatomy and gives different access/visualization.
  • Either can be used for canal occlusion/repair; recent evidence continues to support both as viable approaches rather than one universally superior route. 
https://otosurgeryatlas.stanford.edu/otologic-surgery-atlas/vestibular-surgery/superior-semicircular-canal-dehiscence/#

fields.name: Text
fields.value: If suspect SSCD you need to order a CT T bone with {{c1::Poschl}} and {{c1::Stenver}} reformats

fields.name: Extra
Text
fields.value:

{{c1::Poschl}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
POschl makes the SSC look like an O

A simple mental model:
Pöschl = “hot dog” cut (long axis)
Stenvers = “hamburger” cut (cross section)

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
What are the main evidence-based treatments for chronic bothersome subjective tinnitus?
{{c1::Education/counseling, CBT, sound therapy, and hearing aids when hearing loss is present.}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Extra: Treat identifiable underlying pathology and comorbid insomnia/anxiety/depression separately.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
What treatment has the strongest evidence for reducing tinnitus-related distress?
{{c1::Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: : CBT primarily reduces tinnitus-related distress/functional impact rather than necessarily eliminating the perceived sound.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Bothersome tinnitus + hearing loss →{{c1::hearing aid evaluation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Extra: Amplification increases meaningful auditory input and decreases the contrast/salience of tinnitus.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
Are medications routinely recommended specifically to treat chronic subjective tinnitus?
{{c1::No.}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Extra: Do not routinely use antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, intratympanic medications, or supplements for tinnitus itself. Treat depression, anxiety, insomnia, etc. when independently indicated.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Dupilumab treats CRSwNP by blocking {{c1::IL-4Rα}}, thereby inhibiting {{c2::IL-4 and IL-13}} signaling.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Often particularly attractive when CRSwNP coexists with asthma or atopic dermatitis, or when smell loss is prominent.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Mepolizumab treats CRSwNP by blocking {{c1::IL-5}}, thereby targeting {{c2::eosinophilic}} inflammation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Particularly intuitive in a strongly eosinophilic phenotype and/or eosinophilic asthma.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Omalizumab treats CRSwNP by binding {{c1::free IgE}} and reducing {{c2::IgE-mediated signaling}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Most attractive when there is a strong allergic/IgE-driven phenotype or comorbid allergic asthma; positive allergy testing is not strictly required for CRSwNP biology to involve IgE.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Tezepelumab treats CRSwNP by blocking {{c1::TSLP}}, an upstream epithelial {{c2::alarmin}} that drives downstream type 2 inflammation.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Mechanistically attractive when broader upstream suppression is desired rather than targeting a single downstream cytokine pathway.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In CRSwNP, blood eosinophils {{c1::≥150}} cells/µL support the presence of type 2 inflammation when assessing biologic candidacy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: EPOS/EUFOREA lowered the threshold from 250 to 150 cells/µL.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The SNOT-22 is a 22-item patient-reported CRS quality-of-life questionnaire scored from {{c1::0–110}}, with higher scores indicating worse disease burden

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: Each item is scored 0–5.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In the EPOS/EUFOREA CRSwNP biologic framework, a SNOT-22 score {{c1::≥40}} indicates significantly impaired disease-specific quality of life.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: SNOT-22 measures the patient's disease burden and can be discordant with CT/endoscopic severity.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: In recurrent CRSwNP after prior ESS, a Completion of Surgery Index (CoSI) {{c1::<70::score #}} suggests the patient may derive substantial benefit from revision ESS rather than escalation based solely on presumed medically refractory disease.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: CoSI ranges 0–100, with higher scores indicating more complete prior surgery. Recurrence after a high-completeness ESS more strongly supports refractory inflammatory biology and may shift the balance toward biologic therapy.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The revised 60/60 rule recommends referral for cochlear implant evaluation when an ear has a PTA {{c1::≥60 dB HL}} and unaided word recognition score {{c1::≤60%}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: This is a referral guideline, not a strict candidacy criterion. Each ear is considered independently. Patients outside these cutoffs may still warrant CI evaluation if appropriately fitted hearing aids provide inadequate benefit.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Word recognition score (WRS)}} assesses open-set monosyllabic word recognition presented {{c2::through headphones/inserts at suprathreshold levels}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
WRS is part of conventional unaided audiometry. It assesses how well an ear can recognize speech when the signal is made audible.

Do not confuse WRS with aided speech testing used during formal CI evaluation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Consonant-Nucleus-Consonant (CNC)}} testing assesses {{c2::aided open-set monosyllabic word recognition in an aided condition}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
CNC words are presented with an appropriately fitted hearing aid during CI evaluation.

Because isolated monosyllabic words provide little linguistic context, CNC testing is a relatively demanding measure of the speech information available through amplification.

An aided CNC ≤50% in the ear being considered for implantation supports CI candidacy under ACI Alliance recommendations.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::AzBio}} assesses {{c2::aided open-set sentence recognition}} spoken by multiple talkers.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Scoring is based on the percentage of words correctly repeated. Testing can be performed in quiet or noise.

Sentence context can help the listener reconstruct degraded auditory information, so sentence performance can be substantially better than isolated-word performance.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: During adult CI evaluation, an aided CNC word score {{c1::≤50}} % in the ear being considered for implantation supports cochlear implant candidacy.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
This is an ear-specific clinical benchmark recommended by the American Cochlear Implant Alliance.

Keep it distinct from:
• Revised 60/60 rule → referral
• Medicare ≤60% sentence recognition → coverage

fields.name: Text
fields.value: As of 2026, Medicare defines limited benefit from amplification for cochlear implantation as {{c1::≤60}}% correct on recorded {{c2::open-set sentence::word/sentence}} recognition in the best-aided condition.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
AzBio is commonly used for sentence recognition testing.

Three numbers worth keeping straight:
• 60/60: referral → PTA ≥60 dB + unaided WRS ≤60%
• CNC ≤50%: ear-specific clinical candidacy benchmark
• Sentences ≤60%: Medicare coverage criterion

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A cochlear implant bypasses dysfunctional {{c1::cochlear hair-cell}} transduction and directly electrically stimulates the {{c2::spiral ganglion/auditory nerve}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
A hearing aid amplifies acoustic energy but still depends on cochlear sensory transduction.

A CI instead converts sound into an electrical code and stimulates surviving auditory neurons.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Compared with normal acoustic hearing, cochlear implants provide relatively good {{c1::temporal}} information but limited {{c2::spectral/frequency}} resolution.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Limited spectral resolution helps explain why speech understanding can become excellent while pitch perception, music appreciation, and speech recognition in noise remain more difficult.

A major reason is current spread between neighboring electrodes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Lateral-wall}} cochlear implant electrode arrays are generally designed to emphasize {{c2::atraumatic insertion and preservation of residual hearing}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
These arrays lie along the lateral wall of the scala tympani and are generally thin and flexible.

They are particularly conceptually attractive when preservation of useful low-frequency acoustic hearing is a priority.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Perimodiolar}} cochlear implant electrode arrays position the electrodes {{c2::closer to the modiolus/spiral ganglion neurons}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Reducing electrode-neuron distance can decrease the current required for stimulation and potentially produce more spatially focused stimulation.

The array curves medially toward the modiolus rather than lying against the lateral cochlear wall.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
What is scalar translocation during cochlear implantation?
{{c1::Passage of the electrode array from the scala tympani into the scala vestibuli during insertion.}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The electrode disrupts structures separating the scalae and leaves its intended scala tympani trajectory.

Scalar translocation represents intracochlear trauma and is associated with poorer preservation of residual hearing and potentially worse speech outcomes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The number of functional spectral channels in a cochlear implant is less than the number of physical electrodes largely because of {{c1::current spread and overlapping neural stimulation}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Current from an electrode spreads through conductive cochlear fluid and tissue, so neighboring electrodes stimulate overlapping populations of spiral ganglion neurons.

This channel interaction limits the independent spectral information provided by additional electrodes.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Greater cochlear implant electrode insertion depth provides greater access to {{c1::apical, lower-frequency regions of the cochlea}}, but must be balanced against {{c2::intracochlear trauma and preservation of residual hearing}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Insertion depth is a tradeoff between tonotopic cochlear coverage and atraumatic insertion.

Deeper is therefore not inherently better. Electrode length/depth should fit the patient's anatomy, hearing profile, and goals for residual-hearing preservation.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: During cochlear implant mapping, the {{c1::T-level}} represents the minimum electrical stimulation producing auditory perception, while the {{c2::C-level/M-level}} represents the upper comfortable stimulation level.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Terminology varies by manufacturer.

The electrical dynamic range between threshold and comfortable loudness is narrow compared with normal acoustic hearing. The processor therefore compresses incoming acoustic intensities into this usable electrical range.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Combining preserved low-frequency acoustic hearing with cochlear implant electrical stimulation in the same ear is called {{c1::electroacoustic stimulation (EAS)}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Typically:
• preserved low-frequency acoustic hearing → conventional acoustic amplification
• poorer higher-frequency hearing → electrical stimulation

Preserved acoustic hearing can provide pitch and fine spectral information that a CI represents poorly, improving sound quality, music perception, and speech perception in noise.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: An auditory brainstem implant (ABI) bypasses both the {{c1::cochlea and cochlear nerve}} and directly stimulates the {{c2::cochlear nucleus}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Think anatomically:

Hearing aid → requires cochlear sensory transduction + CN VIII
Cochlear implant → bypasses cochlear sensory transduction but requires a functional auditory nerve pathway
ABI → bypasses cochlea + CN VIII

The classic ABI population is patients with NF2-related bilateral vestibular schwannomas in whom functional cochlear nerve input is absent or cannot be preserved.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Conventional hearing aids primarily improve {{c1::audibility}}, but do not restore normal cochlear processing

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: A hearing aid can make acoustic information loud enough to detect, but a damaged cochlea may still encode that information poorly. This explains why some patients say, “I can hear you, but I can’t understand you.”

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Outer hair cell loss causes loss of normal {{c1::cochlear compression}} and {{c1::recruitment}}, producing a narrowed {{c2::dynamic range}} for hearing.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: The threshold for hearing rises substantially, while the uncomfortable loudness level rises much less. Therefore, simply adding the same amount of gain to every sound would make loud sounds intolerably loud.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Wide dynamic range compression (WDRC)}} provides relatively more gain to soft sounds and progressively less gain to louder sounds

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
WDRC attempts to fit the large dynamic range of environmental sound into the reduced usable dynamic range of a patient with SNHL.

A compression ratio of 2:1 means a 20-dB increase in input produces only a 10-dB increase in output above the compression kneepoint.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Modern hearing aids divide sound into {{c1::frequency channels}}, allowing frequency-specific {{c2::gain}} and {{c2::compression}} based on the patient's hearing loss.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value: A patient with preserved low-frequency hearing but severe high-frequency SNHL should not receive equal amplification across all frequencies. The audiogram therefore directly informs hearing-aid programming.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Poor {{c1::word recognition scores (WRS)}} suggest that simply making speech {{c2::louder}} may not produce good speech understanding.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Pure-tone thresholds primarily assess detection/audibility. WRS assesses the ability to discriminate suprathreshold speech.

Two patients with similar pure-tone audiograms can therefore derive very different benefit from amplification.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Real-ear measurement (REM)}} uses a probe microphone near the tympanic membrane to verify the actual hearing-aid output reaching the patient's ear.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Programming software predicts hearing-aid output, but individual ear-canal acoustics vary.

REM allows the audiologist to compare the measured output at the patient's TM with a prescriptive target and adjust the device accordingly.

Think: programming = prediction; REM = verification.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::NAL-NL2}} is a commonly used prescriptive hearing-aid fitting algorithm that determines frequency- and input-specific amplification targets.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
You do not need to know the algorithm.

Conceptually:
Audiogram → NAL-NL2 target → hearing-aid programming → REM verification

The goal is useful speech audibility while maintaining acceptable loudness.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: A(n) {{c1::open-fit}} hearing aid is particularly useful for patients with {{c2::high-frequency SNHL and preserved low-frequency hearing}}.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
The open canal allows low-frequency sound to reach the TM naturally while the hearing aid provides needed high-frequency amplification.

Benefits include reduced occlusion effect and more natural perception of the patient's own voice.

RIC devices are commonly used for this configuration.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: As required hearing-aid gain increases, a more {{c1::closed}} acoustic coupling/earmold is often needed to prevent sound leakage and acoustic feedback.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
More open fitting
→ less occlusion
→ more natural residual hearing
→ more sound leakage

More closed fitting
→ permits greater gain
→ reduces feedback
→ greater risk of occlusion effect

fields.name: Text
fields.value: Hearing-aid {{c1::acoustic feedback}} occurs when amplified sound from the receiver leaks back to the microphone and is re-amplified.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
This creates a positive feedback loop and produces the characteristic hearing-aid squeal.

Can be problematic in patients that have an open hearing aid and need alot of amplification

Greater gain and inadequate acoustic sealing increase the risk of feedback. Modern hearing aids also use electronic feedback-cancellation algorithms.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: The major benefit of {{c1::directional microphones}} is improvement in the {{c2::signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)}} rather than simply increasing overall amplification.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
If speech is 65 dB and background noise is 60 dB, amplifying both by 20 dB does not change the +5-dB SNR.

Directional microphones preferentially emphasize sound from a desired direction—often in front of the listener—relative to competing noise.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::Remote microphone systems}} improve speech understanding in noise by placing the microphone close to the talker, thereby improving the signal-to-noise ratio before the signal reaches the hearing aid.

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
Instead of trying to computationally separate speech from noise after both reach a microphone at the listener's ear, the microphone captures speech close to its source.

Particularly useful in classrooms, lectures, meetings, and other noisy environments.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::CROS}} is used when one ear is unaidable and the contralateral ear has {{c2::normal/near-normal}} hearing

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
CROS:
Deaf-side microphone → routes signal to good ear.

fields.name: Text
fields.value:
What are the major types/configurations of conventional hearing aids?

{{c1::Behind-the-ear (BTE)}}
{{c1::Receiver-in-canal (RIC/RITE)}}
{{c1::In-the-ear (ITE), including ITC/CIC}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
BTE — behind-the-ear
Microphone, processor, and receiver are behind the ear. Sound travels through tubing to an earmold. Can provide substantial power; commonly used for severe losses and in children. Larger/more visible but durable and flexible.

RIC/RITE — receiver-in-canal/ear
Microphone and processor sit behind the ear. The receiver (speaker) sits in the ear canal, connected by a thin wire. Very common modern configuration and particularly well suited to open fittings and sloping high-frequency SNHL.

ITE — in-the-ear
Electronics are contained within a custom shell in the external ear. Smaller subtypes include ITC (in-the-canal) and CIC (completely-in-canal). More cosmetically discreet, but generally less room for battery, microphones, and other components and less capable of very high output than larger devices.

Key distinction: BTE/RIC have components behind the ear; ITE/ITC/CIC place the device primarily or entirely within the external ear/canal.

fields.name: Text
fields.value: {{c1::BiCROS}} is used when one ear is unaidable the contralateral ear has {{c2::aidable hearing loss}}

fields.name: Extra
fields.value:
BiCROS:
Deaf-side microphone → routes signal to better ear + the better ear is amplified for its own hearing loss.
